en: (Regarding the abiding of the form of Rudra there:
One should meditate upon [the deity] mounted on a ram, resembling the rising sun, with limbs radiant with four arms;
within his lap dwells eternally the form of Rudra, possessing the hue of pure vermilion.

With limbs smeared with ashes, adorned with ornaments, and a white body, he has the form of an elder; three-eyed, he is the bestower of desired boons to the worlds, his hands marked by the gestures of granting fearlessness and performing creation and destruction. || 21 ||

By the qualification "in light," the blue color of the lotus is implied; however, by the previously cited verse from the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, its red color is clearly stated. Furthermore, in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
"Above that, in the region of the navel, is the great city of Maṇipūra."
It was golden-hued, radiant as lightning, and likewise composed of abundant splendor.

By this, the qualities such as having the luster of gold are established as attributes of the lotus. This being the case, the essential point is that since there is a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa-bheda*), one must adopt either one of the two positions for the purpose of meditation, according to the command of Śrīnātha.
He states the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *maṇipūra* in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"Because that city (pura) is filled with jewels (maṇi), it is therefore known as Maṇipūra.

This is the summary of its meaning: above the Svādhiṣṭhāna, at the root of the navel, is the lotus called Maṇipūra, possessing ten petals with the intense luster of a rain-cloud. The petals are radiant with a blue glow and are associated with the upper nasal bindus of the letters ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, and tha.

It is endowed with the ten syllables *da*, *dha*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *ra*, *ū*, *pa*, *da*, and *pha*. Within the pericarp of the lotus is the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*), which is triangular, radiant with a deep crimson glow, containing the seed-syllable *raṃ* within it, and joined with three gates known as *svastika*.
In the previous verse, it was stated that "therein is the fire's own seed-syllable"; this [verse] now specifies that very seed-syllable of fire.

Regarding the phrase "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) and so forth: as to what that seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) is like, he says—mounted upon a ram (*meṣādhirūḍha*), meaning having a ram as its vehicle;

likewise, resembling the newly risen sun (*navatapananibha*), meaning red in color with the hue of the young dawn; likewise, with limbs radiant with four arms (*vedabāhūjjvalāṅga*), meaning whose limbs are shining and beautiful with four arms, i.e., by means of a set of four arms.
The meaning is that it brings forth a golden splendor. The connection with the preceding clause is that one should meditate upon the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) in such a manner.

Regarding this, Rāmavallabha and others have explained [the deity] as being mounted on a ram and having a goat for a vehicle; however, that is incorrect, because elsewhere his having a goat as a vehicle has been stated in such passages as "Agni, seated upon a goat, holding a rosary," and so forth.

"Then one should meditate on [him] seated upon a ram, holding a rosary and a spear"— since this statement, cited in Kālīcaraṇa’s commentary on the *Ṣaṭcakra*, prescribes meditation specifically on the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) as having a ram for its vehicle,
it is inappropriate to abandon the well-known meaning and imagine another sense; therefore, [he is to be visualized] by way of having a ram as his vehicle.
Meditation (*dhyāna*):
[In this lotus, the abiding of the power of Lākinī, and the fruit of contemplating this lotus:
There resides Lākinī, who brings about all auspiciousness, whose four arms are radiant with the Vedas, and whose limbs are brilliant.

Having meditated upon this lotus of the navel— dark-complexioned, adorned with various arrangements such as yellow garments and the like, and intoxicated in mind— one becomes exceedingly capable in the acts of withdrawal or preservation; and from her lotus-like face, the splendor of the mass of knowledge, Vāṇī, shines forth eternally.

(The unstruck lotus and the wind mandala in its pericarp); above that, in the heart, is a beautiful lotus, radiant with the luster of the bandhūka flower, adorned with the twelve letters beginning with *ka*, which are enhanced by the hue of vermilion.
By name it is Anāhata, the life-force; it is a wish-fulfilling tree that bestows more than one could desire.
Here is the mandala of Vāyu, resembling smoke and adorned with a hexagon.
We consider this alone to be correct. Here, it should be noted that because the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*) is present, the deity of fire (*vahni-devatā*) is also present;

for the non-difference between the mantra and the deity is established in all Tantric systems, and thus by the author’s mention of the presence of the fire-seed-syllable, the presence of the fire-deity is also implied. This applies everywhere.

Regarding that, he describes the state of Rudra with the words "in its lap" (*tatkroḍe*). This means in the lap of that seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*); here, the meaning is that he is the bestower of boons (*varada*), granting the desires of the worlds.
Thus, the essential point is this: the seed-syllable of fire, situated in the previously mentioned triangle, has a ram as its vehicle (*meṣavāhana*).
He is red like the morning sun and possesses four arms. Within the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ), the aged Rudra dwells, distinguished by the aforementioned specific attributes;

therein he describes the abiding of the power Lākinī with the words "there she resides. Here, within the pericarp of the lotus, resides that power Lākinī, renowned in all the Tantras. He qualifies Lākinī with the words beginning with "sakala" (possessing all), [describing her] as being clad in yellow garments and so forth.

The meaning is: by means of ornaments such as yellow garments and so forth; she is "adorned" by that "various arrangement," which refers to the disposition of her attire in diverse ways. Alternatively, it may mean "characterized by yellow garments and the like, and likewise adorned with various arrangements.
He states the fruit of contemplating this maṇipūra-cakra with the words: "having meditated upon this... and so on.

Having thus described the maṇipūra-cakra, he speaks of the anāhata-cakra with the words "above that" (tasyorddhe). The meaning is that one should meditate upon the lotus located above that maṇipūra-lotus, in the heart—that is, in the region of the heart—which is called by the name Anāhata, meaning it is designated by the appellation "the Unstruck. He further qualifies this lotus: The meaning is that one should meditate upon the lotus located above that maṇipūra-lotus, in the heart—that is, in the region of the heart—which is called by the name Anāhata, meaning it is designated by the appellation "the Unstruck. He further qualifies this lotus: [as follows].

By the words "sulalitam" and so forth: it is *sulalita* (graceful), very smooth (*susnigdha*), and [the seed-syllable of] wind (*vāyubīja*) along with the presence of the Lord (*īśa*) therein; in its center is the syllable of wind (*pavanākṣara*), sweet and grey like a column of smoke.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord, who is mounted upon a black [bull], resplendent with four hands;

in the midst of that, one should contemplate the stainless one named Īśa, a treasury of compassion, possessing the luster of a swan, and bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and boons with his two hands upon all the three worlds. 24.

It is radiant with beauty, red in color like the *bandhūka* flower; likewise, it is "endowed" (*upakṛta*)—meaning distinguished by or joined with—the twelve syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, such as *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha*, which are colored red like vermilion (*sindūra*) and adorned with the luster of vermilion. In this context, the term used is *upahita*.

In the *Kālīcaraṇaṭīkā*, the reading "upahṛtam" (offered) is seen, and in the *Rāmavallabhaṭīkā*, the reading [is different]; yet in both cases, the meaning there is simply "appropriate. Likewise, while another celestial tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) grants only that which is desired to the petitioner, this *kalpavṛkṣa* in the form of the lotus-pair gives even more than what was desired; such is the intended meaning. [The word] "vāyoḥ" (of the wind).
Here, one should meditate upon the mandala of wind, smoke-colored like smoke, within the pericarp of the lotus. Of what nature is it?
It is adorned with the beauty of six corners. By this, it is shown that the wind mandala is hexagonal. This is explicitly stated in the seventh chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*:
Above this lotus is a pure and beautiful lotus,
adorned with twelve petals and endowed with a crimson color;
in the center of that lotus, within the seed-vessel, is an auspicious hexagonal mandala.
"In the center of the maṇḍala is the beautiful seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Thus, it is understood that the seed-syllable of Vāyu resides within the hexagon inside the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa). Regarding the etymological derivation of the term *anāhata*, the Tantrasāra states:
"The unstruck sound (anāhata) is seen there, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman);
that is proclaimed by the sages as the lotus called Anāhata.
In this context, the phrase "consisting of the Word-Brahman" is an adjective for the lotus under discussion.

This is its summary: above the *maṇipūra*, in the heart, is the fourth lotus called *anāhata*, red as a *bandhūka* flower, very glossy, and having twelve petals. On its petals, one by one, are the twelve syllables—*ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha*—each with the color of vermilion; and in the pericarp is [the syllable] smoky-grey.
"One should meditate on the six-cornered wind-mandala.
Regarding "in its center": in the middle of that wind-mandala is the letter of the wind, *yaṃ*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of wind. (In this pericarp of the lotus resides the power of Kākinī.)
Here indeed dwells Kākinī, yellow like fresh lightning, three-eyed and auspicious, adorned with all ornaments, who joyfully brings benefit to people;
she holds in her hands a noose, a skull-cup, an excellent boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Intoxicated, her heart moist with the essence of full nectar, she wears a garland of skeletons. || 25 ||

The word "should meditate" is to be understood as the ellipsis. He qualifies the seed-syllable of Vāyu with the words beginning with "sweet" (madhura): "sweet" means characterized by sweetness, that is to say, consisting of bliss.
That lotus is celebrated by the sages as being called "Unstruck" (anāhata).
That is indeed the abode of bliss, the supreme state presided over by the Puruṣa.

Thus, from the *Tantrasāra*: "Gray with a mass of smoke" means having a smoky-grey complexion; "resplendent with four hands" means possessing four arms; "mounted upon a black [creature]" means having a black antelope as his vehicle. These four adjectives describe the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vāyu (the Wind). Here, by the presence of the seed-syllable of Vāyu, there is also the presence of the deity Vāyu, who shares that same color and vehicle.
This is to be inferred as before.
Having thus defined the essential nature of the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu-bīja*), he describes the abiding of the Lord within it with the words "in its center" (*tanmadhye*).
The meaning is that one should meditate upon Śiva, known by the name Īśa—that is, called Īśvara—in the middle of that, namely, in the center of the seed-syllable of wind.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth—this is because it is determined that the one named Īśvara presides over the unstruck lotus (*anāhatapadma*). He qualifies Īśa with the words "having the luster of a swan" (*haṃsābha*), and so on; "having the luster of a swan" means white in color, and likewise, [he is the one] who by his two hands protects even the three worlds.
And "bestowing a boon" means granting one;

thus, this is the summary of it: within the previously mentioned circle of wind, there is the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu-bīja*), which is smoke-colored like smoke, has the black antelope as its vehicle, and possesses four arms. Within that [seed-syllable] is [the deity], who holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, is white in color, and consists of compassion.
"One should meditate on Śiva, who is designated as Īśvara.

Here, the meaning is "in the lotus," specifically in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus; the *Kākinī* power resides there. Although this has been stated without specific qualification, it should be understood that the *Kākinī* is situated at the side of Īśa, according to the fifty-seventh chapter of the *Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa*.
"One should meditate upon Īśvara, the Lord of Yogins, within the circle of the heart-lotus.
Having thus described the meditation on Īśvara, one should perform the meditation on his side [upon] Kākinī, the Supreme Goddess.
It should be understood that by this [verse], the fact that Kākinī resides by the side of Īśvara is established. To the question "What is she like?", he says: "navā" and so forth.

"Her heart is moist with the essence of full nectar" (*pūrṇasudhārasārdrahṛdayā*): "full" refers to the essence of nectar which produces complete bliss, located within the interior of the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*). [This refers to the Śakti in the form of a triangle within the pericarp of that lotus, as well as the Bāṇaliṅga.]

Within the pericarp of this lotus, there resides that which is called the Triangle, possessing a body as tender as the tip of a lightning bolt, with its power shimmering at its center; and within that [Triangle],
there is also the Śiva-liṅga known as Bāṇa, radiant with a golden-colored unguent.
Upon his head, he is like a jewel endowed with subtle distinctions, the abode of the splendor of radiant manifestation. || 26 ||

She whose heart is moistened by the nectar-essence flowing from the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the Wick (the individual soul), Śiva, and Śakti— thus it is described in the fifty-seventh chapter of the *Rudrayāmalottara*:
"The subtle Goddess, charming with her triple qualities, whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness..."
"The Kuleśvarī, who delights in drinking nectar, is intoxicated and perfectly full.

We shall clarify this secret in the commentary on the *Sahasrāra*. The rest is clear. This is the summary of its meaning: within the pericarp of this lotus is [the goddess] Trinetrā (Three-Eyed), four-armed, yellow in color, and the performer of auspicious deeds.

Adorned with various ornaments and a graceful arrangement of attire, bringing about the welfare of practitioners with joy, holding a noose, a skull-bowl, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, intoxicated with passion, her heart moistened by the essence of nectar dripping from the thousand-petaled lotus, wearing a garland of skeletons— thus the Śakti Kākinī shines forth.

Regarding the abiding of the Śakti in the form of a triangle and the Liṅga called Bāṇa within the pericarp of this unstruck lotus (*anāhatapadma*), he says with the words beginning "etad" (this): "Of this lotus called Unstruck, which is free from dust, within its pericarp, beneath the seed-syllable of Air (*vāyubīja*), there is a Śakti shining forth; she is designated as 'Triangle' because of her triangular shape. Thus, she is called "Triangle" (*trikoṇā*) due to her triangular form.

She remains renowned by name. Here, because Śakti is described as being triangular in form, it is indicated that, since the triangle has the nature of a *yoni*, she faces downwards. He describes her form: "Lightning"—she whose body is both tender and a mass of radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning, or even equal to the brilliance of ten million times ten million lightnings; she who is situated within that [triangle].
The meaning is that they are situated within the triangle. Here, although there is no difference between the triangle and the power (*śakti*), the phrase "situated within it" is used figuratively;

its sense is "non-different from it. In the fifty-seventh chapter of the *Rudrajāmala*, within the collection of meditations on that sacred seat (*pīṭha*), it says: "One should contemplate the triangle."
The power of the seat (pīṭhaśakti), richly endowed with gold, arising like ten million flashes of lightning,
resembling Kākinī, intoxicated, and active within a full heart-mind.

By this, the non-difference between the triangle and the power (*śakti*) is expressed. As for that which was stated by Kālīcaraṇa— accepting the reading *tadantargataḥ* as an adjective for the phrase "the Śiva-liṅga called Bāṇa"—
[it refers to] the fruit of meditating upon this [liṅga] within the *anāhata* lotus.
One should meditate upon the lotus in the heart, the celestial tree that is the abode of the pedestal of the god Śarva, adorned by a swan that is a lamp-flame devoid of wind,
and possessing the beauty of filaments shimmering within, decorated by the orb of the sun.
He is the Lord of speech and the Lord of the worlds, capable both of protecting and destroying them. || 27 ||
"The *bāṇaliṅga* within the triangle is joined with golden ornaments"—

such statements have been cited as favorable to the support of one's own [sectarian] view; however, even those should be interpreted as referring to the presence of the *liṅga* named *Bāṇa* on the right side of the power (*śakti*) in the form of a triangle, according to the fifty-seventh chapter of the *Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa*.
Having begun with the triangular Śakti (— ),
one should contemplate the Bāṇaliṅga on its right side;
it resembles pure gold, stainless, and possesses beautiful luster.

One should meditate upon the Lord Śiva, who is the bliss dear to Mahālakṣmī, who possesses all forms yet is stainless, from whom the dawning of knowledge and yoga proceeds, whose nature is Brahman and who assumes many forms; he is like the flame of a lamp.
By this, the presence of the Bāṇaliṅga on its right side is designated. And thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with "the one called Bāṇa" is as follows:

in the right portion of the aforementioned triangular Śakti, there also resides the Śivaliṅga known as Bāṇa. Of what nature is it? It is radiant with a golden-colored unguent; that is, it possesses a brilliance as bright as gold. Likewise, on its head (mauli), it is endowed with subtle differentiation.
The meaning is that, like a gem with a minute fissure, or like a tiny dot appearing at the tip of an arrow as if there were a subtle hole above the gem, [it] shines. Regarding "prollāsa":

it means one who is the locus of such splendor (*lakṣmī*) as possesses an intense radiance (*ullāsa*), that is, distinguished by an excellence of beauty; or alternatively, one who possesses the radiance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).

And thus, this is the summary of its meaning: within the previously described unstruck (*anāhata*) lotus-heart, below the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu-bīja*), there exists the Śakti, triangular in shape, soft, and blazing with ten million flashes of lightning; on her right side resides Śiva, known as the Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a luster brilliant like gold, topped by a half-moon and a bindu, and endowed with supreme beauty.

Now, he describes the remaining nature of the unstruck lotus (*anāhatapadma*) and the fruit of its meditation: "One should meditate," etc. That practitioner who meditates upon the lotus in the heart called *anāhata* becomes a lord of speech, equal to Bṛhaspati, a knower of the meaning of all scriptures, and eloquent in speech; likewise, he even becomes a lord capable of protecting or destroying the worlds.

Here, by the word "also" (*api*), the act of creation is likewise included; thus, the meaning is that one becomes capable of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. Alternatively, one becomes a lord of yogis, ever more beloved than the most beloved to the circle of women;
a master of knowledge, successful, with the host of senses conquered, and capable of focused concentration in meditation.
Constantly raining down streams of poetry through prose and the words of verse, he is the deity who bestows fortune and is capable of entering another's city in an instant. (28)
He is not only the Lord of Speech, but also the Lord and Sovereign of the worlds—of what kind? Capable of both protection and destruction.

The meaning is that, having attained this sovereignty which is the fruit of meditating upon this lotus, he is empowered to effect the preservation and the destruction of the world created by the Blessed One. To the question "What kind of lotus is it?", he says: "The celestial tree," meaning it has the nature of the *kalpavṛkṣa*.

The meaning is "that which accomplishes what is desired. Likewise, it is the seat-abode, the place of residence, of the radiant Śarva (Śiva). Furthermore, it is graced by the *haṃsa*—the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—which has the form of a lamp-flame devoid of wind; that is, a lamp-flame that is windless, being free from the movement of air and thus motionless.

The meaning is that the individual soul (*jīvātman*) dwells within this lotus of the heart, as motionless as the flame of a lamp in a windless place. Likewise, those whose interior is adorned by the orb of the sun—the solar disc—and who, for that reason, are radiant, bearing a particular splendor through contact with its ruddy rays; such is the beauty of their filaments (*kiñjalka*), the stamens (*kesara*).
The meaning is that it is its source, its foundational basis. In the fifty-seventh chapter of the Rudrayāmala-uttarakhaṇḍa, concerning the unstruck lotus (*anāhatapadma*), it is said:
"By meditating upon or visualizing these, one becomes the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśa*) in an instant."
There, the Lord should contemplate the attainment of sovereignty for its accomplishment;
there, the foremost of practitioners should contemplate the orb of the sun.
One should meditate upon ten thousand Aruṇas within the center of a lotus filament;
by practicing this for just one month, the yogi shall become a bearer of the cool lunar mark.

By such statements as these, having instructed the meditation on the solar orb within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus, and because the meditation on ten thousand suns is also prescribed for the filaments (*keśara*), it follows that in this present context as well, the filaments are indeed adorned by solar orbs.
And thus, the essential conclusion is this: beneath the previously mentioned *vāṇaliṅga* is the individual soul (*jīvātman*) of the aforementioned form, [situated] in the lotus.
The solar disc within the pericarp and the inner regions of the filaments are resplendent with a multitude of sunbeams.

With another verse, he states another result: "O Lord of Yogis. That practitioner who contemplates this lotus according to the previously mentioned sequence becomes a lord of yogis, the best among yogis; likewise, from the beloved of one surrounded by a host of lovely women, [he receives] night after night.
(There is a pure lotus, and its pericarp is situated in the sphere of space.
At the throat is the stainless lotus called "Pure," having the luster of smoke-colored grey,
illuminated by all the vowels which shine red and manifest upon its petals, belonging to one of radiant intellect.
He sits with his body radiant above the serpent whose luster is like snow, clad in white garments, his circular form resembling the expanse of the sky graced by the full moon. (29)

"Priyatamaḥ" means most beloved. "Jñānīśaḥ" means the best among the wise. Here, by the two terms "Yogīśa" (Lord of Yogis) and "Jñānīśa" (Lord of the Wise), his sovereignty over both action and knowledge is demonstrated. The word "api" is used in the sense of "likewise. "Kṛtī" means a learned scholar. "Jitendriyagaṇaḥ" means one by whom the group of senses has been conquered; by this, [it is shown] that due to the dawning of knowledge, he is free from attachment to sense objects.
It has been stated that the conquest of the senses occurs all the more easily through the complete removal of even those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that exist in the form of seeds.
As it is said in the venerable *Bhagavadgītā*:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."
"Except for taste; even taste ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme.

Likewise, he becomes capable of focused attention in meditation—that is, capable of intense absorption (*abhiniveśa*) in the contemplation of the nature of Brahman. He brings forth showers of poetic nectar.

He is one who is skilled in relishing the continuous nectar-like essence of poetry; likewise, he is like Nārāyaṇa—the deity of Lakṣmī’s sporting (*raṅgaṇa*), meaning the god who is the presiding deity of Lakṣmī’s play. According to Amara: "The words *vṛndāraka* and *daivata* may be used in the masculine. However, in the reading where the letter *na* follows the dental *ta*, the meaning is that Lakṣmī is his "deity of the body" (*aṅganadaivata*). He [is] in the city of others...

One is able to enter another body in an instant; the meaning is that by contemplating this, one attains the fitness for entering the bodies of others. Having thus described the *anāhata* lotus, he speaks of the lotus called *viśuddha*: "Viśuddha... He states the reason for this lotus’s designation as "pure" (*viśuddha*) in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*: [The text continues with the citation from the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.]
"Because purity is extended for the individual soul through the vision of the *haṃsa*,
it is called the pure lotus, known as space, most wonderful.
Thus, in the throat— that is, in the region of the throat— there resides a lotus known as the "Pure" (*viśuddha*), bearing that name.

He qualifies the lotus (*sarasija*) with the words "spotless" (*amala*) and so forth. "Spotless" means free from impurity. Likewise, "having a smoky appearance" (*dhūmadhūmrāvabhāsa*) means that which has a smoky (*dhūmra*) radiance (*avabhāsa*) or luster; by this it is stated that this lotus is smoke-colored.
He describes the arrangement of the letters upon the petals by way of showing their specific qualities, saying "by the vowels" (*svaraiḥ*), [which are] "shining upon the petals" (*dalaparilasitaiḥ*).
On the petals [is the abode of Sadāśiva], his body adorned with arms holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a goad, and a boon-granting mudrā.

In Manoraṅka, the primordial God Śiva dwells eternally, his body inseparable from Girijā; he is snow-white in luster, three-eyed, five-faced, and possesses ten graceful arms, adorned with a tiger-skin garment, and is renowned for the attainment of the power of true manifestation. (30)

It is illuminated in connection with the practitioner whose intellect is radiant and whose mind is purified by the constant practice of yoga— by means of all sixteen vowels, meaning the sixteen vowels from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*), which shine and gleam; [these vowels] have their impurities cast away through uninterrupted cultivation of yoga and have manifested the excellence of knowledge.
The meaning is that only practitioners (*sādhakas*) would be capable of understanding this secret.

Here, although the number of petals is not explicitly stated by the mere phrase "shining with petals," the number sixteen is understood for the petals as well, because the statement "with all the vowels" indicates the presence of the sixteen vowels upon the leaves.
The meaning is that one should contemplate each individual vowel upon each petal. This is clearly stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*:
"In the region of the throat is the [cakra] called Viśuddhi, smoke-colored and beautiful."
"Endowed with sixteen petals accompanied by the vowels beginning with 'a'.

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the location of the sphere of space (*nabhomaṇḍala*) within the pericarp, he says "full" (*pūrṇa*). The sphere of space, most renowned as being like the full moon, the sphere of space which is brilliant and white in color like the full moon, is situated there. He describes the shape of the mandala:
"Vṛttarūpam" means having the form of a circle.
He qualifies the Manu who will be designated by the phrase "in the mark of Manu" in the following verse with the words beginning with "himā-":
"Of what kind of Manu? Of one whose body shines upon a serpent—that is, a white-colored elephant—endowed with the luster of snow."
Of such a one; likewise, "clad in white garments" means wearing white-colored clothing.
(30) Regarding "with arms": with four arms—this is the ellipsis—shining with the noose, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the boon-granting gesture (*varada*).
Here, since the four [attributes] beginning with the noose are mentioned, it should be understood that the number of arms is also four. And thus:
He whose body is adorned with arms possessing the characteristics described by etymology— such a one, [the syllable] *haṃ*, which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the sky (*nabhas*),

dwells eternally, that is, in a manner unconditioned by time and so forth, in the lap (*aṅka*) or bosom of the deity who is preceded by "Sadā" (the god Śiva), renowned through the perfection of this very designation "Sadāśiva. Herein:

Since the abiding of the seed-syllable *nabhaḥ* is mentioned, the abiding of space (*nabhas*) as well should be inferred as before. He qualifies Sadāśiva with the words "three-eyed" and so forth. His body is non-different from Girijā (in this lotus pericarp resides the Śākinī-śakti and the lunar orb).
Within the lotus of the ocean of nectar dwells the pure Śākinī, clad in yellow garments and holding an arrow,
a bow, a noose, and a goad in her four lotus-like hands;
upon its pericarp is the full orb of the moon, devoid of its spot.
The gateway to great liberation is for one whose conduct is esteemed and whose faculties are pure. || 31 ||

The meaning is that he whose body is divided and joined with Girijā is Ardhanārīśvara. Regarding the ten-armed nature and the bull-vehicle of Sadāśiva, the Mahānirvāṇatantra states in its fourteenth chapter:
"He who bears the Gaṅgā, has ten arms, and whose head is adorned by the moon."
By the phrase "resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon, and resplendent upon the bull-throne," [it is meant].
Regarding the word "sudhā" (nectar): within this lotus, in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), resides the power (*śakti*) known as Śākinī. And she...

"Pure" means white in color, even more so than the *sudhāsindhu*, the ocean of nectar; by this it is also indicated that she brings about the satisfaction of practitioners even more than nectar itself. Regarding her presence upon the lunar disc in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), he says "of the *sudhāṃśu*":
the meaning is that in the pericarp shines the complete, stainless, and spotless orb of the *sudhāṃśu*, the moon.

And thus, since the presence of both the sphere of space (*nabhomaṇḍala*) and the lunar sphere (*candramaṇḍala*) within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) has been stated, it should be understood that the lunar sphere is in the center of the sphere of space within the pericarp; therein is the seed-syllable of space (*nabhobīja*); and therein is Sadāśiva as Ardhanārīśvara, together with the Śakti Śākinī. He qualifies the sphere with the word "great" (*mahā-*) [referring to the *maṇḍala*]. [He approaches] the glory (*śrī*), which is the fortune of yoga (*yogalakṣmī*).

The meaning is: having taken as his aim the esteemed doctrine, such a person—one who is devoted to the practice of yoga; for this very reason, "of one with pure senses," that is, a practitioner whose mind has been purified by the practice of yoga—for him, it is the "great door to liberation," meaning it is the cause of the release known as Nirvāṇa.
Here, within the pericarp of the lotus, inside the circular sphere of space (*nabhomaṇḍala*), he describes the abiding of Sadāśiva within the seed-syllable of space (*nabhobīja*).
However, in the eighth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*, it is said:
"In the center of the lotus, upon the lotus-seed-vessel (*varāṭa*), is the most beautiful Janaloka."
Outside of that is a lunar disc which pacifies the blindness of great delusion;
likewise, within the seed-vessel on the Jewel Island is the supreme six-cornered wheel. And in the center of the yantra is a circular form, the Great Lion Throne.
(The fruit of contemplating this lotus:

Having fixed the mind here in this place for an unlimited time, that practitioner becomes one whose yoga is perfected in the self, a poet, an eloquent speaker, a man of knowledge, and one who is exceedingly tranquil in heart.
Beholder of the three worlds, benefactor of all, liberated from disease and sorrow, long-lived, a living soul, and the radiant swan that destroys boundless calamities. || 32 ||
(Between the eyebrows is the two-petaled Ājñā-lotus; in its pericarp resides the power of Hākinī.

That lotus called Ājñā resembles the moon, shining with the light that is the abode of meditation; its body is resplendent with the two phonemes *ha* and *kṣa*, and its petals are the eyes, brilliantly white.
In the midst of that is Hākinī, white as the moon, possessing six faces; she holds a *vidyā*, a *mudrā*, a skull-cup, and a hand-drum with a rosary, her mind pure and radiant. (33)
Above him is Gaurī, and on his right side is Sadāśiva;
he has three eyes and five faces, with three eyes in each face,
his limbs adorned with sacred ashes, and his form resembling the Silver Mountain.
The Lord, wearing a tiger skin and adorned with a garland of jewels,
as well as the all-joy-bestowing Lord, the omnipresent Ardhanārīśvara— by these [descriptions],
there is a moon-maṇḍala outside the seed-vessel (bījakoṣa), a six-cornered wheel within the seed-vessel, and a circle in its center.

Within that is the lion-throne, and there resides Sadāśiva as Ardhanārīśvara; such is the sequence observed here. "Here" refers to one whose yoga is complete within the Self (*ātmasaṃpūrṇayoga*). The rest is clear.
Having thus described the Viśuddha-cakra, he speaks of the Ājñā-cakra: "The Command" (*ājñā*), and so forth. That...
The remainder [of the sentence] is that there exists a lotus with two petals, whose eye-petal is well-known by the name *ājñā*.
Regarding the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this *ājñā*, the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* states in its fourth chapter:
"Therein, the transmission of the *ājñā* is renowned as the 'Command of the Guru' (*gurorājñā*)."
Although it is not specifically mentioned here, it should be understood that the location of this lotus is between the eyebrows. As it is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"The supreme wheel called Ājñā is two-petaled and situated between the eyebrows."
(The mind resides in the pericarp of the lotus of command; within the pericarp, in the triangle, reside the Śiva known as Itara and the Praṇava.
And the mind, well-known in its subtle form, dwells within the interior of this lotus.

In the womb, within its pericarp, one whose heart is most steadfast should contemplate in sequence that other state of Śiva, which shines with the mark of the liṅga, possesses the play of garlands of lightning, is the supreme station of Kula, the awakening of the Brahma-thread, and the primordial seed of the Vedas.
It is white in color, resembling the moon; likewise, it is such that its radiance is through the power of meditation (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, by the two "arts" (*kalā*), namely *ha* and *kṣa*—whereby the word "art" refers to the deity—there is here a metaphorical designation of the "art-ness" in the syllable which serves as the seed of that art. Thus, by means of the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, which constitute the cause for the form of the respective deity to be meditated upon...

The meaning is: "one whose eye-lashes (*netrapatra*) are such that their bodies (*vapuṣ*) are thus beautifully radiant; for this very reason, it is 'suśubhram,' meaning exceedingly white. By the phrase "resembling the moon" (*himakarasadṛśam*), the natural whiteness of the lotus is indicated;
and by the term "suśubhram," the excellence of its whiteness resulting from the conjunction of the letters *ha*, *kṣa*, and *ra*—which are white in color—is suggested.

Regarding the statement "in its center," it means that the well-known power *Hākinī* shines within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) at the center of that lotus. He qualifies her with the words beginning with "the moon" (*śaśi*):
by this, her cool radiance and whiteness are described. Regarding the phrase "the lore" (*vidyā*): the lore is in her hand.

She holds the *mudrā* and so forth, as well as a *japavaṭī*, which is a rosary for recitation. Likewise, she is "one of pure mind," meaning she whose mind (*citta*) is pure. Furthermore, between the eyebrows is the *ājñā*-lotus, white in color and having two petals;
on the two petals are the two extremely pure syllables *ha* and *kṣa*. In the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus resides the power (*śakti*) Hākinī, who has six faces.

The result is that she shines forth, white in color, with six arms adorned with the gestures of knowledge (*vidyā*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and a rosary (*japavaṭī*).
Regarding the word "this" (*etat*): within the center of this lotus called the Command (*ājñā*), the mind (*manas*) dwells.
As to what kind of mind it is, he says: it is subtle in form and beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). If it is beyond the senses, what is the proof for its existence? To this he says:

"Renowned" (prasiddham) means established in all the scriptures. This refers to the location of the Śiva-liṅga called Itara within the triangle inside the pericarp (karṇikā), as stated in the phrase "in the womb" (yonau). Within that pericarp, in the womb-shaped triangle, exists the "state of Itara-Śiva"—the reality whose nature is the Śiva called Itara.
He describes the form of Itara-Śiva with the word "liṅga," meaning it has the shape of a liṅga.

Here he describes the *praṇava* situated therein: "like a garland of lightning. From this point forward, all [the following] are qualifiers of the term "primordial seed" (*ādibīja*). It is characterized by a splendor like a series of lightning flashes; this is the supreme state of *Kula*.
(The fruit of contemplating this is as follows:)

The supreme adept, whose very nature is meditative absorption, becomes one who enters the bodies of others with swiftness; he is a lord of sages, omniscient, all-seeing, a benefactor of all, and a knower of the meaning of all scriptures.
Proclaiming the practice of non-duality, he shines forth, renowned for the attainment of the most extraordinary and supreme siddhi.
He too is long-lived, the creator within the abode of the three worlds, both in its dissolution and its preservation.

By the word *kula*, the power (*śakti*) in the form of a triangle is expressed. Thus, it is that which has for its supreme *kula*—its nature being *śakti*—the triangle as its *pada*, its station. By this, the abiding of the seed-syllable of the Vedas (*vedādibīja*) within the triangle above Śiva, as defined by the etymology, is stated. Likewise, it is that from which arises the awakening of the *brahmasūtra*, that is, the awakening of the *brahmanāḍī*. This refers to this very *praṇava*.

The meaning is that through this splendor, knowledge arises for those situated within the *brahman-āḍī*. The practitioner, possessing a most steady heart, should meditate in sequence upon the *praṇava*—the primordial seed of the Vedas—described in such a manner, as well as *Hākinī* and the others.
Here, although in the third verse, "she who shines as the *praṇava*" (*praṇavavilasitā*) is mentioned in the phrase "in the midst of that, she is Citriṇī, shining as the *praṇava*,"...

Although it has been stated that the *citriṇī* [vein] alone is the manifestation of the *praṇava*, nevertheless, by means of the *praṇava* situated in the *ājñācakra*, one may infer that the *brahmanāḍī* located within the *citriṇī* is also a manifestation of the *praṇava*; thus, the expression "the awakening of the *brahmasūtra*" is well-founded. Nor should it be said that the term *brahmasūtra* here denotes the *citriṇī* vein, for there is no evidence to prove that.

And thus, the conclusion is that within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus named Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the mind; within the pericarp, in a triangle, is the *śivaliṅga* called "the Other" (*itara*); and above that, in a triangle, resides the *praṇava*, possessing a radiance like a garland of lightning.
He states the fruit of this meditation: "Through meditation... One whose self is meditation is one who is steadfast in the meditation upon this lotus.

The supreme practitioner, the best of adepts, becomes one who moves swiftly into another's body; the meaning is that by the power of meditation, he quickly becomes capable of entering the bodies of others. Likewise, the Lord of Sages—the best among those whose nature is contemplation, the omniscient, the knower of all, and the seer of all—is capable of beholding the entire world as if it were an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of his hand, even while remaining in one place. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that he brings welfare to all through his body, mind, and speech; he accomplishes the benefit of everyone, and he is a knower of the meaning of all scriptures. He is a proponent of the practice of non-duality (*advaita*); that is, he speaks of that yoga which consists of the contemplation of the non-difference between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), which is the knowledge of the non-duality of Brahman as established in such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman."
The meaning is that, having personally experienced the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*), he establishes its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatā*).

He is renowned for his supreme, most excellent, and unprecedented accomplishment (*siddhi*)—one not previously attained by other yogis—and likewise possesses long life; the meaning is that he acts as the creator within the abode of the three worlds, namely the creator, destroyer, and sustainer of the three worlds.
(The Abiding of the Letters Constituting the *Praṇava* in the *Ājñācakra*): Within that wheel, there dwells eternally the pure inner self of awakened intellect,
whose light is like a lamp and which is the manifestation of the letters formed as the *praṇava*.

Above that is the half-moon, and above that is the letter *ma* in the form of a shimmering bindu; at its beginning is that *nāda*, laughing with a continuous stream of nectar white as the essence of water.
(The fruit of contemplating the nature of the *praṇava* in the *ājñācakra*):
When the mind has dissolved here in this place, the abode of supreme bliss, one should fix the city [of consciousness] in the supportless state, as well-known through the service of the Supreme Guru.
Through constant practice, the yogi perceives the subtle forms of the friends of the wind (the vital breaths), as well as the stages situated within their midst that possess radiant forms. (37)

Previously, by the phrase "the primordial seed of the Vedas," the contemplation of the *praṇava* was taught; he now specifies that very *praṇava* with the words "within that" (*tadantaḥ*). Within this *ājñācakra*, "within that"—meaning within the aforementioned triangle—resides the light of the phoneme *o*, which exists in the form of the arrangement of the *praṇava* and consists of the combined forms of the letters *a* and *u*.

The connection [of the letters] qualifies that very syllable: its nature is that of a pure and awakened inner self (*antarātman*); likewise, "having light like a lamp" means he whose light is like the radiance of a lamp, which is to say, he is of the nature of luminosity. Above that is the crescent moon (*candrārddha*), a mark in the shape of a half-moon; above that, upon the half-moon, is the Bindu, which is shining and beautiful—he is the bearer of that form.

The letter *ma* dwells [there]; that is to say, the letter *ma* itself exists there in the form of a *bindu*. That *nāda* is situated at the beginning of that aforementioned *ma*, which has the form of a *bindu*. It "laughs" (surpasses) the stream of the flow of nectar-white ambrosia; that is, it is white as mercury (*pārada*) and likewise white as nectar (*sudhā*). Furthermore, it is characterized by the habit of mocking the "stream"—the expansion—of that moon, which is the bearer of nectar. And so:

This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is white with *rasa* (nectar) and which possesses the laughter of a continuous stream of the flow of *sudhā* (ambrosia). By this, the extreme whiteness of the *nāda* is expressed.
And thus, the *praṇava* as defined consists of the *akāra*, *ukāra*, *nāda*, and *bindu*; it is the nature of the inner self (*antarātman*), blazing like the flame of a lamp.
And thus it results that [the deity] is white in color.

Regarding the word "here" (*iha*): when the *praṇava* situated in the *ājñācakra* has dissolved into the mind within this place—the abode of supreme bliss, the locus of uninterrupted bliss—[one attains] that which is well-known through the service of the Supreme Guru.
The practice of yoga obtained through the lineage of gurus— (herein lie the internal distinctions among the sparks of fire and the state of Paramaśiva)—
is like the form of a blazing lamp, and thereafter, it is like the abundance of the rising sun.
The light of illumination, meeting between the sky and the earth,
becomes manifest here in this place as the Lord himself, of full glory and imperishable, like the witness-fire within the orbs of the moon and the sun. (38)

Having bound—through constant practice—the *pura* (the source), which is either the *yonimudrā* or the *khecarīmudrā*, that brings about stability of mind; a *pura* which is "without support" (*nirālambā*), meaning it is such that there is no longer any contact with sense objects (*viṣaya-saṃsparśa*) therein, and thus severs the connection to sense objects; and which has been well-known and correctly attained through service to a skillful teacher who is a supreme teacher.

Through the continuous practice of the *praṇava*, the yogi perceives the portions, parts, or sparks—this is the meaning—of the fires that are friends of the wind. The meaning here is that for the yogi performing yoga, a light resembling scattering sparks of fire attains the state of direct mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣatā*). "Then" means: after the aforementioned practice, within the midst of that...
The meaning is that one perceives even those syllables which constitute the *praṇava*, as words whose forms shine forth intensely within that triangle situated in the center of the lotus.
Regarding what was stated in the previous verse—that "one sees the digits of the friends of the wind"—he specifies this further with the word "blazing" (*jvalat*). Thereafter...

The connection with the preceding clause is: "Immediately upon seeing the sparks of the fire described in the etymology, one sees a light. In response to the inquiry as to what kind of light that is, he says: "having the form of a blazing lamp. The meaning is that the light has a form like that of a blazing lamp. Likewise, it has the abundant radiance of the new sun; "new sun" refers to the sun of the morning time.

In the same way, it is characterized by a radiance like that of the newly rising sun, possessing abundant and profuse light; likewise, it is joined between the sky and the earth. Here, by the word "sky" (gagana), one should understand the void portion situated below the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*) above the previously mentioned *śaṅkhinī* channel. And by the word "earth" (*dharaṇī*), [one should understand...]
Regarding the phrase "the seed-syllable of the earth at that [place]," it should be understood as the earth-maṇḍala located in the mūlādhāra. Thus,
the meaning is that the light— which is joined between the aforementioned space and earth— pervades the entire extent from the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra) down to the mūlādhāra.

"Here" means: in this place, within the pericarp of the *ājñācakra* as described, the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva is present in person; he exists there just as [he exists] within the mandalas of fire (Agni) and of the moon and sun (Candra-Sūrya). Just as Paramaśiva resides within the mandalas of fire, moon, and sun situated in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-kamala*).
The meaning is that it is the same here as well. He qualifies Paramaśiva with the word "pūrṇa" (complete): "pūrṇa" means all-pervading;
"vibhava" means omnipresence, which is the agency of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal [the fruit of the renunciation of breath being attained here].
Having surrendered his life-breaths at this place, which is sweet with the incomparable and supreme fragrance of Viṣṇu, one whose mind is delighted at the time of death attains the Supreme,
Eternal God— the unborn and primordial Person of the three worlds.
And the lord of yogis enters that ancient city known through Vedānta. || 39 ||

He who possesses [that power]—this very Blessed One, Paramaśiva, is the one who, by means of his own sovereign power (*vibhava*), effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all phenomenal manifestations (*prapañca*); this is the meaning. Likewise, he is *avyaya*, meaning his form remains unmodified in every respect; likewise, he is the *sākṣin*, the witness, meaning he is untainted (*nirlepa*). Here, this should be noted: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the agency of creation and so forth belongs to Śakti alone.

Furthermore, because the *Gandharva Tantra*, in its third chapter, states: "Her creation and dissolution arise and cease perpetually," and so forth, it is accepted that Śakti alone is the agent of creation and the rest. Thus, the term "Witness" (*sākṣin*) indicates that [the Self] perceives, in its immutable form, the creation of the phenomenal world and so forth, which is brought about by its own non-differentiated Śakti.
Regarding the abiding of Paramaśiva even in the *ājñācakra*, the *Nirvāṇatantra* states in its ninth chapter:
"Thus, Haṃsa [resides] on Maṇidvīpa; in his lap is Paraśiva;
on the left side is Siddhakālī, whose nature is eternal bliss."

Regarding this, he states the fruit of the relinquishing of life: "here" (iha). At the time of the cessation of life—the moment of giving up the vital breaths—the lord of yogis, with a joyful mind, thinking "Brahman-extinction will be mine," being one whose heart is intensely delighted, [attains] here, in the abode of the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, which is sweet with supreme bliss and delightful with an uninterrupted stream of joy.

Having fixed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in the *ājñā-cakra* and brought about their dissolution according to the sequence of the yoga-instructions, one enters the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*) and attains liberation in *nirvāṇa*; this is the meaning. He qualifies the Person as "the God" (*devam*):
that which has the nature of shining forth in the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and so forth; "unborn" (*aja*), meaning eternal; and likewise, the primordial cause of the three worlds.

The Purāṇa is well-known in all the scriptures by the name "Purāṇapuruṣa" (the Ancient Person). Likewise, it is known through the Vedānta, for according to such scriptural passages as "from which speech turns back, unable to reach it along with the mind," its nature is defined as being beyond the range of speech and mind; thus, even though it is impossible to comprehend it [directly], [it is affirmed that] "all this is indeed Brahman" and "the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
The meaning is that [Brahman] is known through such scriptural passages as these, and is accessible solely through the scriptures that expound Brahman.
Here, by the word "Viṣṇu," the all-pervading Lord Paramaśiva alone is to be understood. As stated in the ninth chapter of the Nirvāṇatantra:

(Above the Ājñā-cakra is the Great Sound in the form of Śiva and Śakti, and the fruit of its vision: Above that [cakra] is the place of dissolution of the vital air, and further above is the half-form of Śiva, which is the Great Sound;
it has the form of Śiva, is peaceful, bestows boons and fearlessness, and is the radiance of pure intellect.

When the yogi, whose character is well-disciplined through service to the lotus-pair of the guru’s feet, beholds [the truth], then the perfection of speech shall always remain in the lotus of his palm. (40)

Because it is stated that Paramaśiva himself resides in the Tapoloka, which has the form of the *ājñācakra*; [the text] declares its quality of bestowing the liberation of *nirvāṇa* in that very same place:
"Sālokya would be in Maharloka, and Sārūpya in Janaloka."
"Union [is attained] in the worlds of austerity (tapoloka), while liberation indeed occurs in that which is above them.

Having thus described the wheel of command (ājñācakra), he now describes the Great Sound (mahānāda) situated below the thousand-petaled lotus located at the head: "the place of dissolution. One who is well-disposed toward the service of the lotus-feet of the Guru’s pair...

The meaning is: by means of service to the lotus feet of the venerable Guru-deva, whose mind is purified through the practice of yoga, and then through the practice of yoga itself; [he becomes] such a yogi whose character (śīla) or nature is pure and filled with a most firm one-pointedness of mind; above that—that is, above the aforementioned wheel of command (ājñācakra)—when there is the form of the Great Sound (mahānāda), which is the essential nature of the Great Sound.
If one should see [it], then the connection is that the perfection of speech shall always abide in his lotus-like palm.
He describes the nature of the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) with the words beginning "the place of dissolution" (*layasthāna*).

The meaning is that the place of dissolution for the vital wind (*vāyu*) is indeed the Great Sound, because its dissolution occurs precisely in the Great Sound, which is the cause of the wind's own emergence. Likewise, it is above Śiva.

In this context, Śiva is Ardhanārīśvara; "half of that" refers to Śakti, and thus "that form" means the form of Śakti. Likewise, "Śivākāra" means the form of Śiva. In this way, by these two terms—*śivārddha* (half of Śiva) and *śivākāra* (the form of Śiva)—it is stated that this Nāda consists of both Śiva and Śakti.
This has been stated in the first chapter of the *Śāradā*:

"The Bindu is of the nature of Śiva, the Bīja is Śakti, and their mutual union is called Nāda; thus it has been declared by those proficient in all the Āgamas. Thus also [it was stated] by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.

Thus, at the beginning of creation, the Supreme Person manifests that eternal Prakṛti, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) and which serves as the substratum for the manifestation of the entire aggregate of principles (tattvas).
Having cited this statement from the *Pāñcarātra* and having declared that its very *nāda* and *bindu* are the forms of the states conducive to creation, [he describes] the *sahasrāra-padmam*.
Above that, on the peak of the Śaṅkhinī in the void region, there dwells a radiant lotus below the Visarga; it has a thousand petals, is as white as the full moon, faces downward,
and is beautiful with a mass of filaments as lovely as the rays of the young sun.
His body is resplendent with the letters beginning with *la* on his forehead and so forth, and he is of the nature of absolute bliss.
When that Śakti, awakened by means of the Nāda and oriented toward the state free from affliction,
is turned toward Śiva, she is then remembered as having the form of the Puruṣa.
Thus it has been said:

"That notion of reality (tattvasaṃjñā), through the proximity of the light of pure consciousness (cinmātrajyotiḥ), desiring to manifest and becoming condensed, at times attains the state of the Bindu."
Thus, even by this statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, the non-difference of Śiva and Śakti alone is established. "Peaceful and of gentle form" (śāntaṃ saumyamūrtim);

likewise, "the radiance of pure intellect" (śuddhabuddhiprakāśam)—that is to say, that from which there is the radiance of pure intellect, which is blazing with knowledge; the meaning is that it is the producer of the knowledge of Brahman.
Now he describes the thousand-petaled lotus situated on the head:
"Above that" means above the aforementioned Great Sound (mahānāda), at the summit—the tip—of the Śaṅkhinī, the channel so named;
in the region of emptiness, the place of the form of void; likewise, below the Visarga, in the lower region of Nature (prakṛti) from the Visarga situated at the Brahma-aperture.

The connection is that [the breath] dwells in a lotus of a thousand petals—that is, ten hundred petals. Regarding the location of the *visarga* at the *brahmarandhra*, the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*, in its second chapter, states:
"Then there is the wind, the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), and beyond that, the *brahmarandhra*."
"In that aperture [is] the Visarga, which is eternal bliss and stainless.
Regarding the fact that the Visarga denotes *prakṛti* (primordial nature):
"The Bindu is said to be Puruṣa (the Spirit), and the Visarga is remembered as *prakṛti* (Nature)."
This has already been demonstrated previously [in the commentary on 1.1].
He qualifies the lotus with the words "illuminating" (*prakāśam*) and so forth. "Illuminating" means having the nature of light (*prakāśa-svarūpa*).
However, in the reading *śūnyadeśaprakāśam*, the meaning is that it is such that its illumination occurs in an empty space. Likewise...
Within that [lotus] is a full moon;
within its pericarp is a lunar disc, within which is a triangle, and within that is the supreme bindu.
Inside that [triangle] resides the pure, perfectly full moon, devoid of the hare-mark.
A mass of throbbing moonlight, with a smile of a continuous stream of smooth supreme nectar,
shines eternally within that triangle; and within that, there is a void in the form of lightning, which is served by all the hosts of gods and is exceedingly secret.
"Brilliant" means having an exceedingly white color, like the full moon. This is stated in the second chapter of the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*:
"The eternal lotus of a thousand petals is white in color and faces downward.
However, in the tenth chapter of the *Nirvāṇatantra*, concerning the [lotus] of a thousand petals: [it says as follows]."
White, red, yellow, black, and even green;
it is adorned with various wonderful forms and diverse colors.
In one moment it is white, in another red, and in another the most beautiful yellow;
in which moment is it black in color, or the supreme green color?
And at what moment, O beloved with beautiful limbs, does it assume its variegated form?
Thus, O Goddess, that lotus is always adorned in various ways.
With these and other words, he describes the different colors according to its various moments: "downward-facing" means having a face turned downwards; "lovely" means having a beautiful form.

Likewise, "like the mass of filaments lovely as the rays of the young sun" means that the mass of filaments is lovely—meaning beautiful—and radiant red, like the rays of the young sun, i.e., the morning sunlight.

[He is] one whose [body] possesses a mass of filaments; likewise, he is one whose body is resplendent with the fifty letters from *a* to *kṣa*, which are placed on the forehead and other parts—such as the forehead and so forth. Since the sequence for the placement of the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) is seen in the form "aṃ namaḥ" and so on upon the forehead, the phrase "by the forehead and others" implies "by the letters beginning with *a*. This is stated explicitly in the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*.
In the second chapter, concerning the thousand-spoked [lotus]:
"It is resplendent with the shimmering letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
Likewise, in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī*: [as follows].
"The thousand-petaled lotus born from the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Thus, the meaning is that this lotus is of the nature of absolute bliss (*kevalānanda*), having the character of uninterrupted bliss (*niravacchinnānandasvarūpa*).
Here, this should be noted: in this lotus, there are twenty revolutions of petals, and for each revolution—
There are fifty petals; on each of those fifty petals, the fifty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa* shine forth.
Regarding the moon-maṇḍala situated in the pericarp of this lotus, he says: "They are equal. Of that...

(The secrecy of the Supreme Bindu and the state of Paramaśiva: That which is most secret must be guarded with effort— that supreme bulb (*kanda*), the source of a mass of intense and supreme bliss, subtle, and shining with the pure form of all the digits of the moon.
In this place dwells the Lord, renowned for the attainment of the state known as Paramaśiva;
he is the essential nature itself, the soul of all, who has transcended both the flavorful and the flavorless, and who is the swan [of consciousness] blinded by the delusion of ignorance. || 43 ||

"Within the lotus" means in the center of its pericarp (*karṇikā*). "Devoid of a hare" means that for this very reason, it is the pure, stainless, full moon; the lunar disc is seated there. He qualifies the moon as "radiant":
"having a mass of shimmering moonlight," meaning that from which masses of shimmering moonlight emanate. And likewise:

"Whose laughter has a continuity made glossy by a mass of supreme nectar"— that is to say, he whose expansion (santāna) or radiance (hāsa) is such that its continuity is rendered smooth by a mass of supreme nectar (paramāmṛta); the meaning is that he generates bliss through a stream of supremely delightful nectar.
Regarding the statement "the triangle" (*trikoṇam*), he describes what is to be meditated upon within the circle of the moon as described in the *Nirukta*:
"Within that," meaning in the center of the lunar disc, there exists a triangle whose form is like lightning, possessing a brilliance similar to lightning.
"Within that" means inside the middle of that triangle; it is extremely secret and is served by all the qualities of the gods.
The connection is that the Void (*śūnya*), which is the form of the Supreme Bindu (*parabindu*), vibrates (*sphurati*).

Regarding the phrase "well-concealed" (*sugopyam*): it means that this Void, as thus defined, must be concealed with effort by practitioners; it should not be revealed to just anyone. He qualifies the Void with the words "of the mass of the stream of supreme, extraordinary joy" (*atiśaya-paramāmoda-santāna-rāśeḥ*).

The meaning is: "of that great liberation (*mahāmokṣa*) wherein there is an abundance of a continuous stream of supreme bliss. It is the supreme bulb (*kanda*), the primary root; it is subtle and difficult to perceive. Likewise, it is the manifestation of a pure form like all the digits of the moon;
here, by the word "digit" (*kalā*), the digit of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇakalā*) which is to be described later is understood—and thus, together with that digit, the digit of Nirvāṇa.

It means that its manifestation is of a pure nature by virtue of the digit of the moon (śaśikalā) currently present; the sense is that even for that which is most subtle— the aforementioned form of the supreme bindu— manifestation occurs through the digit of the new moon (amākalā) and the digit of liberation (nirvāṇakalā) situated within the previously mentioned triangle.

Regarding the statement "here" (*iha*), he describes the abiding state of Paramaśiva within this pericarp (*karṇikā*). The meaning is: "here in this place," that is, above the Inner Self (*antarātman*)—which is otherwise known by the name *Haṃsapīṭha*—situated in the center of the lunar disc located within the pericarp of this lotus.
"Paramaśiva" refers to that which is established through the attainment of the realization (*samākhyāna-siddhi*) of the one designated as Paramaśiva. As for that realization, it is...

The meaning is that he is renowned by the name "Supreme Śiva" (Paramaśiva), which is established through his perfection in all tantras. The connection with the following [word] is: "the God (devaḥ)" who bestows the knowledge of one's own self upon the seeker (yateḥ). He qualifies Supreme Śiva with the words beginning with "the one whose nature is... (*svarūpī*):

"the one whose nature is [it]" (*svarūpī*) means having the form of the Supreme Brahman; "the Self of all" (*sarvātmā*) means the nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) which is the Self of all. Here, "the one whose nature is [it]" (*svarūpī*)...

By the two words "sarva" and "ātman," it is established that although he possesses the nature of all individual souls (*jīvātman*), he does not abandon the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Likewise, by the phrase "rasavirasamitaḥ," it is meant that he has attained both *rasa*— the essence of supreme bliss— and *virasa*— that which is distinct from it,
namely the bliss-essence of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti— even while remaining established in his own essential nature.

The meaning is that he experiences the flavor (*rasa*) of union with Śakti. It has been established in the commentary on the first verse that this very Paraśiva is the essential nature of the venerable Guru (*śrīguru*), and it will be further established in the subsequent verse.
Here, in the fourth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, after describing the *ājñācakra*— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.]
"O Maheśānī, above that, the lotus is always facing upwards;
above that, O Maheśānī, one should meditate upon the Lord Sadāśiva.
Having thus stated the words, [the text specifies] "facing upwards."
It has been stated that one should meditate upon Sadāśiva atop a twelve-petalled lotus facing upward, situated within a thousand-petalled lotus facing downward.
This is also said in the *Pādukāpañcaka-stotra*:
"Ever-present, pure, and wonderful, [He resides] within the interior of the lotus of the Brahma-aperture."
By such means, within the hollow of his sprouted ear-lobes, a line is fashioned by means of the lines of the *akathādi* [vowels];
and by such means, below a thousand-petaled lotus facing downwards, there is one with twelve petals facing upwards.

He describes the presence of Paramaśiva in the form of the Śrī Guru within the triangle situated at the center of the lotus-heart; however, elsewhere in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, it says: "The great thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) is endowed with the three—Nāda and Bindu."
In the three lines starting from the letter 'a', within the triangle formed by the three groups of consonants.

In the center of that, one should draw a triangle starting from the letter 'a' and so forth in a counter-clockwise direction, containing the supreme point (*parabindu*) which consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

By such statements as "within the thousand-spoked [lotus], in the void, adorned with divine archways," and by the words from the first chapter of the *Mahākālītantra* previously cited, [it is established that] the Supreme Śiva resides precisely within the thousand-spoked lotus.

The location has been stated. Thus, through a comparative study of the various tantras, it is established as the final conclusion that since two distinct systems are understood, one should adopt whichever method follows the tradition of one's own guru.
However, according to the venerable Paramahaṃsa Bhagavat Pūrṇānanda, the residence of Paramaśiva is held to be in the *sahasrāra* (thousand-petaled lotus) itself.
It should be noted that there is not even a slight mention of a twelve-petaled lotus at the base;
for the Blessed One, discharging an unceasing torrent of the stream of nectar, bestows supreme self-knowledge upon the yogi of pure intellect.
He is the Lord of All, the overflowing stream of the succession of all happiness; he is known by the name of the Supreme Swan (Haṃsa). || 44 ||

Regarding the phrase "sudhādhārāsāram" (the essence of the stream of nectar): Paramaśiva has been defined as *sudhādhārāsāram*; *sudhādhārā* means a stream of nectar (*amṛtapravāha*), and *sāra* means the most excellent. Thus, the meaning is that it is a sentence consisting of a mantra which is like the essence of the stream of nectar. And so, this mantra-constituted sentence, which bestows bliss like nectar, is *niravadhi*, meaning eternal and always present.
For the sake of the practitioners' attainment of the goals of human endeavor, [the Lord] releases Himself by manifesting in the form of the venerable Guru.

For the ascetic practitioner—whose mind is pure, whose heart is purified through service to the feet of the venerable Guru accompanied by supreme devotion, and whose mind is fixed upon the deity to be realized—the "knowledge of one's own Self" (*svātmajñāna*) arises; that is, the knowledge of both "one's own self," which is the individual soul (*jīvātman*), and the "Self," which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The meaning is that [the scripture] directs or teaches the knowledge of the non-difference between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), as established by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

Here, this should be noted: the aforementioned Supreme Śiva himself, appearing in the form of the venerable Guru, having descended upon the earth in the form of the initiation-guru (*dīkṣāguru*), [bestows] upon practitioners the initiation of various deities to be worshipped and their respective mantras, which consist of nectar.

It accomplishes the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). This has been established in detail by other authorities as well, such as those stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Kulārṇava*: "He who is bound by human skin is himself Paraśiva," and so forth.
The commentary on the first verse of the first chapter, beginning with "the full moon shining upon the thousand-petaled lotus," has been provided by us [elsewhere] and is not elaborated upon here.
Regarding the phrase "they are equal": beneath Paramaśiva is Sarveśa, the Lord of all, who is Haṃsa.

The inner self (antarātman), consisting of both Puruṣa and Prakṛti, remains [there]. Regarding the nature of the Haṃsa within this inner self consisting of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, it is stated in the commentary on the first verse of this work:
"The letter *haṃ* is said to be the Bindu, and the letter *sa* is remembered as the Visarga."
This has been established by such elaborations as the words of the *Prapañcasāra*. To the question "Of what nature is the *haṃsa*? he says:

"It is the overflow of the wave of the continuum of all happiness. This means that it is that from which there issues forth the wave—that is, the series—of the continuum, the expansion, of all happiness; its meaning is that it brings about an uninterrupted and abundant abundance of happiness.

By this very reasoning, since an overflow of a distinctively different kind of bliss arises from that [source], its nature as consisting of such bliss should also be inferred, just as a "treasure-element" (*dhanadhātu*) is characterized by possessing an abundance of wealth. Likewise, he is known by the name "Supreme" (*parama*); "Supreme" is another name for him, or it is "Paramahaṃsa."
(In this pericarp of the lotus is the abode of all the gods:
the Śaivas call it the station of Śiva, the Vaiṣṇava hosts speak of it as the Supreme Person, while some and others generally call it the station of Hari and Hara.
Even other lords of sages, who delight in the essence of bliss from the pair of the Goddess’s feet, [seek] that stainless station of Prakṛti and Puruṣa which is the foot of the Goddess. 45.
(This is the fruit of the knowledge of this lotus:
Having understood the place here, the best of men, with his own mind fixed in discipline,
shall not exist in saṃsāra again, nor shall he be bound once more within the three worlds.
For that skillful man of disciplined mind, his power shall always be complete; he possesses the ability to create and destroy, as well as the power of flight and speech that is perfectly pure.
He says that this very place is the abode where all deities reside, referring to it as "the abode of Śiva" (śivasthāna). The Śaivas, the worshippers of Śiva, declare this to be the abode of Śiva;

the Vaiṣṇava groups declare it to be the abode of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person. Others, the worshippers of both Hari and Hara—the meaning being the Śāktas who delight in the nectar of the bliss of the Goddess’s pair of feet—declare this to be the station of Hari and Hara.

They say that this is the foot, the abode of the Goddess; the meaning is that other lords of sages and even the best of yogis also declare, "This is the stainless abode of Prakṛti and Puruṣa. By this, it should be understood that this is the abode of all the gods, each according to their own object of worship.
He states the fruit of this lotus-knowledge (*padmajñāna*) [with the words] "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in this thousand-petaled lotus;

having known the station, that is, having understood that the abiding of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) is right here—this is the meaning. Regarding this, the reading *atra idaṃ sthānaṃ jñātvā* ("having known this station here") is supported by Kālīcaraṇa. *Niyatanijacittaḥ*: one whose own mind is fixed, meaning one's own mind is directed toward one's respective chosen deity.

By which such an excellent man, the best of practitioners, shall not exist again; the meaning is that he does not undergo the taking up of rebirth in *saṃsāra*. Regarding this, he states the reason: "bound within the three worlds. The sense is that he is not bound in heaven, the mortal realm, or the netherworld (*pātāla*), because of the exhaustion of all karma—both auspicious and inauspicious—and because of the non-arising of further karma that would serve as the cause for experience. Furthermore, of him...

The connection is as follows: for the wise person, there shall always be the complete power to accomplish all tasks—to perform their desired deeds, to take away what is undesired, and to avoid it; likewise, they shall possess the ability to travel through the sky and a perfectly pure speech.
(Within the triangle inside the pericarp of this lotus is the abode of the digit of the moon):
Here resides that sixteenth digit of the Moon, pure and like a sister to the infant Sun; it is the supreme [digit], whose form is a single part of a hundredth of a subtle fiber from a dust mote.
Her body is as delicate as a garland of lightning; she is eternally risen with her face turned downward, bearing a stream of nectar flowing from an overflowing succession of perfect bliss. || 47 ||

(That is the abiding of the *nirvāṇakalā* within the crescent moon: That digit known as *nirvāṇa*, which is higher than the highest, exists contained within that [moon], having the form of a single part of a hair-tip divided a thousandfold.
The Blessed Lady is the presiding deity of all beings, ever-arisen in awakening; she possesses a form as transient as the crescent moon, yet her splendor is equal to that of all the suns.
Regarding the abiding of the *amā* digit within the triangle situated inside the thousand-petaled lotus described in the *Nirukta*, it says: "Here she resides.

Here, within the triangle at the center of the pericarp, that well-known digit of the moon—which consists of one part out of sixteen parts, is a digit (*kalā*) born of the same womb as the infant sun (*śiśusūrya*), and is red in color like the morning sun—namely the digit called *amā*, resides. He now describes the nature of the *amā* digit:
In the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, as cited in the *Tithitattva*:
"O Goddess, the New Moon (*amā*) is said to be the sixteenth part;
it is the supreme *māyā*, established as the sustainer of the bodies of embodied beings."
He qualifies the *kalā* (digit/aspect): "pure" (*śuddhā*), meaning free from blemish. "Dustless" (*nīrajā*):
she is of the nature of a single part of a hundredth part of a very fine lotus fiber—that is, of the nature of a single portion of a hundredth part of a subtle, stainless thread.
Likewise, she is the supreme (*parā*) power (*śakti*). Her body is as tender as a flash of lightning.

She is distinguished by a soft, radiant splendor resembling a garland of lightning; she is eternally risen, meaning she possesses perpetual light because she is devoid of decay or arising. She is downward-facing (adhomukhī), that is, with her face turned downwards. She is full and all-pervasive, possessing a succession of bliss—a continuous stream of bliss. Likewise, she pours forth an overflowing stream of nectar.

"Dharati" means that she exists as such, in the sense that she flows with abundant nectar (*amṛta*). Such a digit (*kalā*) named Amā resides within the triangle at the center of the thousand-petaled lotus; this is the meaning.
He speaks of the digit of Nirvāṇa residing within the digit of Amā: "Nirvāṇa... [referring to] that which is contained within it, of that...

Within the Amākalā resides the Nirvāṇakalā, renowned as the bestower of liberation. In the center of this [Amākalā] shines the supreme, unprecedented Nirvāṇa-śakti, which is the abiding state of the Nirvāṇa-śakti whose nature is the internal Bindu (— ).
She who possesses the radiance of ten million suns, the mother of the three worlds, whose single form is but a ten-millionth part [of her true nature],
who is more secret than the tip of a hair, and who bears a stream of overflowing love that is boundless—
she who is the life-force of all, joyfully bringing the awakening of reality into the minds of sages. (49)

The etymological derivation of the term *nirvāṇakalā* is that it is the digit (*kalā*) that bestows [liberation] and is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). He qualifies it as "from the supreme" (*parāt*), meaning it is higher than the supreme (*parāt paratarā*) and most excellent. The reading *parā paratareti* is found in the *Kālīcaraṇadhṛta*; in that case, however, the meaning is that it is the digit *amā* (the new moon) which is supreme, and the digit *nirvāṇakalā* is even higher than that. It is of the nature of a single part of a hair-tip divided into a thousand portions.

The meaning is that she is of a form consisting of a single part out of a thousand parts of the tip of a hair, thus being exceedingly subtle. Here, the elision of the vowel *ā* in the word *vibhajitasya* is an archaic (ārṣa) usage for the sake of meter. Being (*satī*), although difficult to perceive due to her extreme subtlety, she is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpā*) because she is established in all systems of thought. She is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*) of living beings (*bhūtānām*, i.e., sentient beings), having consciousness as her essential nature. She is the perpetual dawning of awakening (*nityaprabodhodayā*). Regarding "perpetual awakening": [text continues]
