The meaning is that she is the "Bestower of the Knowledge of Brahman" because the arising of that knowledge occurs through her.

She possesses a curved form equal to the crescent moon, being as crooked in shape as the half-moon; likewise, she possesses a radiance equal to all the suns, meaning she is endowed with a splendor like that of the twelve Adityas. He now states the essential nature of the digit of the new moon (amā-kalā) and the digit of liberation (nirvāṇa-kalā).
In the second chapter of the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*:
"Here, the ever-arisen digit of the new moon (*amākalā*), devoid of increase or decrease, resides;
in its center is the curved seventeenth digit called Nirvāṇa."
He speaks of the abiding of the power of nirvāṇa within the portion of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇakalā): "of this" (etasyāḥ). The connection is as follows:

in the middle region of this portion of nirvāṇa, the supreme power of nirvāṇa—which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and likewise unprecedented (apūrvā), meaning it has nothing prior to it because it exists at the beginning of the creation of the entire phenomenal world—shines forth.
It distinguishes the power of Nirvāṇa: she possesses a radiance like that of ten million suns, a splendor resembling infinite suns;

likewise, she is the mother of the three worlds, giving birth to the three realms consisting of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla); likewise, she is of the nature of a single part of the tip of a hair, meaning she is most subtle. For this very reason, she is exceedingly secret, being difficult to perceive due to her subtlety.

She is "one who bears the stream of overflowing love without limit," meaning she bears that stream of love which flows and pours forth incessantly—an infinite stream of supreme nectar produced by the bliss of *sāmarasya* (divine union). She is "the life-force of all," meaning she is the very nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) for all living beings. Likewise, she dwells with joy—that is, with delight—in the minds of sages, within the hearts of yogins.
The grammatical connection is as follows: the supreme power of liberation (*nirvāṇa-śakti*), bearing the awakening to reality (*tattva-bodha*) and existing in the form of the *bindu*, shines forth.
(The abode of the Supreme Brahman is within that power of liberation.
In the midst of its interior lies the stainless, eternal state of Śiva, accessible through yoga.

Some wise ones describe that state called Brahman as eternal bliss, consisting of all happiness, and the light of pure consciousness; others call it the Vaiṣṇava state; and some fortunate ones speak of it as the one known as Haṃsa, which awakens one to the path of liberation. (50)
(The Sequence for Raising Kuṇḍalinī):

Having learned from the mouth of Śrīnātha the sequence that illuminates the path to great liberation, the virtuous practitioner— whose character is disciplined by the constant practice of restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)— should recognize the Goddess by means of the syllable HŪṂ alone.

In this context, although the phrase "in the middle of this" indicates that the power of Nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-śakti) resides within the digit of Nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-kalā), it should be understood that its location is above the *nāda*. As it is stated in the second chapter of the Kaṅkālamālinītantra:
"Know that she who is called Nirvāṇa, who has entered within, is of the nature of fire and is the awakener."

"Sound (*nāda*) is unmanifest; above that is the power of Nirvāṇa, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, the supreme [power] of all, whose form is the source (*yoni*). Thus it is said. He describes the abode of Śiva within that aforementioned power of Nirvāṇa with the words "of that" (*tasyāḥ*), meaning "of that power of Nirvāṇa."

In the midst of the interval, within the internal void, exists the stainless, the pure—meaning free from the impurity of *māyā*—the state of Śiva, the locus of the Supreme Brahman. He describes its essential nature: it is eternal, meaning its nature is perpetual; it is accessible to yogis, meaning it is to be known solely through yoga properly practiced by yogis; and it is designated as "eternal bliss" (*nityānanda*), that which is both eternal and bliss.

The meaning is that because its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is such, it is designated as "eternal bliss" (*nityānanda*); this is the worldly convention regarding that which is "Brahman, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānanda*), according to scriptural texts (*śruti*). Thus, by the very name "eternal bliss," practitioners (*sādhaka*) celebrate it. Likewise, it consists of all happiness (*sakalasukhamaya*), meaning it is the source of happiness for all; indeed, all practitioners [perceive] it precisely as consisting of happiness.

The meaning is that they experience that. Likewise, "the illumination of pure consciousness" (*śuddhabodhaprakāśa*) means that from which the illumination of pure consciousness—that is, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—proceeds; or alternatively, it is called "the illumination of pure consciousness" because it illuminates pure consciousness.
He states the different names for this according to different traditions, beginning with "some": "some," namely, certain wise Vedāntins, [regard] that...
Some speak of the state of Śiva, which is designated as the Supreme Brahman; others, the Vaiṣṇavas, speak of that Vaiṣṇava state;

certain yogins speak of that which is called Haṃsa, named after the swan; while others discourse on something ineffable—the awakening of the Self, the locus of self-realization, which is liberation itself. And thus:

It should be understood that although there are differences in terminology due to the diversity of traditions, this state is the ultimate goal for all practitioners, whether they belong to the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, or other schools.
One whose nature is pure and awakened brings about [this state] in the center of the door of Brahman for the virtuous.
Having pierced through that form of the Liṅga by means of the successive application of wind and fire, [he beheld] the heated [substance].

Having thus described [the path] up to the thousand-petaled lotus, he teaches the sequence for raising the Kuṇḍalinī within the thousand-spoked [lotus] with the words "by the syllable *huṃ*. One who is habituated to the practice of *yama* and *niyama*— where *yamas* are defined as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*), and *niyamas* [are likewise defined]...

"Suśīla" means one whose conduct (*śīla*) consists of the repeated practice (*samabhyāsa*) of those limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*) whose characteristics were previously stated— namely, purity (*śauca*), contentment (*santoṣa*), austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*). This refers to one who is devoted to the constant and most rigorous practice of yoga, performing it correctly with long duration, reverence, continuity, and respect.

Having abandoned practices that obstruct yoga, the renowned yogi, being established in the state of a *śiṣṭa*, learned from the mouth of the Guru— the venerable *Śrīnātha*— the *Krama* which illuminates the path to great liberation; that is, having understood the procedure for the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *sahasrāra*.

One whose own nature (*svabhāva*) is pure consciousness— that is, one who has attained the state of Brahman itself through the grace of the venerable Guru— is such that his own being is established in the Supreme Brahman, which is pure consciousness and consists of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). Having drawn the vital air (*pavana*) into the interior of the body by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), he proceeds by means of the sequential application of the vital air and fire toward that well-known Goddess Kuṇḍalinī.

The fire, sustained by the practice of *kumbhaka* (breath retention) and ignited by the aforementioned wind, is the fire of desire (*kāmāgni*) situated within the triangle inside the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra*. By the mutual friction of these two, that well-known Goddess—
the *kuṇḍalinī* residing in the *mūlādhāra*, who encircles the *svayambhū-liṅga*, exists in the form of a sleeping serpent with three and a half coils— is heated.

The meaning is "having awakened. Having pierced the aperture of the *svayambhū-liṅga*, which has the form of that *liṅga*, [the yogin] "places" (the meaning is "establishes") [the consciousness] in the middle of that which was described in the third verse as being situated at the mouth of the *brahmanāḍī*—namely, the "Brahma-door" (*brahmadvāra*) which shines forth at its opening, a region delightful with the essence of nectar (*sudhāsāra*). The *brahmanāḍī* itself is mentioned in the third verse.

As for the claim made by a certain commentator— who, having derived the word *nāḍī* from the verbal root *naḍ* (to go), fabricated a groundless meaning for the term *brahmanāḍī* as "the void portion within the *citriṇī* channel, which serves as the path for Kuṇḍalinī’s journey to the presence of Paramaśiva," and concluded that there is no other channel within the *citriṇī*— that is incorrect.
Īḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Citriṇī,
and Brahmanāḍī— these five channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed to be situated therein.

Thus, because the *Brahmanāḍī* is defined as being one of the five [channels] mentioned in the eighth chapter of the *Toḍalatantra*, and because the essential nature of Kuṇḍalinī has already been demonstrated previously, this verse shows the sequence for the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī from the *Mūlādhāra* up to the *Brahmadvāra* by means of the syllable *Hūṃ*. Through the *Hūṃ* [syllable], [Kuṇḍalinī...]
He states the sequence for awakening [Kuṇḍalinī] in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī* (the method of Kuṇḍalinī-yoga):
"Having pierced the three liṅgas, [she enters] that supreme Rasa-Śiva, the blazing subtle abode."

That goddess, of pure essence, like a flash of lightning, extremely subtle and appearing as a shimmering thread, reaches every lotus from the channel called Brahman and shines intensely; by means of her characteristic subtlety, she suddenly effects that state which is the nature of bliss known as liberation. (52)
The supreme goddess Kuṇḍalī is born from the syllable Hūṃ;
by means of the Haṃsa mantra, Kuṇḍalī sustains her own body as the Self.

"In conjunction with the intensified fire, together with the mind and the vital winds, one should lead the supreme Kuṇḍalinī, accompanied by the individual soul (jīvātman), upward. Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"By means of the path of the junctions of the six cakras, and likewise by way of the suṣumṇā,
one should lead the Goddess to the thousand-spoked [cakra] with the mantra *haṃsa*.
Here, by the aforementioned earlier statement beginning with "by the syllable *huṃ* alone," the raising of Kuṇḍalinī by means of the syllable *huṃ* is declared.
However, by the subsequent statement beginning with "by way of the path of the junctions of the six cakras," a difference in sequence is observed regarding the *haṃsa* mantra.
In the second chapter of the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*, it says:
"O Daughter of the Mountain King, having drawn forth the individual soul (*jīvātman*) by means of the *praṇava* alone..."
Taking the vital breath (prāṇa) along with its fragrance (gandha) together with Kuṇḍalinī,
the practitioner should bring the Goddess to the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra] by means of the mantra "So 'haṃ tu."

By this, it is taught that one should lead the individual soul (jīvātman) from the heart to the *mūlādhāra* with the *praṇava*, and then, by means of the *haṃsa-mantra*, effect the awakening of the *kuṇḍalinī* together with that individual soul.
Having led the life-force from the heart to the lotus of the mouth by means of the *haṃsa-mantra*...
Having raised Kuṇḍalī from the Supreme Deity by means of the syllable HŪṂ.

Thus, by the statement of the *Kālīkulāmṛta*, it is understood that the leading of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) to the *mūlādhāra* is performed with the *haṃsa* mantra, and the raising of Kuṇḍalinī together with the individual soul is performed with the syllable *hūṃ*. And so, by considering the sequence of preceding authorities,
one ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is that having led the individual soul into Kuṇḍalinī with the *praṇava* (oṃ), one raises [her] with the *haṃsa* mantra.

It is understood that according to another [tradition], one leads the individual soul (*jīvātman*) there by means of the *haṃsa* mantra and then raises it up by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. However, the author’s own position is that the second alternative alone is intended, as indicated by the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "by *hūṃ* alone. Now, he describes the sequence for joining the *kuṇḍalinī* at the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) with the words "having pierced," etc. That Goddess has been thus described.

(The sequence for the union with Kulakuṇḍalī in the Śiva consisting of the previously mentioned Bindu: Having led that Kulakuṇḍalī, together with the individual soul (jīva), by means of dissolution, the wise one [should place her] in the supreme Lord Śiva, the abode of liberation, in the dwelling of the pure lotus.
The lord of yogis, resting upon the pair of lotus feet of his guru, meditates in samādhi upon the Supreme Goddess, who is the embodiment of consciousness and bestows the desired fruit. 53.

The meaning is as follows: having pierced the three signs— namely, the self-arisen sign (*svayambhū-liṅga*) situated in the *mūlādhāra* wheel, the sign called the arrow (*vāṇa-liṅga*) situated in the *anāhata* wheel, and the sign called the other (*itara-liṅga*) situated in the *ājñā* wheel— and having removed the obstruction of the path to the *sahasrāra* created by these signs, [one proceeds] through the channel known as Brahma, that is, the aforementioned *brahmanāḍī*.

Having reached all the lotuses in succession— from the *mūlādhāra* to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, then the *maṇipūra*, and then the *anāhata*— in this manner, she, whose essence is pure *sattva* and whose nature is the consciousness of the fourth state (*turya*),
shines forth like lightning, possessing a brilliance resembling an electric flash, and her form is that of a radiant thread characterized by extreme subtlety.
That Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, whose very form is like that of a shimmering, radiant lotus fiber,
[resides] within the midst of that Supreme Śiva— who possesses supreme splendor and a subtle radiance— in His stainless, eternal state of Śiva, which is accessible only to yogis.

The meaning is: having proceeded in due order to Śiva, who is of the nature of the supreme *bindu* as thus described, or to Paramaśiva; he suddenly brings about—that is, accomplishes—for practitioners liberation in the form of bliss known as *mokṣa*, which is of the nature of uninterrupted bliss.
Now, he describes the sequence for the union of Kuṇḍalinī with Śiva, who is of the nature of the supreme Bindu characterized by Nirukta: "Having led," and so forth.

The "Lord of Yogins" (yogīśa)—meaning the best of yogins—is one who rests upon the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru, taking sole refuge in the lotus-feet of the venerable Guru; he is "intent on that," meaning he is devoted exclusively to Samādhi, which is characterized by the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. [He leads] that Kulakuṇḍalī, whose characteristics have been described.
Having led the life-force (jīva) from the heart to the lotus of the mouth by means of the *haṃsa* mantra together with the life-force—
according to such statements from the previously cited *Kālīkulāmṛta* regarding the time [of death]— by means of that life-force which has been led from the *anāhata-cakra* to the *mūlādhāra*.

Together with the individual soul (*jīvātman*), having led [it] by means of the process of dissolution (*layakrama*) into the presence of the supreme Lord— either into the supreme Lord Śiva in the form of *Parabindu*, who is the highest master (*svāmin*), or into the proximity of that supreme Lord in the form of Paraśiva through the power of dissolution— he describes the station of the Lord by way of showing its attributes as "pure" (*śuddha*). His abode is the pure lotus, the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*).
The meaning is: "existing in such a state" refers to residing in the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*); likewise, "in the abode of liberation" means in the place that brings about liberation.
Regarding the upward movement of Kuṇḍalinī together with the individual soul (*jīvātman*), the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, in its fourth chapter, states:
"In conjunction with the intensified fire, by means of the mind together with the vital airs..."
"One should lead the supreme Kuṇḍalinī, together with the individual soul (jīvātman), upwards.
Having thus described the yoga of Kuṇḍalinī at the thousand-petaled lotus (sahasrāra), he explains the method of meditating upon her: "One should meditate," etc.

This means she is in the form of one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), who bestows desired fruits—that is, she grants the fruits one seeks—and she is the supreme [Kuṇḍalinī] in the form of the Supreme Bindu (para-bindu).

Or [one may meditate on her] as having the form of Paraśiva, and likewise as having the form of consciousness (*caitanya*). By this, it is implicitly stated that one should contemplate her non-differentiation from Śiva—who possesses the same forms—by way of her own nature as *parabindu* and her nature as consciousness. This is clearly stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, concerning Kuṇḍalinī:
"O Maheśānī, one should lead [the energy] from the mūlādhāra to the sahasrāra;
one should contemplate the supreme Śakti residing in Śambhu as being in a state of oneness.
There, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī in the form of one's chosen deity. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, it was stated in the root-text: "by virtue of dissolution. As for the method of upward extraction according to the sequence of dissolution:

having brought the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the *anāhata* wheel to the *kuṇḍalinī* situated within the cavity of the triangle inside the pericarp of the *mūlādhāra* lotus by means of the *haṃsa* mantra, [one dissolves] the seeds of Indra, Brahmā, Kāmadeva, and so forth, which reside in the aforementioned triangle, into the earth.

Having caused the earth to dissolve into the principle of smell (gandhatattva), which is its own cause, one should dissolve the individual soul (jīvātman), the Kuṇḍalinī, and the principle of smell into the Svādhiṣṭhāna by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. This is stated in the second chapter of the Kaṅkālamālinītantra concerning the Mūlādhāra lotus: [The text continues: ...the Mūlādhāra lotus... [as described].
O Goddess of gods, within its pericarp is a most beautiful triangle;
likewise, O Goddess of gods, one should contemplate the letter *laṃ* in that which is called the triangle. Having meditated upon Brahmā there, one should then meditate upon Kāmadeva.
Having spoken thus and so forth, [the Lord said]:
"O Mother Girijā, O Gaṇeśvarī, having brought these down to the earth,
O beloved, their center is in the form of a *liṅga* encircled by Kuṇḍalinī."
Having thus determined the essential nature of the self-arisen *liṅga* and the *kuṇḍalinī*,
O Maheśvarī, daughter of the Mountain King, one should lead the previously mentioned earth into the *gandha* [element] and then,
by means of the *praṇava* alone, draw forth the individual soul (*jīvātman*).

"Taking the vital breath (prāṇa) along with the fragrance together with Kuṇḍalinī, O Goddess, the practitioner should cause it to enter the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra] by means of the mantra 'So 'haṃ'. Regarding this statement, the instruction that the drawing-in is performed with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the raising is performed with "So 'haṃ" represents another tradition (*matāntara*); this is not [the present author's view].

That it is "approved by Pūrṇānanda" has been explained in detail in the commentary on the fifty-first verse, beginning with "the Goddess by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. Thus concludes the procedure for the upward movement of Kuṇḍalinī from the Svādhiṣṭhāna. Thereafter, [one should contemplate] the water-seed (*va*), Viṣṇu’s power (*śakti*), and so forth, situated within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) there, as well as water within water.

Having brought about the dissolution of the individual soul and Kuṇḍalinī into the *rasatattva* (the principle of taste), which is their own cause, one should dissolve that *rasatattva* into the *maṇipūra* cakra by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. As it is said in that very same work: "In its pericarp [one should contemplate] Varuṇa, and there also one should contemplate Hari."
O fair-faced one, having visualized the youthful Śakti Rākiṇī, [one should worship her].
O fair-faced one, having brought water located in the seat of the tongue-faculty, as well as desire and attachment,
and these along with fragrance and taste to Śiva;
O beloved, having led the individual soul, Kuṇḍalinī, and the vital essence into the Maṇipūraka through supreme yoga, that lotus has ten petals.
Thus ends the procedure for the upward movement to the Maṇipūra [cakra].

Then, having brought about the dissolution of the fire-seed (vahnibīja), Rudra, Lākinī, Śakti, and the rest— which shine within its pericarp— into the light, and that light into the principle of form (rūpatattva) which is their own cause, one [dissolves] that principle of form, the individual soul (jīvātman), and Kuṇḍalinī [into the next level].

One should dissolve [the object] into the *anāhata-cakra*. Regarding that, it is said in that very same place concerning the *anāhata-padmam*: "O lady of beautiful hips, the practitioner, having meditated upon fire within its pericarp, [should know that] Rudra himself is the agent therein for the withdrawal of all."
One should meditate upon that captivating [deity] as united with the power of Lākinī;
there, O Śivā, one should contemplate the sense organ of sight as consisting of radiant light.
"O fortunate one, O highly blessed one, having brought this essence into the form [of the *kuṇḍalinī*],
one should lead the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the form of the *kuṇḍalinī* into the *anāhata* [cakra].
Thus ends the procedure for the upward movement to the *anāhata*.

Then, having brought about the dissolution of the Lord of the Seed-Syllable of Air (vāyubījeśvara), Kākinī, Śakti, and the others— residing within the pericarp of the Anāhata-cakra— into the element of Air, and [having dissolved] that Air into the principle of Touch (sparśatattva), one should dissolve that principle of Touch, the individual soul (jīvātman), and Kuṇḍalinī into the aforementioned Viśuddha-cakra.
This is stated in that very same work concerning the Anāhata-cakra:
In its pericarp is Vāyu, who dwells in the abode of the individual soul (jīva);
there also is the circle of the womb, adorned with the Bāṇa-liṅga.
"O Malakāriṇī, having joined these— the Kākinī conjoined with Śakti, Vāyu, and the sense of touch— with Form (rūpa), place the Jīva, Kuṇḍalinī, and Touch into Viśuddhi. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the procedure for the elevation of the pure wheel (*viśuddhacakra*).
Following this, [one should contemplate] the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*), Sadāśiva, and Śākinī, situated within the pericarp of this sixteen-petaled lotus;
[furthermore, one should effect the descent of Kuṇḍalinī back to the *mūlādhāra* and the satiation of one’s chosen deity with the flow of nectar].
Having drunk from Paraśiva that supreme nectar which has the hue of lac, the beautiful Kuṇḍalinī then enters the root through the path of Kula by virtue of the great arising of full bliss;
with a steady mind, she should satiate the deity with that stream of divine nectar.
The yogi [perceives] that which resides within the vessel of the cosmic egg, known through the lineage of yoga. || 54 ||

Having brought about the dissolution of Śakti and the others into space, and the dissolution of space into the principle of sound (śabdatattva), one should dissolve that subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), as well as the individual soul (jīvātman) and Kuṇḍalinī, into the aforementioned Ājñācakra. As it is said in that very same work concerning the Viśuddha [cakra]: "In its pericarp are space and Śiva, joined with Śākinī."
Having established both speech and hearing in space, O daughter of the mountain.
"O Śaṅkarī, my beloved, having brought these [elements] to touch and sound,
one should place the life-force (jīva), Kuṇḍalinī, and the sound into the Ājñācakra.
Thus ends the procedure for the upward movement through the Ājñācakra.

Then, having brought about the dissolution of all others—the Śiva, Hākinī, Śakti, and so forth—residing within the pericarp of the *ājñācakra* into the mind, one should lead the individual soul (*jīvātman*), the *kuṇḍalinī*, and the mind to the *sahasrāra*.
As it is said in that very same [text]: "O Maheśvarī, [one should lead] the individual soul, the *kuṇḍalinī*, and the mind as well."

"One should also apply the mind to the thousand-petaled great lotus. Thus, here is the sequence of dissolution (*layakrama*): the essence of the word as explained by etymology (*nirukta-śabdatattva*) is to be dissolved into the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego into the Great Principle (*mahattattva*); the Great Principle into the subtle primordial nature (*prakṛti*) known as Hiraṇyagarbha; and that [nature] into the Supreme Bindu (*parabindu*). As it has been said:
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa* cited in Kālīcaraṇa’s commentary on the *Ṣaṭcakra*:

"In the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), he takes away space along with sound; that [space] also in the Great Principle (*mahat*). And the Great Principle in the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the cause of all powers, which is supreme."

"One should contemplate that everything, from earth onwards in due order, is dissolved therein— that supreme Vaiṣṇava cause which is of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. Thus, it follows that for all things, beginning with earth and including those dependent upon them, their dissolution occurs into their respective causes.

Furthermore, he describes the descent of Kuṇḍalinī from the *sahasrāra* to the *mūlādhāra*: "having the luster of lac" (*lākṣābham*). Then that Kuṇḍalinī, having drunk the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*)—which possesses a color like lac—from Paraśiva, [she does so] because of the great arising of eternal bliss (*nityānandamahodayāt*), wherein there is a great emergence of eternal bliss.

From that state, "from that path of the family" (*kulapathāt*), the ablative case is used in the sense of eliding the suffix *lyap*. Having reached the path leading to the previously described thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*),

she enters— that is, she penetrates— once again into the root, her own abode in the form of the *mūlādhāra* cakra, by the very same sequence through which she had previously gone to the thousand-spoked wheel.
The meaning is that, having returned in sequence, it remains encircling the *svayambhū-liṅga* in the form of three and a half coils.
This is clearly stated in the fourth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, concerning the *sahasrāra*:
"O Supreme Goddess, there resides Sadāśiva Mahādeva."
Having gone there, the Great Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the Supreme Deity, [resides].
The Goddess Rūpavatī, who sports in the exhilaration of desire,
gladdened the supreme Śiva with the fragrance of her lotus-like face.
Having awakened her, O Supreme Goddess, one should dwell above that, O Beloved;
for Kuṇḍalinī, O Śivā, kisses the lotus-face of Śiva.
O Goddess of gods, O Beloved, Sadāśiva may sport for even a single moment;
O Supreme Goddess, at that very instant, nectar is produced, O Goddess.
O Goddess, the nectar arising from that is like the juice of lac;
with that nectar, O Mistress of the Gods, one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
Having satiated the deities of the six chakras there with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should bring [the nectar] back to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
Thus, the sequence of the descent of Kuṇḍalinī from the Sahasrāra to the Mūlādhāra is also clearly demonstrated in that very place:
having described the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī beginning with "Always [visualize her] sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts," and so forth.
Having meditated thus, O Śivā, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
having recited the Mātṛkā-mālā, one should bring it to the Ājñā-cakra.
There, one should unite the supreme Kuṇḍalinī with the other Śiva-liṅga;
having meditated upon her there as consisting of Brahman, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, having led her into purification, one should unite her with Śiva;
meditating upon that chosen deity, O beloved, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having led her into the heart-lotus, one should unite her with the arrow;
meditating upon her in the form of the Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having led her to Maṇipūra, one should unite her with Śiva;
meditating upon her in the form of the Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having led her to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, one should unite her with Śiva;
having united them, O Priyaṃvadā, one should recite the mantra while meditating upon the Goddess.
(The Fruit of Knowledge of the Sequence of the Six Chakras): Having understood this supreme sequence with a restrained mind, the yogi, joined in meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
[attains the goal] through the arising of the flow of fragrance from the pair of lotus feet of the venerable initiation-guru.

In this cycle of existence, he is never born, nor does he ever perish; at the time of dissolution, he is tranquil, the foremost among the virtuous, and delighted by a succession of perfect bliss. || 55 ||
(The fruit of studying this section on the six chakras:

The yogi who, established in his own true nature, studies this stainless, pure, and well-guarded sequence— the primary cause for the door to liberation— during the night, at the two twilights, or during the day;
The mind of one whose inner thoughts are fixed upon the pair of lotus feet of the glorious and venerable Guru will surely dance with joy at the station of his chosen deity. (56)
[Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Yoga," in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the Paramahaṃsa Śrīpūrṇānanda. || 6 ||
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should lead it to the *mūlādhāra*.

There, one should meditate upon the self-manifested (*svayambhū*) Liṅga, radiant like a jasmine flower, and so forth. Regarding the statement "that," he describes the satiation of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) by means of the stream of nectar produced by the aforementioned method: "with a steady mind" refers to the practice of the yoga described above.

The meaning is that the yogin, distinguished by firm conviction, should satisfy the deity—the chosen goddess—with that previously mentioned stream of divine nectar, whose nature has been experienced through uninterrupted practice of yoga and which is known through the succession of yogas. He qualifies the deity by stating "situated within the vessel of the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍabhāṇḍe*); the "vessel" (*bhāṇḍa*) of the cosmic egg means its receptacle, which is in the form of the womb (*yoni*).
The meaning is that Kuṇḍalinī is situated there.

Having thus described the procedure of the six cakras, he states the fruit of that knowledge: "Having known," etc. A yogin who is joined with, or devoted to, samādhi—having attained [this state] through service to that stream of fragrance which exists in the pair of lotus-feet of the venerable Dīkṣā-guru—[attains the goal].

From the arising of that succession of the bliss of Brahman-knowledge, having understood this sequence—the aforementioned method—one is not born, nor is one produced, within saṃsāra; even at the time of dissolution, during the period of cosmic destruction, one is not destroyed. Through the succession of eternal bliss, by means of the experience of the bliss of the nature of Brahman as a continuous flow, he becomes tranquil and the foremost among the virtuous.

He states the fruit of studying this section on the six cakras with the words "he who has studied": he whose nature is to take refuge in the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Śrī Guru; likewise, he whose inner mind is restrained—that is, one whose mind is restrained within the inner self—and who is such a yogi, established in his own nature, meaning one whose being is situated in his own Self—at night.
Whether at night during the two twilights— morning and evening— or by day, for that yogi who studies this exposition of yoga, which is the cause for opening the door to liberation,
his mind dances within the state of his chosen deity, the feet of his own beloved divinity. The meaning is that, through the power of this yoga,
by beholding the true form of his own chosen deity, his consciousness attains an exceeding degree of joy therein.

[The Seventh Chapter] (The characteristics of sacrificial pits, their classifications, the nature of the girdles and other features, the different types of pits according to the distinction of castes, the procedure for performing oblations on a leveled mound when it is impossible to construct a pit, and the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.)
(Declaration of the description of the nature of the sacrificial pits) I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pits according to the tantras. (The square pit)
Then, one should mark it all around with a cord measuring one cubit.
Having divided it into four squares, one should drop the diagonal cords;
thus the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) becomes a square that bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 2 ||
In the fifth chapter,

by the statement "Then the wise mantra-practitioner should fashion the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) to his own right" (5.109), the construction of the pit has been indicated; now, its specific form is described with the words beginning "Of the pits," and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the word *kuṇḍa*, the *Viśvasāra* as cited in the *Tantrasāra* states:
"O Goddess, on the earth (*kau*) a beautiful cavity (*vila*) is seen; therefore it is called *kuṇḍa* for the benefit of practitioners. Thus it is said.
Regarding the description of the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) to be discussed there:
"Indeed, all pits, such as the *yoni* and others, arise from the square (*caturasra*).
By this statement from the *Siddhāntaśekhara* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, [it is established that] in another tantra, in the twenty-ninth chapter, the square pit is [the basis].
Having proceeded [with the description], it is stated:
"In that regard, I shall describe other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to you according to their measurements.
By this statement, since the square nature of the other sacrificial pits is declared, the first [pits described] is the square sacrificial pit.
He characterizes [it] with the words "one cubit" and so forth. "On all sides" means in the four directions. "Consisting of four compartments" refers to the aforementioned *yonikuṇḍa*:
having divided the field into five parts, one part is [set aside] in the east.
One should place [the marks] upon that thread, extending from the sides up to the middle.
Then, one should rotate the pair of lines directed westward from each of those respective half-measures,
individually and correctly, as far as the three corners.
When it is done in this way, the established pit (kuṇḍa) becomes like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
A pit facing north, known as the "womb" (yoni), bestows spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 5 ||
(The triangular pit: A wise person should draw a cord thirty-two finger-breadths long all around,
so that it takes the form of a triangle with its face toward the east, as previously described.
The triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhis).
(For the circular pit: Having divided that area into eighteen parts, one should cast one part outwards;
then, having fixed a cord in the center, one should rotate [the circle] using that measurement as the radius.
Then the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be circular and facing the east, which is unsurpassed.

The meaning is that one should draw one line from the center of the square toward the western end and another line from the north toward the southern end. When this is done, four compartments are produced. Regarding the "corner-lines," the meaning is that there are two lines: one from the southeast (āgneya) to the northwest (vāyavya), and another from the northeast (aiśāna) to the southwest (nairṛta). The digging will be described later.

Regarding the *yoni-kuṇḍa*, he says: "The field. Here too, having prepared a square as before, one should divide that field into five parts; this is the meaning. In that case, the division into five parts should be made specifically of the northern portion of the line cast from south to north. This was stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "In that regard, regarding the division of the entire area of the field..."
Because there is no purpose [for dividing the middle line], only the middle sūtra should be divided.

Regarding the phrase "in that field": having divided the previously mentioned field made into a square into eighteen parts, one should cast one of those eighteen parts outside; the meaning is that one should place it all around the outside of the circle to be drawn.

"One should rotate" means: having placed a thread at the center of the aforementioned field— that is, in the middle region equal to that— the thread should be rotated by that measurement from the aforementioned seventeen parts [to form the] half-moon-shaped *kuṇḍa*.
Having divided the field into ten parts, one should discard them in order from top to bottom;
then, one should assign one [part] each to the left and right corners.
Having laid down two cords according to the measurement and a cord for the chord as it should be,
one should then drop a single cord from the middle of those up to the end of the upper measurement.
One should rotate it by that same measure so that it forms a half-moon;
for the purpose of killing, this is always recommended when facing south, while [the other] is for facing north.
(Padmakuṇḍa) Having raised up the circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa),
the practitioner should fashion three circles from the center; however, in the first portion, he should place the pericarp (karṇikā).
The best of teachers should fashion the filaments outside of that, the centers of the petals outside of those, and the tips of the eight petals outside of those.
Having drawn the pericarp with a height of three finger-breadths, one should then bury it;
the lotus-pit (padmakuṇḍa) is said to have its filaments in the lower portion.
(The Procedure for Digging the Kuṇḍas): I shall describe the digging of the kuṇḍas according to the tantras.
One should cause a beautiful excavation to be made measuring fifteen aṅgulas. (14)
The meaning is that one should rotate [the cord] inside the eighteen parts situated on the exterior. This is clearly stated in the *Vaśiṣṭhasaṃhitā* cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having divided the field made into a square into eighteen parts..."
"Having set aside one part outside, one should rotate [the cord] with that to form a circle.
(In the case of quadrangular and other types of fire-pits, the girdles (*mekhalā*) also possess the same shape as the pits; whatever the form of the pits, such is the form of the girdles. 15.
(Resolution on the Girdle) A wise man should fashion the girdle leaving one finger-breadth from the neck;
he should increase it accordingly for a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit.
For others, it extends up to ten cubits, with each [subsequent part] increasing by half a finger-breadth individually.
(The height of the girdles:
Here, the height of the principal girdle is stated to be nine finger-breadths;
the height of the outer girdle is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths.
The height of its outer girdle should be two finger-breadths. || 17 ||
(Vistāraḥ) The auspicious girdles should be made with a width equal to one-fourth of the altar's breadth. || 18 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the *kuṇḍas*": it should be understood that in this manner, the sequence of the girdles (*mekhalā*) in each respective case is to be determined—namely, that in a square *kuṇḍa* the girdle is square, in a triangular *kuṇḍa* it is triangular, and in a circular *kuṇḍa* it is circular.
He states the location of the girdles with the word "neck" (*kaṇṭha*); the neck, however, is that which lies all around between the *kuṇḍa* and the girdle.

The term *pradeśa* refers to this. Thus, the meaning is that one should construct the girdle (*mekhalā*) after leaving a space of one finger-breadth all around the exterior of the neck (*kaṇṭha*), which has been defined as such. This is the rule for a pit (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit; however, in the case of two-cubit pits and larger, the neck increases by half an inch at each successive stage.

Previously, by the passage beginning with "whatever the form of the pits (*kuṇḍas*) was," it was established that the girdles (*mekhalās*) have the same shape as the pits. Now, he states their height: "The primary... and so forth. There are three girdles;
among them, the height of the first is nine finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*), of the second five finger-breadths, and of the third two finger-breadths.
The meaning of the commentary:

Having stated the height of the girdles (*mekhalā*), he states their width with the words "Vedas and fires" (*vedāgni*). Thus, the first [girdle] is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width, the second is three finger-breadths in width, and the third is two finger-breadths in width; such is the meaning.

In this regard, the following should be noted: by the statement "the excavation is fifteen finger-breadths [in depth]," etc., the fifteen-finger-breadth dimension of the excavation is established; [this constitutes] the primary [method], while [the subsequent passage] provides an alternative procedure for making the excavation.
Alternatively, a pit measuring twelve finger-breadths should be dug. || 19 ||
(Therein, the distinctions regarding the measurements of the girdles:
The auspicious girdles are twelve, eight, and four *pramāṇāṅgula*s [in height]; all the girdles are four *aṅgula*s wide. || 20 ||
(An alternative sequence for the altar and the girdle:
Now, in the case of a single girdle, one should dig [the pit] to a depth of eight digits (aṅgulas).
The girdle should be four digits wide and six digits high.

The height of the girdle (*mekhalā*) is also taught to be nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Thus, by combining the fifteen-finger-breadth depth of the pit (*kuṇḍakhāta*) with the nine-finger-breadth height of the girdle, it is established that, in ultimate reality, the pit measures twenty-four finger-breadths.
And so it is said:
"One should dig downwards as deep as the width of the pit, making it level.
By this statement from the *Saurakāṇḍa* of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*, cited in the *Vaidikasarvasva*,

which states that the depth of the excavation should be equal in measure to the width of the pit, it is understood that this refers to its being equal to the measurement of the primary girdle (*mekhalā*).

This has been clearly stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, which upholds the entire essence of the Vedic tradition: "The measurement of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should include the excavation together with the upper girdle (*mekhalā*).
The same applies elsewhere as well.

He states another alternative regarding the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the girdle (*mekhalā*) with the words "it should be made. Thus, according to this alternative, the pit of the *kuṇḍa* is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in measure, and the primary girdle is also twelve finger-breadths in measure;
by combining these two measures of the pit and the girdle, [the total becomes twenty-four finger-breadths].

It should be understood that the depth of the pit (*khāta*) is established as being equal in measurement to the width of one cubit (*hasta*). In this ritual manual (*kalpa*), the primary girdle (*mekhalā*) is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height, the second is eight finger-breadths in height, and the third is four finger-breadths in height.
As for the width, however, it is four finger-breadths for all three girdles; thus, the result is that there is no variation in the measurement of width as there was previously.
It is stated clearly in that very same [text]:
"The first [altar] should be made beautiful, four finger-breadths high;
the second eight finger-breadths, and the third twelve finger-breadths."
"One should make the width of all [the enclosures] four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*). Thus it is said.

Regarding the procedure for digging and so forth in a *kuṇḍa* with a single girdle (*mekhalā*), he says "Now" (*atha*). Here, one should dig to a depth of eighteen finger-breadths (*aṣṭādaśāṅgula*)—that is, the measure of the "elephant-ender" direction (*gajāntaka-dig-aṅgula*). The height of the girdle is six finger-breadths, and its width is four finger-breadths.
(An alternative ritual for constructing the sacrificial pit:
Alternatively, one may indeed dig every sacrificial pit measuring exactly one cubit.
For a pit of one cubit, it is taught that starting from two cubits and so forth, the depth of the excavation should be stated to be equal to the width of the pit.
(Regarding the girdle:
Five girdles should indeed be made with [the widths of] five, six, four, three, and two [finger-breadths].
(Regarding the alternative options therein:)
Alternatively, it should be made threefold, measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
Alternatively, a single girdle provided with three, four, or two finger-breadths [in width] is proclaimed as superior, middling, and inferior, respectively. || 25 ||
(The variations in the dimensions of the girdles according to the variations in the dimensions of the fire-pits:
In a fire-pit measuring one fist, [the girdles] are measured at two, one, and half an aṅgula;
but in a fire-pit measuring one aratni, they are increased by three, two, and one aṅgula respectively. || 26 ||
He states another alternative with the words "or else" (*athavā*). "Single" (*ekā*) means this sequence pertains to a pit (*kuṇḍa*) of one cubit;
"two cubits" (*dvihasta*) means the sequence is proclaimed for [pits] of two cubits and so forth. To the question "What then is that?", he says "as far as" (*yāvat*) and so on.
Here he states the threefold method for the girdle (*mekhalā*), beginning with "the girdles. Therein, in order, six, five—

One view is that there are five girdles measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively. Alternatively, another view is that there are three girdles measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths in sequence. Or yet another is that there is a single girdle measuring four finger-breadths. Regarding the term "supreme": therein, the first option of five girdles is supreme; the second option of three girdles is middling; and the third option of a single girdle is inferior—this is the meaning.

Now, he demonstrates the different measurements of the girdles (*mekhalā*) according to the different measurements of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), beginning with the words "measured by a fist" and ending with "by the wise in all cases. Regarding the phrase "measured by a fist": here, the primary girdle is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) wide, the second is one finger-breadth, and the third is half a finger-breadth; it is the same for the others as well. Regarding the phrase "measured by a cubit (*aratni*)": they are measured at three, two, and one finger-breadths respectively.
In a pit measuring one cubit, the girdles are four, three, and two finger-breadths wide;
in a pit of two cubits, they are six, four, and three finger-breadths wide.
In a four-cubit [stūpa], the girdles (mekhalā) are to be known as measuring eight, six, and four aṅgulas;
however, in a six-cubit [stūpa], they are to be measured by ten, eight, and six aṅgulas.

In a sacrificial pit measuring eight cubits, the girdles (mekhalās) should be known by the wise to be respectively twelve, sixteen, and twenty finger-breadths in height and width; in a ten-cubit pit, they should be fifteen, twenty, and twenty-five finger-breadths, respectively, on all sides.
(Now, the Yoni: In the western part of the pit, the wise [practitioner] should fashion a well-characterized yoni in the center, either in the shape of an aśvattha leaf or triangular. || 30 ||
One should make it possess a length, width, and height of six, four, and two finger-breadths respectively; the tip of the yoni should be one finger-breadth wide and slightly turned downward.
The *yoni* of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *muṣṭi*, one *ratni*, and one *hasta* is thus described.
(3|2|1) "One" refers to four, three, and two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). (4|3|2) Regarding the "girdle" (*mekhalā*): it consists of six, four, and three finger-breadths. (6|4|3) Regarding "four":

it is endowed with eight, six, and four finger-breadths. (8|6|4) In the case of six *hasta* (six-cubit) pits, [the measurements] are ten, eight, and six finger-breadths. (10|8|6) Regarding "eight": [the sequence follows]. (8...)
"By twelve, ten, and eight [units]" (-) (12|10|8); "ten cubits" means "endowed with fourteen, twelve, ten fingers" (-) (14|12|10).
By this, the traditionalists maintain that the arrangement of the girdles (*mekhalā*) for the medium size of every *kuṇḍa* has been demonstrated.
Having defined the girdle, he defines the vulva (*yoni*), saying "of the *kuṇḍa*": this is the vulva of the *kuṇḍa*.

It should be made upon the western girdle (*mekhalā*). This is stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradā*: "In front of the Hotṛ priest, the vulva (*yoni*) of these [girdles] is above, like an *aśvattha* leaf.
"Of these" refers to the girdles.

"Six": in this ritual manual (*kalpa*), the meaning is that the length of the womb (*yoni*) is six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the width is four finger-breadths, and the height is two finger-breadths. However, another ritual manual will be explained later.
(The specific details regarding sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits and so forth.)
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the width of the vulva (yoni) by one finger-breadth for each successive pit.
One should likewise extend the tip of the vulva by a distance of two barley grains.
(Another method for making the womb-vessel: Alternatively, the wise one may prepare the womb-vessel in another manner:
twelve finger-breadths in length and likewise eight finger-breadths in width. 34.
The practitioner of mantras should fashion the womb (yoni); its tip should be two finger-breadths wide. One should increase the measurement up to ten cubits in sequence, as previously described.
The stalk from the rear of the womb is four finger-breadths long and possesses a cavity;
its width at the base and tip is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively.

Since no specific measurement is mentioned for the "twelve," it should be understood here as well that the height is two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*). This is clearly stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The yoni is twelve finger-breadths in width and [twelve] long finger-joints (*dīrghārka-parvan*) in length."
Her elevation is two finger-breadths; (........................................).

Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should make the womb (*yoni*) three parts wide at its center, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, and twelve parts high, with a small cavity for the insertion of the jar. Thus.

"Twelve parts high" means it should be two *aṅgulas* in height. Regarding this, the *Śāradātilaka*, in its third chapter, states that a hole must be made in the center of the womb (*yoni*) within the described base: "Starting from the surface, there should be a stalk; the center of the *yoni* must have a perforation."
Regarding the phrase "the stalk (*nāla*) is said [to be] by way of the womb": "from root to tip" means from the base up to the top;

the connection is that it is intended to have a width of three, two, and one finger-breadths respectively. Thus, the meaning is that the base of the stalk is three finger-breadths wide, the middle is two finger-breadths, and the tip is one finger-breadth.
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"To the west of the yoni, the stalk (*nāla*) should be four finger-breadths in length;
its width is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively, tapering toward the tip."
The location and other details regarding the *nāla* (tube) are clearly stated in the *Narapati-jayacaryā-vimarṣiṇī*, as cited in the *Vaidikasarvasva-ṭippanī*:
"(Regarding the *nābhi*:
one should cast a lotus-like *nābhi* within the *kuṇḍa*, or [one that] has the form of the *kuṇḍa* itself."
The navel of those whose hands possess a single jewel-muṣṭi is due to its state of elevation. || 37 ||
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the wise one of noble intellect should increase [the measurements] by two or three finger-breadths,
and likewise increase the navel by a sequence of two barley-corns for each.
(Regarding the avoidance of the yoni and the navel in the yoni-pit and the lotus-pit:
One should avoid the yoni in the yoni-pit, and one should avoid the navel in the lotus-pit. || 39 ||
(The sequence for the emanation from the navel:
Having divided the locus of the navel into three parts, the wise one should draw the pericarp in the central portion and eight petals in the two outer sections. (40)
The area situated outside the girdles is called the *sthalam* (platform). The *nāla* (stalk) is square, originates from the *sthalam*, and has a perforation in its center.
"The stalk should be thick at the base and fine at the tip, and it should be beautiful;
one should fashion it starting from the outer surface of the external girdle.
Here, having constructed an altar (*vedi*) four finger-breadths in height and width, with six external girdles (*mekhalā*), one places the stalk upon it.
"One should place [the fire]," says Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Regarding the creation of the opening for the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) upon the second girdle (*mekhalā*), the *Vaidikasarvasva* states:
"To the west of the womb (*yoni*), the tube (*nāla*) should be six finger-breadths in length."

"The wise man should then make a cavity above the second girdle for the purpose of placing the enclosing stick (paridhi) between the two girdles. Regarding the phrase "within the pit" (kuṇḍāntaḥ): the meaning is that the navel (nābhi) should be made measuring six, four, or two finger-breadths (aṅgula). In the case of the measure of a fist (muṣṭi)—
The meaning is that the height of the navel is two *aṅgulas* in the measurement of the *ara*, three *aṅgulas* in the measurement of the *ratni*, and four *aṅgulas* in the measurement of the *hasta*.
However, in other cases, there is an increase of two *yavas*.
The meaning is that one should not construct the aforementioned *yoni* in a *yonikuṇḍa*, nor a *nābhi* in a *padmakuṇḍa*.
(The distinction of the sacrificial pit according to the number of oblations:
For fifty [oblations], it should be the measure of one fist; for one hundred, the measure of an aratni;
for one thousand, the measure of one cubit; and likewise for ten thousand, two cubits.
(The sequence for increasing the size of the sacrificial pit): By extending the measurement of the corner-cord of a one-cubit pit on all sides, that pit shall become two cubits in size.
In this very manner, the wise person should cause all of that to increase.
(Regarding that, another sequence:
Now, another view from the Toḍalatantra is being proclaimed. (44)
In a pit measuring one cubit (hastamātra) on all sides, one should increase it by four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula);
by that measure, it is declared to be two cubits (dvihasta).
(Regarding the dimensions of the sacrificial pit according to the different types of *homa*, such as the *lakṣa* and others:
In a *lakṣa-homa*, the pit is four cubits; in a *daśalakṣa-homa*, it is six cubits;
in a *koṭi-homa*, it is eight cubits, and likewise ten cubits.
(In that regard, another alternative:
Or else, one may have it made at one cubit for one hundred thousand [repetitions],
and likewise increase it by one cubit for every ten hundred thousand, up to ten million.
Beyond ten cubits, there is no sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in any of the scriptures whatsoever.
(The defect resulting from a deviation from the prescribed measurements of the pit: If the pit is larger than specified, one becomes ill; if smaller, there is loss of wealth.
In a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken boundary line (*mekhalā*), death occurs.
(The nature of the sacrificial pit as being the very form of one's chosen deity:
One should know the form of the sacrificial pit to be the supreme body of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (50)
The head should be in the east, and the arms in the south and north respectively;
the fire-pit is said to be the belly, and the feet are in the west.
(The differences in results based on the squareness and other characteristics of the fire-pit):
A square pit is the cause for peace, prosperity, nourishment, and growth;
a Yoni-shaped pit bestows speech, while a Bhaga-shaped pit effects attraction.
The circular [mandala] bestows prosperity; it consists of three half-moons and is known as Padma. It is the cause of all wealth and bestows nourishment. || 53 ||

(The differences in sacrificial pits according to the distinction of caste: A square pit is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, and a circular one is considered suitable for kings; a semi-circular pit is for merchants, while a triangular one is for those born of the Śūdra class.
(Regarding the square fire-pit as common to all castes, there is another opinion:
Some teachers say that for all [castes], the [pit] is square. (55)
(The fault of being devoid of a girdle and other ornaments: Indeed, in the case of one devoid of a girdle, there is grief; if it is excessive, there is loss of wealth.
A *kuṇḍa* fashioned without a *yoni* is said to bring about the destruction of one's wife.
A *kuṇḍa* that is devoid of a neck is declared to cause the destruction of one's offspring. (56)
(Regarding the performance of the fire-oblation on a sacrificial mound when the construction of a fire-pit is impossible:
One should perform the daily or occasional fire-oblation on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 57 ||
The meaning is that the *candra-ardha-tritaya* refers to the half-moon-shaped pit (*ardhacandrakuṇḍa*) and the triangular pit (*tryasrakuṇḍa*).

Regarding the word "always" (*nityam*), the meaning is that one may perform the rite on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) when the construction of a pit is impossible. The definition of the sacrificial mound is stated in the third chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*:
(The Characteristics of the *Sruk* and *Sruva*) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva*. (58)
The Guru, having taken one of the trees— either *śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or *kṣīri*—
should divide it into thirty-six parts, each measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in length.
The *daṇḍa* shall consist of twenty parts; the *vedi* shall be made with eight of those parts.
The *kaṇṭha* is measured by one part, and the *mukha* is measured by seven parts.
The width of the neck is proclaimed to be one-third of the altar;
the mouth should be equal to the neck, and one should fashion the mouth-passage for the exit of the clarified butter with the measurement of a little finger (kaniṣṭhā). || 61 ||
"One should make that very beautiful [altar] out of sand, measuring one cubit [in area],
four-cornered on all sides, and endowed with a height of one finger-breadth.
Having thus described the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he promises to explain the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in due order:
Now, therefore:
"Thirty-six" means that the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) should be known to be thirty-six finger-breadths long, reaching to the length of the arm, and resembling a plantain flower.

Thus, by the scriptural statement cited in the *Vaidikasarvasva*, it is taught that "the measure of the *sruks* is the length of a forearm. Accordingly, one should divide a piece of wood—such as *khadira* or another specified type—that measures exactly one forearm, into thirty-six parts;
of these, twenty parts constitute the shaft (*daṇḍa*), eight parts the bowl (*vedikā*), and one part the neck (*kaṇṭha*).

"One should fashion the mouth with seven parts. When this is done, there will be an inclusion of thirty-six portions within it. Regarding the width of the neck and so forth, he says: "by one-third of the altar" (*vedītryaṃśena*); the meaning is "by one-third of the aforementioned altar. "Equal to the neck" means consisting of one part out of the three parts of the altar-base (*vedikā*). "The mouth" is for the exit of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) to be offered.

One should fashion the path for the exit of the oblation at the mouth according to the measurement of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhāṅguli*). The meaning is that such an aperture must be made in the mouth for the purpose of the exit of the oblation, so that the insertion of the little finger occurs therein.
This aperture is to be made with a heated iron rod; as it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The wise one should cause a passage below the neck for the exit of the clarified butter, and he should perform the piercing at the mouth with a heated iron probe. Thus it is said.
"The pericarp is to be fashioned in the center of the altar, occupying one part."
One should construct a pit all around it using one part of that [measurement] on the exterior. || 62 ||
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and outside by half a part;
one should arrange the petals all around with one part.
The molding (mekhalā) for the mouth-altar (mukhavedī) should be on all sides measuring half a part.
At the base and the tip of the staff (daṇḍa), there should be two pots (kumbhas) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively;
the gong (gaṇḍī) should be made with eight parts of the staff's width, which is declared to be the circumference of the staff.
The back portion of the altar (vedi) should be six parts wide and shaped like a tortoise.
He shows the procedure for the altar (*vedi*) and its enclosures (*mekhalā*) and so forth in the passage beginning with "in the middle of the altar" (*vedīmadhye*).
In the central region of the aforementioned altar, one part is for the pericarp (*karṇikā*); outside that, one part all around is for the hollow pit (*avaṭa* or *garta*);
outside that, three parts are for the excavation (*khāta*); outside that, half a part is for the circle (*vṛtta*); and outside that, one part all around is for the petals (*dala*).

The meaning is that one should fashion the girdle (*mekhalā*) at half the measure on all sides of the *nirukta* and the *mukha*. In this way, it follows that there is the pericarp (*karṇikā*) [1], the pit (*avaṭa*) [1], the excavation (*khāta*) [3], the circle (*vṛtta*) [½], the petals (*dalāni*) [1], and the girdle (*mekhalā*) [½].

Regarding the phrase "with the staff" (*daṇḍa*): "with the fingers of the qualities and the Vedas" means that at the base of the staff there is a jar (*kumbha*) measuring three fingers, and at the tip...
It is four finger-breadths [in thickness].
Regarding the term *gaṇḍī*: *gaṇḍī* refers to a ring-shaped encasement; he states its measurement as "by two parts of a *yama*.
The phrase "at the root and at the tip" should be understood here as a reference back to what was previously stated.

"The *gaṇḍī* at the base and the tip of the staff should be like a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*)," according to the statement of Somaśambhu cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa. Thus, the meaning is that there should be one *gaṇḍī* at the base of the staff occupying two parts, and another of the same dimension at the tip. He states the width of the staff with the words "of the staff."
The meaning is that the circumference—the width—of the staff is said to be six parts.
As it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The circumference of the middle of the staff is declared to be six finger-breadths.
One should draw the face of either a swan, an elephant, or a boar.
The characteristic of the back part of its mouth is thus described for the *sruk* ladle.
(The characteristics of the *sruva* ladle:
One should fashion the *sruva* from twenty-four parts;
its handle is declared to be measured by twenty-two parts. 66.
The swelling (ānāha) consists of four parts; its head, which receives the oil and ghee, is one karṣa.
One should bury it in the mud to the depth of two parts, shaped like the footprint of a deer.
At the base and the tip of the handle, two vessels should be fashioned as ornaments like bracelets;
the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle are declared to be exactly as previously described.
(The arrangement in their absence): But in the absence of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, another method is stated. || 69 ||
Regarding the phrase "of the swan": the connection is that one should draw [the mark] on the back part of the face of this *sruk* ladle. "Of the boar" refers to the *potrin*, the wild boar.
Having thus described the characteristics of the *sruk*, he describes the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle with the words "four... and so forth, referring to the *sruk* mentioned previously.
The meaning is that one should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts. The connection is that the measurement of the handle (*daṇḍa*) is by twenty-two parts.

"Circumference" (*ānāha*) means width. Regarding the word "karṣa": it consists of two parts; it is that which holds a *karṣa* of clarified butter—that is, it is suitable for receiving a *karṣa*-measure of clarified butter—and that is its head (*śiras*). The connection is that one should bury [the rest of the handle]. He states the measure of a *karṣa*:

Rāghavabhaṭṭa states: "Ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* are declared to be a *karṣa*. Regarding the term *paṅka*: his head is such that its shape is like the shape of a deer's footprint (*mṛgapada*) in the mud.

The connection [is as follows]: "In the scripture held as the very essence of the Vedas, the *sruva* ladle should be one cubit in length and provided with four corners, such that it always appears beautiful, like the hoof-print of a cow in soft mud. Thus it is said.
"And as before" means that this sequence for arranging the *kumbha-gaṇḍī* should be performed according to the previously established order of the *kumbha-gaṇḍī* fashioned with garlands.
The oblation is offered with two middle leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
Alternatively, when the rite of oblation is performed in brief with two leaves of the Aśvattha tree. || 70 ||
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the Paramahaṃsa Śrīpūrṇānanda. || 7 ||
[The Eighth Chapter] (The Procedure for Homa) (The Declaration of the Intention to Describe the Rules for Homa)
Now I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) according to the Śakti-tantras.
First, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), beginning with the inspection (vīkṣaṇa). (The eighteen purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit.
One should first cause the eighteen purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit to be performed. || 1 ||
One should perform the inspection with the root mantra; sprinkling is considered to be done with the arrow-mantra.
Striking is performed with that same [mantra], while sprinkling with *darbha* grass is considered to be done with the armor-mantra.
The excavation and the removal of the earth are performed with the Astra-mantra;
the filling [of the pit] and the leveling are likewise performed with the Hṛdaya-mantra and the Astra-mantra.
One should perform sprinkling with the armor mantra, pulverizing with the weapon mantra, and cleansing with the armor mantra; thereafter, one should perform the anointing.

Thus, having explained the section on the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the seventh [chapter], he now describes the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) in this [eighth] chapter: "Now" [he says]. And therein:
"In that sacrifice, one should consecrate the sacrificial pits with these aforementioned consecrations."

Since the necessity of performing the purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskāra*) is heard from such statements as the fifth chapter of the *Śāradātilaka*, he first describes those very rites [beginning with the word] "first" (*ādau*).

"With the root-mantra" (*mūlena*) means with the mantra to be given; "with the arrow" (*śareṇa*) means with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*); "with that very same arrow" (*tenaiva śareṇaiva*) means with that very same weapon-mantra.

Regarding the term *khananam* (digging): it is the extraction of earth, that is, the lifting up of the soil from the pit. *Pūraṇam* (filling) is the pouring of other earth into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Here, the connection is as follows: one should perform the digging and the extraction of the earth with the *astra-mantra*, and likewise, the filling with the *hṛdaya-mantra*—namely, the word "namaḥ"—and the leveling with the *astra-mantra*. This is clearly stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*:
In the fifth chapter,
one should likewise fashion the digits (kalās) of the Moon, Sun, and Fire;
and one should worship the formation of the three threads with the heart-mantra.
The transformation into a vajra is performed with the Astra-mantra and auspicious kusha grass using the Hṛdaya-mantra;
the form of the four-way intersection is the opening of the eyes by means of the Netra-mantra.
The Āvasathya fire should be in the middle part, and likewise the Āhavanīya fire to the east and the west; then the Anvāhārya fire is in the southern region.
Then, the knower of mantras should contemplate the Gārhapatya fire as a portion;
or else, he should gaze upon the fourfold [set] with the root mantra and with the Śara mantra.
Digging and lifting [the earth] are performed with the Astra-mantra; filling it is done with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
leveling is with the Astra-mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be with the Varma-mantra.

Regarding "sprinkling" (*secanam*): by means of the *heti-mantra* and the *astra-mantra*. "Washing" (*mārjanam*), "anointing" (*vilepanam*), "the conceptualization of the digits of the Moon, Sun, and Fire" (*somasūryānalakalākalpanam*), and "the triple-threading" (*trisūtrīkaraṇam*)—these four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are to be performed with the *varma-mantra*;
this is the resultant meaning. "Triple-threading" (*trisūtrīkaraṇam*) is the wrapping [of the thread] with three threads.

Regarding "vajrīkaraṇam" (the act of making into a vajra): by means of the *astra* mantra, *vajrīkaraṇa* is the making firm like a vajra. By means of the *hṛdaya* mantra, with auspicious *kuśa* grass, one should perform the rite consisting of the form of a crossroads—that is, the construction of four paths in the four directions. However, in the reading "catuṣpathaṃ bhāgarūpam," it means that which has the nature (*rūpa*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) of a division (*bhāga*), namely a partition (*vibhāga*).

One should construct a crossroads, but not a crossroads of any other kind; this is the meaning. By "with the eye" is meant [the mantra] *vauṣaṭ*; by this, there is the "cutting of the eyes," which is the opening of the sense organs.
And thus: (1) gazing, (2) sprinkling, (3) striking, (4) pouring over, and (5) digging.

(6) Removal of earth, (7) filling, (8) leveling, (9) sprinkling, (10) pounding, (11) sweeping, (12) smearing, (13) the conceptualization of the digits of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, (14) the drawing of the three lines, (15) worship, (16) the transformation into a vajra, and (17) the division of the four paths; (18) the removal of the axle— these are the eighteen purificatory rites of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Sprinkling and striking with Darbha grass, and sprinkling with the palm turned upwards;
these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are declared to be performed with the Kavaca mantra alone.
(The fire offering on a sacrificial mound):
Alternatively, the best of practitioners should perform the fire offering on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
which is a mandala made of sand with a height equal to the thumb and middle finger.
One should cause the site to be purified by smearing it with cow dung, making it square and one cubit in measure, and by performing the fourfold rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).

The wise one should draw three lines extending from west to east; each should be known to be one span in length, representing Mukunda, Īśa, and Indra. (These are the three lines with their tips pointing east. 12.
Regarding the inability to perform the eighteen consecrations (*saṃskāra*) as previously described, he states an alternative ritual consisting of a set of four consecrations:

"the tetrad. The word "tetrad" refers to the four consecrations; this is the ellipsis. He specifies that tetrad with the words "by means of the root [mantra]": namely, (1) gazing with the root mantra, (2) sprinkling with the *śara* mantra, and (3) striking with *darbha* grass by means of that same [mantra].
Sprinkling with the *varma* mantra (4). Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) means sprinkling over (*abhyukṣaṇa*). This is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā*:
"Alternatively, one should consecrate those [objects] by means of the four [purifications], beginning with visualization (*vīkṣaṇa*).
The *Tantrasāra* states this explicitly:
"Beholding with the root mantra, sprinkling with the *śara* [mantra] is prescribed;
striking with *darbha* grass using that same [mantra], and sprinkling with the *varma* [mantra] is prescribed.
Thus, the meaning is: "by means of the four [rites] beginning with beholding," as previously stated by the words "the fourfold," etc. And so it is.

The performance of the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is the primary rule; in its absence, the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) are performed there. On the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), however, only the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection are required.
(Three lines with their tips pointing north.)
With the heart-mantra itself,
one should draw three lines from south to north, representing Brahmā, Vaivasvata (Yama), and the Moon.
One should place the writing stylus there by joining the index finger and the thumb;
having gathered the dust from them, one should sprinkle it with the Praṇava.
(The sequence for the arrangement of the Yoga-pīṭha):
And the Yoga-pīṭha [should be made] with vermilion, camphor, and saffron, or with grain-flour, or with yellow pigment (*haridrā*) powder in the center. || 15 ||
Having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, and a square enclosure provided with doors, one should place a flower in the center of that with the *bālā* mantra. || 16 ||
He describes the sequence for the construction of the Yoga-pīṭha with the passage beginning with "And the Yoga-pīṭha" and ending with "one should deposit.
Although only the triangle and the hexagon are explicitly mentioned here, [the sequence is as follows]: first the triangle; outside of that, the hexagon;
outside of that, a circle; then an eight-petalled lotus; and then the outer square (bhūpura) provided with four gates, as stated in the root text.

The sequence should be understood as follows: "it must be written. Otherwise, the passage to be mentioned later—"the eight forms on the eight petals"—would not be logical, because there is not even a slight mention of the preparation of the petals prior to that. Therefore, what is stated here as "a triangle and a hexagon" is intended with the purpose of determining the *yogapīṭha* situated within the fire-diagram (*vahniyantra*). But in ultimate reality:

Beyond the six-cornered figure described in the *Nirukta*, the circles and other elements must also be drawn. This is clearly stated in the thirty-first chapter of the *Gandharva Tantra*, which sets forth the rules for fire-offerings (*homa*):
"Having first drawn three lines toward the south, immediately thereafter..."
And the lines shall have the nature of Vaivasvata, Brahmā, and Ananta.
Immediately following this, one should worship the *pīṭha* there according to the successive distinctions of the deities of the *pīṭhas*.
One should worship Maṇḍūka, Rudra, Ādhāra, Kūrma, and Śūkara.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in the cardinal directions of the seat (pīṭha), and those [four] preceded by A- in the corners above the seat. || 18 ||
(Yogapīṭhārcana) Then, the knower of mantras should again worship the Yogapīṭha with the Tāra mantra.
*Tāra*, *māyā*, *kāmeśī*, and *kāmeśvarayutā*, followed by *yogapīṭha* ending with *namo*: this is declared to be the *pīṭha-mantra*. || 20 ||
(Meditation on Kāmeśvarī):
In the center is the goddess, the mother, the mother of the universe, Kāmeśvarī, who is exceedingly mature and resembles a blue lotus. (21)
"O Goddess, having first drawn a triangle in the center, one should thereafter construct a most beautiful hexagon outside it according to the prescribed rule;
and outside that, an eight-petaled lotus with a beautiful pericarp [should be made] by means of a circle," and so forth.
With the Bālā mantra to be mentioned later—*bālayā ai klī sauḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "the unprecedented" (*apūrvān*): previously, *dharma*, *jñāna*, *vairāgya*, and *aiśvarya* were introduced. By the term "unprecedented," it refers to those [qualities] such as *dharma* and the rest which have the letter *a* as their prefix; [these are to be placed] in those corners.
It should be understood that by including the meaning "one should worship," the worship of Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya in the corners is taught;
[this is performed] with the *tāra*, which is the *praṇava*.
"Tāra" refers to the *praṇava* (Oṃ). "Māyā" is Hrīṃ. Thus, "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Yoga-pīṭha joined with Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī"—this is the meaning of the *pīṭha-mantra*.
Having meditated upon her as united with Kāmeśvara, one should worship her with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
One should worship Kāmeśī with the seed-syllable of Śakti and Kāmeśa with the mantra of the one to be accomplished (sādhya). || 22 ||
(Regarding the piling of the fire-altar:
It may be produced from the house of one learned in the Vedas, or born from a sun-crystal, or even produced from a fire-drill, and placed within a vessel of gold or other precious metal. (23)
The practitioner should bring it covered with a copper vessel or similar object;
or else, he should place what has been brought upon a bronze dish.
Therefore, the officiating priest should bring forth something by means of the seed-syllable of fire (vahnibīja). || 25 ||
(The fire-consecration:
