One should perform the inspection with the root mantra, carry out the protection with the weapon mantra, sprinkle with the armor mantra, and likewise perform the veiling. 26.
(Regarding the binding of the directions, etc.
Having performed the binding of the ten directions, one should display the *dhenumudrā*. || 27 ||
Having circumambulated the sacrificial pit three times from left to right while reciting the mantra,
one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyād) toward the southwest using the kūrca and the weapon-mantra.
(The subsequent duties: Afterwards, having transferred the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*), one should kindle the fire.
Regarding "from the south": having taken up the fire from one's own right side, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times.

This is the meaning. Regarding the term *kūrca*: by the word *tāra* (the "high-pitched" sound), the root mantra is to be understood as that which is being uttered. *Kūrca* is *hūṃ*, and the *astra* is *phaṭ*. Therefore, having recited the root mantra, [one says] *hūṃ phaṭ kravyādebhyaḥ svāhā*; this is the procedure for relinquishing the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*).
The authors of the *Tantrasāra* explain it in exactly this way.

Then, according to the principle of a lamp lighting another lamp, the knower of the mantra should worship [the deity] as it flashes forth in all directions through the path of the breath, while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Placing his knees on the ground and the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hūṃ*) from the fire [mantra],
he should cause the pure one to rise with this [mantra] ending in *ṅe namaḥ*.
(The Installation of the Fire):
With the thought that it is the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should cast the fire into its womb, facing oneself, within the previously mentioned mandala. 31.
(The kindling:
First with the *vyāhṛtis*, and afterwards with the fire-mantra, [forming] a circle:
"O Citpiṅgala, slay, slay; burn, burn; cook in two ways!"
"O Omniscient One, give your command, svāhā!"—with these words, the wise one should kindle the fire.
(Jvālinī Mudrā):
Having made the two wrists level and the hands with fingers extended,
having joined the two middle fingers, one should place the two thumbs in between them.
And the supreme practitioner should display this Jvālinī mudrā. || 33 ||

Regarding the word "at first" (*ādau*): here, having first uttered the circle together with the *vyāhṛtis*, one subsequently utters the fire-mantra (*vahnimantra*). By the use of the word "and" (*ca*) here, it is understood that the circle comes at the beginning of the fire-mantra as well. Thus, it results in the mantra for igniting the fire being: *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ cit piṅgala hana hana daha daha paca paca sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā*.
Regarding the specific procedure for kindling the fire, the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa states:

"Those who are about to offer oblations and those who have already offered into the fire should not blow upon the fire with their hands, winnowing baskets, or wooden ladles (*sruva*), nor should they do so with fans and the like."
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth.
(The worship of Agni:
"I revere Agni, the kindled one, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations."
Golden-colored, stainless, blazing, and facing in all directions. || 34 ||
Having thus performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) of the fire according to the injunctions of Manu, the wise one,
having uttered the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*), should worship the form of the Fire-god.

Having uttered the Bāla-mantra, one should write "Āṃ so'ham. Having uttered the fire-consciousness (vahnicaitanya), ending in the letter Ṅ and joined with the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu), one should contemplate the fire within the womb of Kāmeśvarī by means of this mantra. || 36 ||
(Throwing the fuel stick: Having silently cast into the fire a fuel stick of the length of a span, smeared with ghee at both its base and tip;
(The placement of the deities and others upon the tongues of the fire):
One should place the deities upon the tongue. || 37 ||

The deities, the ancestors, the gandharvas, yakṣas, pannagas, piśācas, and rākṣasas should be assigned by the practitioners to these [parts] respectively: to their own characteristic marks, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, the eyes, and the limbs. (38)
Regarding "the seed-syllable of desire" (*kāmabīja*): thus, the sequence of worship is *klīṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*.
Regarding "the Bālā-mantra": thus, one should contemplate Vahni within the womb of Kāmeśvarī with the mantra *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ āṃ so'haṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ*. This is the meaning.
"Silently" means: having silently offered a fuel-stick (*samidh*) the size of a span (*prādeśa*) into the fire.

"Upon the tongue" means: upon the seven tongues of the fire, such as Hiraṇyā and so forth, which are to be described later. One should install the deities. He states those very [deities]—(the installation of deities in the six limbs):

Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—these are the names mentioned. A wise person should apply these, ending in the dative case, sequentially to the six limbs. || 39 ||
(The assignment of deities to the eight limbs of Agni):
Thereafter, one should assign the eight forms [of Śiva] in sequence, preceded by the Praṇava;
everywhere, along with Agni, one should assign the mantra of Jātavedas.
One should also place Saptajihva, Havyavāha, and Aśvodara; then Vaiśvānara and Kaumāratejas; and Viśvamukha and Devamukha—one should assign these [deities] to these locations. (41)
One should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the head, the right shoulder, the side, the hip, the left anus, its region, and the side-part. 42.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the deities" (*devatā*): "in these" means in the seven limbs, namely the private organ, the anus, the head, and so forth; the meaning is that one should install these deities in these [limbs]. And thus, according to the tradition: having first installed the seven tongues in the seven limbs such as the linga, one should then install the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) upon those tongues.

He describes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities upon the limbs of the Fire-god with the mantra beginning "Sahasrārcis" and so forth. The meaning is that one should join the six limb-deities—beginning with Sahasrārcis and ending with Dhanurdhara, each in the dative case—with the six limbs. Thus: *Oṃ sahasrārcciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā*; *Oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya* [śikhāyai vaṣaṭ].
The sequence concludes with "To the crest-lock, Vaṣaṭ.

Regarding the phrase "the eight forms": the meaning is that one should perform the placement upon the eight limbs, beginning with the head of Agni, using the name of Agni preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending in the dative case.
The connection is that one should place the eight forms, beginning with Jātavedas, ending in the dative case. And this...
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed in a clockwise direction. As it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā*:
"One should perform the placement of the tongues of Fire within one's own body by means of the mantras.
Thus: "One should place the tongues of the Fire-eater within one's own body with the [appropriate] mantras."
Everywhere—in one's own genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes—(43).

Those beginning with *sā* and ending with *i*, joined with fire (*ra*), wind (*ya*), and the left ear (*u*), and endowed with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, are proclaimed as the mantras of the tongues. (44)
The preceptor should place the eight forms of Jātavedas upon his own body:
on the head, the two shoulders, the two sides, the two hips, and again on the hips, the two sides, and the two shoulders.
One should assign them in due order by way of circumambulation;
they are called Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana.
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, while another is called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas is [another], and Viśvamukha is remembered as Devamukha.
These forms of Fire (Vahni-mūrti) consist of the words beginning with "Tārāgnaye" and ending with "Namaḥ."
Thus [it is said]: they do not end with *svāhā*, but rather end with *namaḥ*.

Accordingly: *Oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ*—thus on the head; *Oṃ agnaye saptajihvāya namaḥ*—thus on the right shoulder. Such is the sequence of application. This ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed upon the eight petals of the described yantra, which constitute the eight limbs of Agni.

It should be performed. It should be understood that this is because it is stated in the thirty-first chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, beginning with "To Agni Jātavedas" and so forth, regarding the eight petals.

Regarding the phrase "one should place": the connection is that one should place the seven tongues upon the seven limbs mentioned—the penis, anus, head, and so forth—using the mantras that will be described hereafter. He states the mantra, beginning with "Sādi": those ending in the letter *ya* [are to be placed] in reverse order, starting from the letter *sa*.

The seven letters ending in *ya* are each joined with fire (*ra*), as well as with the letter *ya* combined with the long vowel *ū* (the left ear of wind), and further endowed with the *bindu*, the *nāda-kalā*, and the half-moon (*candrārdha*). Thus, the meaning is that they are joined with these. Accordingly, "sarayū, obeisance to Hiraṇyā" is for the *liṅga*; "ṣarayū, obeisance to Kanakā" is for the anus.
"Śarayu, obeisance to Raktā"—thus on the head; "Varayū, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā"—thus on the face. This is the sequence of application.

Since no specific [sequence] is mentioned here, it should be understood that the sequence itself follows the tongues as they are divided by the distinctions to be described later, such as the *sāttvika* and others.
(The threefold nature of the tongues.)
The tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities in their functions.
(Therein, those prescribed for *sāttvika* rites:
Hiraṇyā, Kapilā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atirūpā are considered suitable for the *sāttvika* sacrificial ritual. (46)
(Those prescribed for the rājasika action are:
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and likewise Candralohitā; Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālinī.
The tongues designated as characterized by the quality of passion (rajas) are employed in rites performed for desired objects.
(Those ordained for tamasic action: Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojavā, Lohinī, Kanakā, and Kālī are declared to belong to the tamasic [category].
(Regarding the last [seven], they are devoted solely to cruel rites:
These seven are worshipped by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites. || 48 ||
The colors of the tongues should correspond to their respective names; these tongues belong to Kalyāṇaretas. (49)
(Strewing the grass): Having thus disposed his body, he should perform the strewing; having sprinkled with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) upon the middle girdle situated there.

Regarding "with the water for the *arghya*": the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) is performed with the *vālā* seed-syllable. As it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "Then, having sprinkled [the area] above the girdles with pure waters by means of the *vālā* [mantra]. Regarding "the root-cloth":
[it is laid out] with its tip pointing north in the eastern direction, and with its tip pointing east in the south. Then...
The tip should face north in the west, and sequentially eastward in the north. || 51 ||
Having made a covering with the root [mantra], the practitioner should spread [the materials] three times over it;
upon this, he should sprinkle water with the root mantra.
(The Installation of the Enclosing Sticks):
The most excellent of gurus should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the cardinal directions, excluding the east.
Having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, the forms of Brahmā and the other deities are to be established within them. (53)

That which has complete covering is [the fire]; likewise, having covered the base, the remainder is with the front [of the grass]. This strewing (paristaraṇa) should be performed with *darbha* blades that are hollow in the middle. As it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā*:
"One should strew with hollow *darbha* blades upon the central girdle."

In the *Tantrasāra* as well, it is stated: "One should wrap [the fire] three times each with *darbha* grass that is hollow in the middle, covering the base with the tips, starting from the middle girdle.
Regarding the term "should cast," it refers to the enclosures (*paridhi*). The definition of the enclosure is stated in the *Kātyāyana-saṃhitā*:
In the fifteenth section:
the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are the size of an arm, straight, with their bark intact, and free from blemishes;
they are three in number, with their tips notched, and according to some, they are placed in the four directions.
"One should place two enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) on both sides with their tips pointing eastward, and another behind with its tip pointing north;
if there is yet another, it should be placed in the east with its tip pointing north.
Thus it is stated in the *Pañcarātra* as cited in the *Vaidikasārvabhauma*.

"Then the enclosing sticks (paridhis) should be placed; they should be made from the wood of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, with their bark intact, measuring one cubit in length and twelve finger-breadths in width.
Thus says Āpastamba, as cited in the *Vaidikasarvasva*. There are three enclosing sticks.
[The wood may be] from the *palāśa*, *kāśmarya*, *khadira*, *udumbara*, *bilva*, *rohitaka*, or *vikaṅkata* trees, or whatever trees are fit for sacrifice, and so forth.
And thus there are three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*): two with their tips pointing eastward in the south and north, and one with its tip pointing northward in the west.
This is in accordance with the previously cited statement of Kātyāyana: "If another enclosing stick is to be placed, it should have its tip pointing northward in the east."

By the phrase "excluding the east" (*mūle prācīvarjam*) in the root text, it precludes that other ritual procedure which was stated as having the form of laying down four enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
The meaning is that an enclosing stick is not to be prescribed for the eastern side.
(The meditation on the fire).
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, golden-hued, bearing the spear and the svastika,
enriched by the splendor of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with excellent ornaments of gold.
One should meditate upon him who is clothed in white garments, seated upon a lotus,
possessing three eyes, radiant, and with matted hair and the like rising upward from his crown.
(The mantra for the invocation and worship of Agni: O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come hither from the west; O Lohitākṣa, at the conclusion of all [the rites], accomplish the rituals.
One should perform the invocation of Vahni with the mantra ending in the wife of Vahni (Svāhā).
Having worshipped Agni with this,
[the sequence for the worship of the seven tongues of Vahni follows].
One should worship Rasanā in its mouth. || 57 ||
Starting from the northeast, in the hexagon and in the center, the best of practitioners should worship the six-limbed enclosure according to the application of the previously mentioned mantra. (58)
On the eight-petaled lotus within the circle of the earth, one should [worship] the lords of the directions belonging to the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).

He states the mantra for the invocation of Agni as "vaiśvānara... and so forth. Thus, the mantra results in: "O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O Lohitākṣa, accomplish all rites, svāhā! By means of this...

By means of the mantra beginning with *niruktavaiśvānara*, it should be understood that both the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the worship (*pūjana*) of the Fire are to be performed by this very mantra. Having thus described the worship of the Fire, he explains the worship of the seven tongues within its mouth, starting with the words "in its mouth" (*tanmukhe*).

Accordingly, outside the previously mentioned triangle, in the six-cornered figure, one should worship Hiraṇyā and the other six [tongues] in the order beginning from Īśāna, and [the seventh] in the center.
The meaning is that one should worship the seventh [deity], Sarayū, by means of the previously mentioned mantra-union with the mantra beginning "Obeisance to Hiraṇyā" and so forth.

Regarding the instruction "one should worship the six-limbed enclosure," the meaning is that one should do so according to the previously stated sequence, namely: "Oṃ, obeisance to the thousand-rayed one, to the heart," and so on.
(Furthermore, the meditation on the fire and other rites must be performed.)
Furthermore, the best of practitioners, having meditated upon Vaiśvānara, should perform worship. || 59 ||
(The Purification of the Vessels): One should sprinkle the vessels with arghya water for the sake of purification;
then, having turned them toward oneself, one should consecrate them with the Bālā mantra.
One should cast water and flowers into the pair of vessels for the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī*.
Having turned the *sruva* ladle face-down and heated it three times, the knower of mantras,
taking it with his left hand, should cleanse it three times with *dūrvā* grass.
One should cast the dūrvā grass, from its base up to its tip, into the fire;
then one should place it upon a bed of kuśa grass on one's own right side.
(The Consecration of the Clarified Butter):
Having placed the vessel for the clarified butter in front, one should perform its cleansing with a blade of *śara* grass.
Having established the *pavitra* strainer therein, the wise practitioner should face the northeast.

Regarding the phrase "the eight forms" (*aṣṭamūrtīḥ*): the meaning is the eight forms mentioned everywhere in connection with Agni, beginning with the mantra *manuvijjātavedasam*. The practical applications for this, such as *oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ*, have already been demonstrated previously.
Here, the *Śāradā-tilaka*, in its fifth chapter, also describes the worship of other deities.
"On the petals, one should worship the forms holding a spear and a svastika;
on the tips of the petals, the Mothers are to be worshipped along with Aṣitāṅga and the other Bhairavas;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions according to the described characteristics. Thus it is said.

And the *sruva*—by the word "and" (*ca*), it means both [the *darvī*] and the *sruva*. "With the face downward" means having taken it with the face upward, one should turn it face-downward and heat it; such is the meaning. "From the base, etc. means one should cleanse it three times from the base up to the tip. However, in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*:
Thereafter, taking up the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and turning them face downwards,
the preceptor should heat them three times in the fire while holding *darbha* grass;
he should then purify their tips, middles, and bases respectively with those blades of grass.
Having placed the clarified butter (ghṛta) right there and performed the purification through inspection and other rites,
one should cast the charcoal into the wind and then into the midst of the clarified butter.
Having kindled a blade of darbha grass, one should cast it away while reciting "idantāpanam";
the illumination is declared to be performed with the heart mantra.
Having taken clarified butter, charcoal, and darbha grass, one should cast them into the fire;
then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should hold that purifier (pavitra).
Then, one should pour clarified butter through the middle of that very [channel] in reverse order;
next, one should sprinkle the purifier three times with the heart-mantra.
One should cast that ghee into the fire and consecrate it with the *bālā* mantra.
(Offering of Incense and Lamps) One should properly diffuse incense so that it fills the sacrificial pit and the pavilion;
one should also arrange rows of lamps upon all the tiers of the altar.
(Preparatory rites for the fire-oblation:
One should cast into the clarified butter a pair of darbha blades, each a span long and tied with a knot. (69)
Having meditated upon the pair of the white and black fortnights (the consideration of the three nāḍīs in the clarified butter) and the nāḍikā on the left;
Iḍā is on the right, Piṅgalā is on the left, and Suṣumṇā is in the middle portion.

By this sequence beginning with "ityādi," the cleansing (*mārjana*) of the base, middle, and tip is prescribed. It is observed that the commentator Rāghavabhaṭṭa has taught the cleansing of the base, middle, and tip of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles respectively by means of the base, middle, and tips of the *darbha* grass, stating: "by the roots of the *darbha*, its [the vessel's] root; by the middles of the *darbha*, its middle; by the tips of the *darbha*, its tip," and so forth.
(The Fire-Eyed Face-Opening Homa):
Having meditated, one should offer clarified butter from the right portion using the *sruva* ladle with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
saying "Svāhā to Agni," into the right eye of the fire.
Likewise, taking [the offering] from the left, one should then offer it into the fire in the left eye with the heart-mantra, saying: "Svāhā to Soma! (72).
Taking clarified butter from the center and offering it into the eye on the forehead of the fire,
one should sacrifice with the mantra "To Agni and Soma, Svāhā," using the Heart-mantra.

Having taken a portion of clarified butter from the southern part with the *sruva* ladle while reciting the heart-mantra, he should offer it into the mouth [of the fire] with the words: "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭikṛt. (74)
The Guru should cause the weapon (heti) to fall upon the portion according to the sequence of oblations of clarified butter;
thus he should perform the opening of the eyes and faces of the fire.
"Along with a *prādeśa*" means that one should cast a pair of darbha blades, joined at their knots and measuring a *prādeśa* in length, into the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

"White" means that one should meditate upon one of the two previously mentioned portions of clarified butter as the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and the other as the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). "On the left" means the *iḍā*, the lunar channel; "on the right" means the *piṅgalā*, which is by implication the form of the sun.

The connection is that one should meditate upon the *suṣumṇā* in the center, which consists of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire. "With the *hṛdāṇu*" means with the heart-mantra, namely "namaḥ. Here, the connection is that one should take clarified butter from the right side with the *hṛdāṇu* and offer it into the fire with the mantra "agnaye svāhā. This has been clearly stated by the author of the *Tantrasāra*: "with the mantra 'namaḥ' using the *sruva* ladle."
Taking clarified butter from the southern portion, one should offer it into the right eye of the fire with the mantra: *oṃ agnaye svāhā*.

This same sequence applies to what follows as well. Regarding the term *hetim*, it refers to the residue of the oblation (*āhuti*). Thus, the meaning is that from whichever portion the clarified butter is taken for a specific offering, one should pour the residue of each subsequent oblation (*pratyāhuti*) into that same portion, according to the previously stated sequence of clarified butter offerings.
"Thus for Agni": by this, the meaning is that one should perform the opening of the eyes and the mouth of Agni in sequence by means of these four oblations beginning with "Svāhā to Agni.
(The Mahāvyāhṛti-homa).
And one should perform the oblation of the Mahāvyāhṛtis, offering four times with the mantra beginning with "Tārā."
"Bhūḥ" is for Agni and the great Earth, accompanied by the word "vahnivallabhā";
from the word "bhuvaḥ," it is for Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarīkṣa), according to the sound. || 77 ||
The mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) is prescribed for the sake of divine and great [attainments].
After the word "nakṣatra," there follow the words "svara" (sun), "āditya" (sun), and "candramas" (moon), all ending in the feminine suffix ṅīp. || 78 ||
To the three [words], *svāhā*, and after the word ending in *apad* (non-word), again the words *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*;
likewise, *agnī*, *āditya*, and *candramasaḥ* ending in the dative (*ṅe*), as well as *nakṣatre*;
those ending in the ablative (*bhyas*), and from the directions (*digbhyaḥ*), and for the great one, the beloved of Fire (*mahate vahnivallabhā*). (79)
(Brahmārcana:
Having duly worshipped Brahmā to the south, the best of practitioners [should proceed]. (80)

He describes the *mahāvyāhṛti-homa*, which is to be performed immediately thereafter, beginning with the words "mahā" and so forth. The connection is that one should offer oblations in four ways with the four mantras to be described, preceded by the syllable *TĀRĀ* (or *TĀRA*) and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
Thus, having first joined the *praṇava* to each of the four mantras to be described, one should perform the *homa* with those mantras conjoined with the *praṇava*.
This is to be known. And thus: (1) *Oṃ bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai mahate ca svāhā*; (2) *Oṃ bhuvo vāyave antarikṣāya ca divyāya mahate ca svāhā*;
(3) *Oṃ svar ādityāya candramase nakṣatrebhyaḥ svāhā*; (4) *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar agnaye ādityāya candramase nakṣatrebhyo digbhyo mahate ca svāhā*. Thus [it is said].

The four mantras reach their conclusion. In works such as the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* and the *Gandharvatantra*, a partial difference in the form of these mantras is observed. Here, after the author of the *Tantrasāra* has described the oblation following the aforementioned *Sviṣṭikṛt* offering, he prescribes an oblation with the *praṇava* and *vyāhṛtis*, followed by another oblation as prescribed in the respective *kalpa*s, beginning with *Oṃ*.

The fire-oblation (homa) has been described with the mantras beginning with "Bhūr agnaye. However, in the thirty-first chapter of the Gandharva-tantra, the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa is not mentioned prior to the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) such as conception (garbhādhāna); rather, the oblation with "Oṃ bhūr agnaye" and so forth is prescribed after the homa stated in the Kalpa. Thus, a difference in sequence is observed.
(The consecratory rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation:
Thereafter, one should perform the consecratory rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*).
"O Fire, I am performing this; hereafter follows this impregnation. (81)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should pronounce the "bride of fire" (Svāhā) at the end;
having thus offered seven oblations, one should likewise cast the sacrificial fuel sticks.
In this sequence, he performed the Puṃsavana and then the Sīmantonnayana;
having completed the Jātakarman, he then proceeded to sever the umbilical cord.
One should offer a sacrificial ladle (prādeśa) five-finger-breadths long, joined at its base and tip with clarified butter, while reciting: "Oṃ, svāhā to Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī. (84)
The practitioner should unite the parents of the fire with Svāhā;
he should employ the name of the fire preceded by the name of his chosen deity.
Next, the rite of going forth is declared, followed by the first feeding of solid food; then indeed the tonsure, the initiation, and the return home. (86)
Marriage and other auspicious rites [should be performed under these], while killing and other cruel acts [should be performed] during cruel [periods]. || 87 ||

Now, he describes the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the fire, beginning with the words "This... and so forth. Thus, the practical application culminates in the formula: *oṃ idam agner garbhādhānaṃ karomi svāhā*. With this mantra, one should offer seven oblations (*āhuti*) for each rite. However, in the *Tantrasāra*, according to the tradition of Sundarī, it is: *oṃ agner garbhādhānaṃ kalpayāmi ai namaḥ*.
Thus, the sequence of the ritual application has been stated: "one should offer each oblation one by one.
Regarding the word *jātā* ("born"): it is for the purpose of removing the umbilical cord and severing the channel (*nāḍī*).
This has been stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: [The citation follows.]
"Having meditated upon the newborn as having this form, one should perform the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
Having removed the umbilical cord and then purified the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*), [one should proceed].
And regarding marriage: in auspicious rites, the sacraments end with marriage; however, in cruel rites..."
The meaning is "ending with the killing [of the enemy].
(The fire-oblation for the tongues, limbs, and deities:
One should perform the fire-oblation separately for each using the mantras of the tongues, limbs, and forms in their proper sequence.
One should perform six oblations for the fire with the six-limbed mantra;
the wise practitioner should perform the homa for the eight forms according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and poured it four times into the *sruc*,
the preceptor, rising while remaining composed in mind, should offer oblations into the fire with the *agni-mantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of perfection.
(The Gāṇapatya Homa): One should first offer ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇapati mantra;
one should also offer them four times with that same mantra used in its entirety.
The mantra of that [deity] is said to consist of the six seed-syllables beginning with Tārā, joined with each preceding one individually as well as all together. (91)
Regarding the *homa* for the tongues, limbs, and forms [of the fire-god], it says "in sequence": that is, for the tongues, limbs, and forms previously mentioned.
One should offer one oblation (*āhuti*) for each. As it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Śāradā-tantra*:
"With the mantras of the tongues, limbs, and forms, one should [offer] to the fire in sequence according to the rule."
The best of those who know mantras should offer one oblation for each [deity].

Regarding the word "atha" (now): having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and poured it four times into the *sruc* offering-spoon, and having covered that *sruc* with the *sruva*, the preceptor, with a concentrated mind, should offer oblations with the fire-mantra beginning with "vaiśvānara" and ending in "vauṣaṭ"—this is the connection.
Regarding the word "maha": first, at the outset, [he should offer] ten times with the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati which is about to be described, in its distributed form (*vyasta*).

The meaning is that one should offer one oblation for each [syllable] and then four oblations with the entire [mantra]. In this regard, he teaches the oblation by dividing [the mantra] with the words beginning "Tārādi" (the Seed-syllables beginning with Tāra). The meaning of the phrase "with the six seed-syllables beginning with Tāra joined one after another" is as follows: since the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is mentioned first in the forthcoming statement explaining the extraction of the mantras—beginning with "Śrīṃ"—the first [syllable] is Oṃ.

The oblation (*homa*) is performed with "svāhā" at the end of the *praṇava* (i.e., *oṃ svāhā*). Then, for the second oblation, the mantra is "oṃ śrīṃ svāhā," where the oblation is performed with the *śrī*-seed-syllable joined with the previously mentioned *praṇava*. Then, for the third oblation, it is "oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā"; here too, it is with the *māyā*-seed-syllable joined with the *praṇava* and *śrī*. The same applies to the subsequent ones as well.
(The Mahāgaṇapati Mantra):

[One should utter] the Praṇava, then *śrīṃ*, then the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), then *smaraṃ* consisting of *glauṃ*, then the letter *pa* with the five [vowels] ending in it, joined with the Bindu, then *gaṇapatiṃ* ending in *ṅ*. (92)
At the end of *vara* one should write *varadam*, and at the end of *sarva* one should write *janam*;
"me vaśam ānaya svāhā" is that which ends with the twenty [syllables] and concludes with *gajāntaka*. || 93 ||
This face is declared to be common to all goddesses. || 94 ||

He describes the sequence for extracting the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati with the words beginning "Praṇava" and so forth. Thus it is: *oṃ śrī hrī klī glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. "Ending in twenty, [it is] Gajāntaka": that which has the number eight at the end of the count of twenty; such is its nature.
This means that the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati consists of twenty-eight syllables. It is clearly stated in the *Mantrakoṣa*:
"One should first utter the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhū, and Vighna; then [the word] Gaṇapati ending in the dative case (ṅe), followed by the word 'Varada' at the end of 'Vara'."
Having said "bring all people under my control at the end," followed by two *ṭha*s—
this twenty-eight-syllable mantra, beginning with Tārā, is thus proclaimed.

"Tārādyaḥ" means beginning with *tāra* (Oṃ). Regarding the reading "glaumāntakaṃ tataḥ" in the root text, the term *āntakam* means that which has *ā* at its end (*ā-ante yasya*), thus referring to *pañcāntakam*; in this sense, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *gām*. Furthermore, in the commentary on that manuscript, the sequence for extracting the mantra is demonstrated as: Oṃ Śrī Hrī Klī Glau Gāṃ Gaṇapataye, and so forth. However...

Since the seed-syllable *gam* is seen in the *Mantrakoṣa*, the *Tantrasāra*, the *Gandharvamahānirvāṇa*, and other texts, the reading *āntakam* has not been inserted into the root text. Here, this should be noted: the sequence for the tenfold oblation previously mentioned in such passages as "one should first offer ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇapati mantra" is as follows: (1) *oṃ svāhā*; (2) *oṃ śrīṃ svāhā*; *oṃ*... [etc.]

Śrīṃ Hrīḥ Svāhā (3) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīḥ Klīṃ Svāhā (4) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīḥ Klīṃ Glauṃ Svāhā (5) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ Svāhā (6) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Svāhā (7) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Varavarada Svāhā (8) | Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīḥ Klīṃ Glauṃ...

*Gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ svāhā* (9). *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā* (10). Thus, having offered ten oblations in this manner, one should offer four oblations with the entire mantra together; this is what is meant by the phrase "four times with that very [mantra] in its entirety."
(The worship of the Root Goddess in the mouth of fire):
Having visualized the King of Yantras, accompanied by a multitude of rays, within the mouth of fire, one should invoke the Goddess, the illustrious Tripurasundarī. (95)
The wise practitioner should worship her, who is in the form of fire, with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
[This is the oblation that effects the unification of the fire and the deity.
He should offer it into her mouth twenty-five times while reciting the root mantra.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with clarified butter; this indeed is the unification of the faces.
(The Fire-Channel Union Homa): Contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity with one's own self,
one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
This is declared by those who know the scriptures as the "joining of the channels" (nāḍīsandhāna). || 97 ||
(The Homa for the Deities of the Enclosures): Thereafter, one should offer one oblation each for the sake of the deities of the enclosures.
(The Procedure for the Homa of the Root Deity)
Then, having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should perform the optional oblation (kāmyahoma).
Having uttered the root mantra ending with "svāhā," and saying "this [is] for the deity," one should offer oblations into the blazing fire and perform the prescribed number of repetitions all around.
(On the Determination of those Authorized for Tantric Homa):
The twice-born possess authority for the performance of tantric homa.
(The Special Case of the Śūdra)
If one is desirous of worldly pleasures, even a Śūdra may perform the rite of oblation (homa). || 100 ||
Having set aside the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*), one should perform the oblation ending with the Heart-mantra.
This doctrine, which accords with authoritative Tantras, has been proclaimed from the Vārāhī-tantrarāja. (The authority of this stated sequence) 101.
Regarding "Vahnimukha" (the Fire-mouth): the King of Yantras is the Śrīyantra to be described hereafter.
"Unification of the mouth" means the conceptualization of non-difference between the Root Goddess and the Fire-mouth.
(The differences in results according to the different tongues [of fire] during the homa).
Offering oblations in the tongue of fire located to the northeast of Īśa bestows success;
in the southwest for rites of pacification, in the west for the rite of immobilization,
in the northwest for eradication, and in the center for the rite of killing.
(Various sacrificial vessels according to the difference in intention:
A vessel made of gold, silver, stone, or clay is prescribed for rites such as pacification (*śānti*).
One fashioned from *vilva*, *akṣa*, or *śigru* wood is used for rites such as killing (*māraṇa*) and uprooting (*uccaṭana*). 103.
(The three mudrās prescribed for the fire sacrifice:
Three mudrās are traditionally taught for the homa: the mṛgī, the haṃsī, and the kasturī. (104)
The *kastūrī* is formed by contracting the fingers; the *haṃsī* is joined with the little finger;
and the *mṛgī* consists of the little and index fingers—these are remembered as the three mudrās. (105)
(The application of these mudrās:
In sacrifice and in rites for pacification, the Mṛgī and Haṃsī are proclaimed [to be used]. (106)
In all rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), musk is highly recommended.
(Regarding the specific [mantras] for the six rites and the fire-oblation *homa*: the seed-syllables (*jāti*) end with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.
In pacification, subjugation, as well as in paralyzing, causing enmity, and killing. || 107 ||

He states the different sacrificial vessels according to the difference in purpose (*kāmanā*): "Of gold," etc. Regarding "in rites such as pacification" (*śāntyādiṣu*): the meaning is that for pacification (*śānti*) the vessel is made of gold; for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), it is made of silver; for immobilization (*stambhana*), it is made of stone; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), the vessel is made of clay; and for killing (*māraṇa*), causing flight (*uccāṭana*), and so forth, the vessel is traditionally said to be fashioned from *vilva*, *akṣa*, and *śigru*. *Vilva* is well known. *Akṣa* [is the *akṣa* tree].
*Vayaḍā* is its common name; *śīgru* is the *śobhāñjana*. The meaning is that a vessel fashioned from the wood of either of these should be employed for rites such as killing (*māraṇa*).
Regarding *namaḥ*: likewise, in rites of pacification (*śānti*), mantras end with *namaḥ*, while in rites of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), they end with *vaṣaṭ*.
The meaning is that the ritual applications should be performed in this sequence, ending with *vauṣaṭ* for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*).
(Kumārī-pūjā) Now, the practitioner of mantras should worship both a young maiden (*kumārī*) and a married woman (*suvāsinī*).
(Śrīvidyā-pūjā) Thereafter, one should worship Śrīvidyā with the Bālā-bījas according to the prescribed rule. || 108 ||
(The Mahāvyāhṛti-homa and the Pūrṇāhuti):
Having performed the Vyāhṛti-homa for the Goddess, one should perform the Pūrṇāhuti;
having filled the *sruk* with clarified butter and placed a flower at its tip. (109)
Rising with the sacrificial ladle (sruva) and the grass-bundle (sadarbha), one should perform the covering; then,
holding [the vessel] with joined palms while reciting the root mantra at its conclusion,
one should offer a continuous stream of oblations in the form of barley, preceded by shouts of victory.

The oblation of the Great Vyāhṛtis (*mahāvyāhṛti-homa*) for the Goddess has been stated previously. He now describes the procedure for offering the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the words beginning "pūrṇā" and so forth, and "ghṛtena" and so forth. Thus, having filled the large ladle (*sruk*) with clarified butter using the small dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and having placed a flower at the tip of the ladle, he stands up; then, taking that large ladle full of clarified butter—covered by the small spoon together with *darbha* grass—in his joined palms, he proceeds.

One should offer a stream [of oblation] into the fire in the form of barley—that is, having the same thickness as a barley grain—using the root mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ*. Regarding this, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* have stated that after offering the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra beginning "From here onwards" (*itaḥ pūrvam*) and the root mantra, one offers the *pūrṇāhuti* with this mantra of self-surrender (*ātmasamarpaṇa*). The authoritative source supporting that explanation is as follows:
It has not been shown [there]. In the eighteenth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*, it says:
"O Dear One, having performed the naming of the fire, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
again, one should offer the final oblation with the mantra of 'offering to Brahman' (*brahmārpaṇa*)."

From this statement, as well as from the fact that it is stated in the *Tantrasāra* beginning with "with the root [mantra]" (*mūlena*), it is understood that after offering one final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, one should again offer a final oblation with the mantra "Brahmārpaṇam. Otherwise, the word "again" (*punar*) would be redundant. However, in the thirteenth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
Having performed the full oblation with the *sruc* ladle using the root mantra,
the preceptor should dismiss the deity— along with its limbs and retinue— from the water-pot (*kumbha*).

By this, the offering of the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra alone has been stated. However, in the present context, because two distinct ritual acts are prescribed— namely, "one should offer a stream in the form of barley" and "likewise, one should offer eight oblations in sequence"— it follows that there is no mention anywhere of a *pūrṇahoma* consisting of eight oblations.
(The fire-offering of the mantra for self-surrender): One should offer eight oblations in sequence with the mantra of self-surrender. 111.
(The Mantra for Self-Dedication):
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, and thereafter the root mantra; having said "from this time forward," one should then recite "prāṇa-buddhi... [and so forth]. (112)
However, because of the authority over the body and its functions, one acts through the mind, speech, and physical deeds during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (113)

One should likewise recollect [the transgression] with the two hands, the two feet, and the belly; that which was remembered, that which was spoken, and likewise that which was done by the penis. (114)
Let even that which is "all" be an offering to Brahman, like the beloved of Agni;
and let my own Praṇava be the entire deity to be accomplished. With the word "Ṅe" at its end, the Tāra (Oṃ) thus offered is the mantra for the perpetual offering of one's own self.

From the mention of the *dhānā* and the offering of the *pūrṇāhuti*, it is understood that this offering of eight oblations (*kāṣṭāhuti*) performed with the mantra of self-surrender (*ātmasamarpaṇa*) is indeed distinct from them. Thus, since differences of opinion are not observed here across various tantras, one should adopt whichever position is appropriate according to the tradition of one's own guru; such is the direction [of the teaching].

He describes the nature of the mantra for self-surrender (ātmasamarpaṇa-mantra) with the passage beginning "The Praṇava" and ending with "the mantra for the offering of the self. Thus, first the Praṇava, then the Root Mantra, and then: "Whatever [I have done] prior to this, through my vital breath, intellect, body, and faculties, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, by mind, speech, or action..."

"Whatever has been thought by the two hands, the feet, the belly, and the genitals; whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done—may all that be an offering unto Brahman, Svāhā! Oṃ, my entire self, [name], is surrendered to the deity [name]. Oṃ Tat Sat.
Thus concludes the mantra for the surrender of the self. Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the eighteenth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
O Pārvatī, one should then offer oneself and all ritual actions with the Great Mantra specifically to her whose nature is Brahman. (The sprinkling and worship of the fire.)
Having sprinkled water [around it], the wise one should worship the fire with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
(The Great Vyāhṛti Oblation and the Tongue Oblation):
Having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, the preceptor shall offer one oblation each for the tongues and other parts of the Fire, using their respective mantras. (117)
(The dismissal of the fire with a prayer: O Fire, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!
When another rite is about to commence, please remain present here with respect.
Having thus made this request to the fire, one should dismiss it with the words, "Forgive me. || 118 ||
Having united the fire with one's own self, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given;
in the case of occasional rites (naimittika), one should offer the enclosing sticks (paridhi), but in the daily rites (nitya), one should not burn them at all.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 8 ||
Three times prior to this, and thereafter,
[the functions of] the vital breath and the intellect cease at the end of the authority over the body's attributes during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Then by mind, then by speech, and thereafter by action;
then by the two hands, then by the two feet, and thereafter by the belly.

O Goddess, whatever was previously remembered, whatever was subsequently spoken, and whatever may have been done— whether it pertains to me or to what is mine— all that, and furthermore everything beyond that;
"Likewise, [the mantra] 'May it be offered into the Brahman at the end of the sound within you;

Svāhā!'—this is said to be the mantra ending in *svāhā* for the offering of one's own self. Regarding "into Agni," the remainder is that [one should do so] by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. This has been stated in the *Tantrasāra*:

As before, having sprinkled with water upon the girdle (*mekhalā*) and joined the fire to oneself by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*—thus [it is said]. Regarding "occasional" (*naimittika*): in an occasional rite, one should burn the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) previously placed; the ellipsis is that one should cast them into the fire. However, in a daily (*nitya*) rite, one should not burn them. As it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "One should cast the enclosing sticks along with the coverings into the fire; however, the distinction lies in the occasional rite."

"One should burn these in a ritual action (*karma*), but one should not burn them in a daily rite (*nitya-karman*). And in the *Śāradā-tantra* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*: "The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should burn them in an occasional rite (*naimittika*), but never in a daily rite.
[Ninth Chapter]

(The differences in results based on the difference in substances for the fire-oblation, the differences in the quantity of the oblation-substances, and the procedure for abandoning hostile mantras) (The promise to define the oblation-substances):
Now, as a relevant digression, I shall state the characteristics of the substance used in the fire-oblation. (1)
(The differences in results according to the difference in substances for the fire-oblation:
By offering jasmine, *mallikā*, and *jātī* flowers mixed with honey,
and by performing a homa filled with clarified butter, mastery over speech (*vāgīśatva*) is produced.
And this is not otherwise for one who is deluded, mute, or like a stone.
Through oblations of *karavīra* and *javā* flowers mixed with clarified butter, the world is brought under control;
indeed, all women become submissive and turn into servants.
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations of red karavīra flowers smeared with honey along with guggulu resin, one shall bring under one's control twenty rulers of the earth.
With *karavīra* flowers smeared with honey, one may bring the king, along with his retinue, under one's control.
For seven nights, the wise one should offer oblations with ghee,
using *pāṭala*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *śatapatra*, and *jāti* flowers, accompanied by the recitation of the [Soma] hymn.

Having established the section on fire-offerings (*homa*) in the previous exposition, in this exposition he first teaches the various substances used as implements for the fire-offering, as well as the specific fruits attainable through fire-offerings performed with those respective substances,
beginning with the words "mālati" and so forth.

"Anointed with honey" (madhvakta) means the king together with his limbs— that is, the king accompanied by the constituent elements of sovereignty such as ministers, friends, and the treasury. "With the moon" (śaśinā) means with camphor.
By worshipping with or offering oblations of fresh *mālatī*, jasmine, *mallikā*, lotus, and *kiṃśuka* flowers— whether mixed or unmixed—
one attains all prosperity and becomes a master of speech through wisdom. (7)
An oblation with red lotuses bestows all prosperity;
with red water-lilies, the world is brought under control and kings become submissive in an instant.
By means of blue lotuses, even the most wicked are brought under control; it cannot be otherwise.
By means of white lotuses, one certainly obtains prosperity and eloquence through the performance of oblations.
By offering *kahāra* flowers, the practitioner of mantras may take away good fortune and wealth;
however, by means of the fruits and flowers of the *vakula*, great good fortune is produced.
By offering camphor and saffron mixed with musk into the fire, even death itself shall be conquered by the practitioner.
By performing oblations with *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, the practitioner of mantra obtains great and radiant, supreme prosperity, and may even paralyze this entire world.
Having offered śrīkhaṇḍa, aguru, karpūra, and likewise guggulu as oblations,
one shall bring under one's control the wives of kings, great lords, and gods.
All the worlds indeed come under his control; of this there is no doubt. || 13 ||
"By mixed [flowers]" means by those already mentioned flowers, such as *pāṭala* and so forth, combined together; or else, by unmixed [flowers], or by any one of them—this is the meaning.
By "campakas and *pāṭalas*" is meant "by mixed [flowers]"; [it refers to] the *homa* performed with unmixed *pāṭala* flowers.
Because it has been stated previously:
"One afflicted by the fear of poverty shall obtain a kingdom through a hundred-thousand-fold fire-offering (lakṣahoma) using śrīkhaṇḍa, which is sandalwood."
The pacification of difficult calamities occurs through the oblation of a pala of the three sweets.
One will certainly destroy the enemy's army with *mahāpala*;
by performing a *homa* at a crossroads at night, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). (15)
By performing a fire-oblation at night with goat’s meat smeared with blood,
combined with the three sweets, according to the procedure taught by the Guru,
one shall bring the entire great fortress of Mahārāṣṭra under control.
Having separated the honey, milk, and ghee, the wise man should offer them as oblations;
thereby, longevity, wealth, health, and prosperity arise for men. (17)
Through oblations with honey mixed with milk, one shall destroy death;
through the mixture of curd and honey, one shall obtain good fortune and wealth.
With mustard seeds and salt, one may agitate this world;
by means of oblations, one shall bring wicked people under control—of this there is no doubt. (19)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with curd, one shall bring untimely death under control.
A wise man should offer one hundred and eight oblations of ghee mixed with milk;
by means of guggulu resin combined with honey and ghee, he shall bring even a lord of kings under his control.
By performing oblations with curd, honey, milk, and parched grain, the best of practitioners will certainly become a destroyer of diseases, a benefactor of the world, and a conqueror of death.

Regarding "trimadhu": Rāghavabhaṭṭa, citing the *Prayogasāra*, states that "trimadhura" consists of milk, honey, and ghee in equal proportions: "Milk, honey, and ghee—these together are known as trimadhura.
*Rājikā* refers to black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *rājikā* applies to both black mustard and a furrow in a field."
Health is attained through an offering of one hundred and eight oblations of ghee and milk;
by the mere performance of a homa with sesame seeds and clarified butter, one shall accomplish all rites.
Having offered white oblations, the knower of mantras should perform the rite of paralyzing the enemy;
and by the oblation of guggulu resin, he shall destroy all miseries.
Even enemies quickly come under one's control through the oblation of sandalwood;
indeed, by means of an oblation of red sandalwood, both men and women are brought under subjection. (25)
By the oblation of camphor, the speech of men becomes submissive;
indeed, by the oblation of musk, all beings become subject to the power of the mantra-practitioner.
Through the oblation of sesame seeds and rice, all peace shall prevail in the home;
through the oblation of sugar and jaggery, one shall accomplish all undertakings. || 27 ||
By means of an oblation of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), one may bring the great grahas under control. || 28 ||
By means of an oblation of ripe jujube fruits mixed with sugar, the practitioner brings the three worlds under his control; indeed, there shall be an increase of grain. (29)
Through the offering of ten-ingredient incense, incomparable good fortune shall arise;
by the offering of a full pomegranate, one may bring even the great planetary spirits under control.
By means of a complete offering of *vara* flowers, one shall bring kings under control;
by an offering of *mātuluṅga* fruits, Kṣatriyas will certainly come under one's sway.
White sugar;
by means of an offering of *kuṅkuma*,
and indeed by an offering of orange fruits, Vaiśyas become submissive.
Indeed, by means of an oblation of *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruits, Śūdras become submissive.
Through one hundred thousand oblations of grape fruits, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained; of this there is no doubt. || 33 ||
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of plantain fruit, ten kings will certainly become submissive; of this there is no doubt.
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of dates (kharjūra), kings become subject to one's will;
this occurs exactly twenty times over, without a doubt. (35)
Through oblations of coconut fruits, prosperity arises without delay;
by a mere hundred thousand [recitations], the knower of the mantra will certainly become equal to a king. (36)
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of ripe mango fruits, the knower of mantras shall bring the earth,
bounded by the four oceans, under his control.
Through oblations of *jambū* fruits, women are brought under control; through *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourds, the daughters of the Daityas;
and through *bilva* fruits or their leaves, one obtains supreme Lakṣmī from the fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
Through oblations of sugarcane stalks, happiness is attained, and by them, princesses are won over.
(The Measurement of the Materials for the Homa) Now I shall describe the measurement of the materials which grants success in the fire-oblation:
one should offer a full flower, and even a lotus in its entirety. (39)
The wise one should offer kusumbha and vāṇa flowers as desired;
likewise, sesame seeds by the count of a hundred and black mustard seeds by the count of a hundred. (40)
The parched grain should be the measure of a handful, the clarified butter likewise one karṣa;
the milk should be half a mouthful, and the cooked rice should be the size of a single morsel.

Large fruits such as the pumpkin (kuṣmāṇḍa) and likewise the citron (mātuluṅga), as well as pieces of sugar-candy and other fruits pleasing to the mind, certainly bring about [the desired result]. || 42 ||
One should offer plantain fruit divided into four pieces, provided it is not cut too small;
one should also offer jackfruit kernels and mangoes mixed with honey. (43)
In former times, a single piece of sugarcane was a cause of satisfaction for the mind;
yet now, there would be entire bunches of grapes, oranges, and dates. (44)
There should be guggulu and half a betel nut, as well as saffron;
camphor the size of a guñjā seed, along with musk, saffron, and [the same amount of] safflower. || 45 ||
Aloe-wood and sandalwood may be used together with betel nut;
likewise, all fruits that are pleasing to the mind are suitable for the oblation. 46.
Having offered oblations pleasing to the mind, the wise person should shake off everything else;
this shall be the measure of the oblation (and its alternative method).
Another method is now stated. || 47 ||

The curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti), and the flattened rice as well as the parched grain (śaktu) should likewise be so; the molasses should be one karṣa, and the quantity of sugar should be half a pala.

In the ancient site at the mountain region, half a mouthful is the measure for the sacrificial porridge (caru); one leaf is prescribed [as the portion]. The citron (mātuluṅga) is traditionally divided into four pieces, and the jackfruit (panasa) into ten. || 49 ||
The wise know that coconuts are split into eight parts;
a bilva fruit is divided into three parts, and a kapittha fruit is split into two.
Other fruits should be cut into pieces, and the fuel-sticks should be ten finger-breadths long;
the rice should be a single handful in measure, as should the red mung beans and the barley.
There should be half as much rice, and sesamum seeds measured by a *culuka*;
there should also be twenty black peppercorns, the size of *tintiḍī* seeds. (52)
(Regarding the specific case when the substance is not mentioned: When the sacrificial substance is not specified, sesame seeds and clarified butter are said to be the oblation. || 53 ||
Regarding "fuel-sticks" (*samidh*): they are ten fingers long, measuring one span (*prādeśa*). The characteristics of fuel-sticks are stated in the eighth chapter of the *Karmapradīpa*:
"A fuel-stick should never be taken as thicker than the thumb."
Nor one from which the bark has been stripped, nor one infested with insects, nor one that is split.
In fire-offerings, a wise person should use fuel-sticks that are no more nor less than a span (prādeśa) in length, possessing two branches, not having leaves, and not lacking in potency.
Those that are shattered, split, short, crooked, thick, thin, double-ended, worm-eaten, or long should be carefully avoided.
Those bitten by worms and those that are elongated should be avoided with great effort.
In the first chapter of the *Gṛhyāsaṃgraha*:
"A [fire-drill] that is split causes the destruction of one's lifespan; one with cracks brings about disease;
a short one is said to cause misfortune; and a crooked one leads to ill fortune."
If she is stout, she creates obstacles; if she is emaciated, she increases one's enemies.
Indeed, in both ways, she destroys wealth, as well as one's wife and dear kinsmen.
"One bitten by an insect brings great fear, and one that is too long will take away one's sons;
therefore, with every effort, one should avoid those [lines] and cause them to be avoided. Thus ends the procedure for abandoning hostile mantras.
Now, the proper procedure for the abandonment of hostile mantras is fully explained.
Having become pure and composed, on an auspicious day,
the preceptor should commence the excellent rite for the destruction of all suffering.
(Placing the Vessel): First, in that beautiful hall, the wise one should place the jar upon the mandala according to the sequence of the initiation rite, and fill it with auspicious waters. (56)
(Therein, the worship of the deity to be accomplished along with the enclosures:
Having invoked the deity there by reciting the mantra in reverse order,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worshipped [the deity], one should worship the enclosures.
Having thus worshipped the deity of the mantra, the twice-born practitioner of mantras, having offered oblations of even cow-ghee with the reverse mantra, [should proceed]. (58)
(The Offering to the Guardians of the Quarters):

Thereafter, one should duly present an offering (*bali*) of milk-rice to the deities in the cardinal and intermediate directions, according to the sequence of mantras that will be described hereafter. (59)
(Therein, the *bali* mantra for Indra:
Oṃ! Come, O Indra, Lord of the Suras, O Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī!
Salutations to you; accept this *bali* consisting of flowers, incense, and so forth. (1) || 60 ||
Oṃ! Come, O Lord of splendors, O bearer of oblations, O bestower of boons!
Accept this well-worshipped offering of flowers, incense, and other gifts. (2) || 61 ||

Previously, in the second chapter, the mantras of enemies were described. Now, he states the sequence for the ritual abandonment of those mantras which yield undesirable results, beginning with the words "Now, of the abandonment of enemy mantras," and so forth.
The phrase "having performed the sakalīkaraṇa" implies [the performance of it] by means of the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra).
(To Yama): Oṃ! King of the Pretas, come hither, you whose luster is like crushed collyrium;
accept this offered oblation, and being well-pleased, become the granter of boons. (3) 62.
Oṃ, homage to you! O Lord of the Rakṣasas, O Nairṛta, you have come here;
accept this offering, worship, and so forth, presented by me with devotion. (4) || 63 ||
(To Varuṇa): Oṃ, come, O guardian of the western quarter, O lord of the world; salutations be unto you!
Having accepted this worship offered with devotion, may you attain delight. (5) || 64 ||
(To Vāyu:
Oṃ, O Prabhañjana, Lord of Life, come hither with your retinue;
accept with respect this offering presented by me according to the ritual rules. (65)
(Kubera and Candra): Oṃ! May Kubera and the Lord of the Stars, the best of gods, come hither;
being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, may you both grant me boons. (7) 66.
(For Īśāna: Oṃ, O Lord, come here, O Blessed One, O Master consisting of all knowledge!
Honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be present for the sake of prosperity. (8) 67.
(Brahmā): Oṃ! Come, O Brahmā, Lord of all the gods;
accept this worship and dispel all my obstacles. Salutations be unto you. (9) || 68 ||
Oṃ, come, O infinite one, bestower of boons, unmanifest Viṣṇu, leader of the universe!
Honored with supreme devotion, may you be the giver of happiness to me. (10) 69.
(Adoration of the Deity to be Accomplished) Thereafter, one should worship the deity of the mantra together with his retinue,
using flowers, incense, and other offerings, while reciting the mantra in reverse order.
(Prayer:
Then the wise one should pray to the worshipped deity of the mantra.
(In that regard, the mantras:
O Lord, though my intellect was wavering, I have both received and honored the nature of the mantras, whether by looking toward them or not looking at all.
Therefore, always dispel this agitation of my mind.
May my evil be destroyed and may eternal welfare prevail;
may your purifying devotion alone extend auspiciousness to me. (73)
Having thus prayed, "This is the subsequent duty," one should write the syllables of the mantras in reverse order upon a leaf and worship them with *amalaka*, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having again placed it upon the water-pot with supreme devotion. || 74 ||
Then the wise man, having tied that leaf upon his own head,
should bathe with the auspicious waters from the consecrated jar, which are imbued with mantras.
Furthermore, having filled another jar with water while remaining self-controlled,
one should place the mantra-leaf within it and then perform worship.
In the midst of that, on the bank of a river or in another pure body of water,
one should place ten Brahmins and worship them according to one's capacity.
In the reverse order— that is, by way of inversion—
[is the result arising from the performance according to the etymological explanation].
For one who has performed the rite in this manner, the afflictions arising from the mantras of enemies [are neutralized].
They are surely destroyed, there is no doubt; through this process, clarity of mind gradually arises.
He is born exceedingly prosperous and his own lineage prospers in due course;
this doctrine of the *Mālinīvijaya* has been declared as being in agreement with authoritative texts on this ritual procedure. (79)
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 9 ||
[Tenth Chapter] First, the five-syllable [mantra]; then, the single-syllable; then, the various types of mantras consisting of three peaks (*kūṭa*) and four peaks.
(The promise to explain the *Śrīmattripurasundarī-vidyā*)
Now I shall declare that Vidyā which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra—the Goddess who consists of all scriptures and whose form is the cause of all. (1)
I bow to the illustrious Tripurasundarī, who brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution, who bestows liberation, and who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
I shall proclaim its mantra, which bestows all accomplishments.
(The fifth Vidyā):
First, the fifth Vidyā is described here, which is difficult to obtain on earth. (3)

Having thus established in detail the sequence of initiation (dīkṣākrama) together with its ancillaries through the successive illuminations mentioned above, he makes a formal promise to define the essential nature of the Śrī Tripurasundarī Vidyā with the words "Now" (atha). He states her essential nature with the passage beginning with "the one who carries across the ocean of saṃsāra" and ending with "Śrī Tripurasundarī. Regarding the phrase "Śrī Tripurasundarī":
Regarding the etymological derivation of the word *Tripurā*, the second chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* states:
"Because she places three cities (*pura*) before [herself], that Supreme Goddess is known as Tripurā; likewise, she is so called because of her excellence of beauty."
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*, as cited in the commentary on the *Tripurāmahopaniṣad*, it is also stated: "Her maṇḍala is a triangle, and her city-walls consist of three lines;
her mantra is said to have three syllables, and likewise her form is threefold."
"The Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is threefold for the creation of the three deities;
since everything is a triad of triads, Tripurā is considered to consist of three syllables.
Regarding the word "tasyāḥ" (of her): it refers to Tripurasundarī. Many divisions of Tripurā will be demonstrated in due order.
That supreme Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), consisting of five peaks, is difficult to attain;
it is eternal, bestows liberation, is pure, grants happiness, and destroys suffering. || 4 ||
(The five-element nature of the world consisting of the five peaks:
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of the fivefold Goddess;
it arises from earth, water, fire, air, and space. (5)
(The nature of Earth and the other elements as the powers of their respective deities:
Earth is the power Brāhmaṇī, and likewise water is Nārāyaṇī;
fire is Rudrāṇī belonging to Rudra, and wind is Īśvarī belonging to Īśa.
Likewise, Māheśvarī is space, and she is the power of Maheśvara;
consisting of the five deities, there are five [deities] and five powers of the fifth.
(An Exposition of the Five Powers Consisting of the Five Peak-Syllables of Etymology) The first is to be known as Kāmeśvarī, and likewise the auspicious Vajreśvarī;
the third is Bhagamālā, and the fourth is Tripurasundarī. (8)
And the fifth power is eternal, having the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
(The nature of the fifth [vowel]):
That which is the Great Cause of the worlds, whose form is supreme bliss—from that [Cause] arises the form of the Goddess, which is devoid of rising and setting. 10.
Therein, he first explains the fifth [verse] with the words "tatrādau" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "consisting of five peaks" (*pañcakūṭātmikā*):
it means that its nature consists of the *vāgbhava* peak, the three *kāmarāja* peaks, and the *śakti* peak.
By the passage beginning with "the earth is Brāhmaṇī, the Śakti," etc., it has been established that the earth and the other elements possess the nature of the Śaktis of Brahmā and the other deities.

He states the result of that [inquiry] with the word "five" (*pañca*). The meaning is that one should know that the five elements beginning with earth, which consist of the five deities previously mentioned—Brahmā and the others—are the five powers (*pañcaśaktayaḥ*) of the fifth [vowel]. By this, the fact that the phonemes of the *Mātṛkā*, which consist of the five elements, constitute the components of the mantra is explained. However, the specific details are found in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
This is to be understood from the second chapter.
It is devoid of rising and setting, transcending both destruction and prior non-existence.
In its gross state it possesses a gross form; in its subtle state, it possesses a subtle form.
Through the distinction between the gross and the subtle, she is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
This Power is non-different from Śiva:
that Lord who is the Sovereign of the Universe, abiding pervading the entire universe, is indeed that Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe, established through her all-pervasive nature. (12)
That very fifth Vidyā, consisting of five peaks, is supreme;
by the grace of that very fifth [Vidyā] alone, Śiva and the others possess their lordship and other attributes.
She is meditated upon by Śambhu, and through her grace, Śiva becomes the all-pervading Lord.
And through his compassion, the lordship over the worlds was obtained;
by him, Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā, and Viṣṇu himself attained the state of Viṣṇu.

He states the threefold form of the Goddess as "grossness," etc. Here, this should be noted: in the Āgamas, the threefold form of the deity is seen through the division of gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and supreme (*para*). Among these, the form established by meditation, characterized by distinct heads, hands, feet, and so forth, is the gross; the form consisting of mantra is the subtle.

But the supreme form (*pararūpa*) is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and is accessible through the worship consisting of internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). As it is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:
"The gross [form] is [known] by its entire name, and likewise the subtle is the body of mantra."
"But the supreme form, O Śivā, is known through the act of *arpaṇa* as worship. Thus it is stated.

This was clearly explained by the venerable Bhāskararāya in his commentary on the *Tripuropaniṣad*: "The deity has three forms—the gross (*sthūla*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the supreme (*para*). Among these, the first is that which is described in the respective verses of meditation (*dhyāna-śloka*); the second..."

The first consists of the respective root-mantras (*mūlamantra*), while the third consists of worship (*upāsanā*). Since the deity is threefold, worship is also threefold, distinguished by external sacrifice (*bahir-yāga*), recitation (*japa*), and internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). Thus, the meaning of the passage beginning with "in its grossness" (*sthūlatve*) is as follows: when worship is gross, that is to say, in the worship of the form (*mūrti*) presented through meditation, that deity is of a gross form; [whereas] in its subtle state...

In subtle worship consisting of the recitation of mantras, she exists in a subtle form; however, in supreme worship in the form of internal sacrifice—which is described as being devoid of the distinctions between gross and subtle—she is the deity whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman. This is the meaning.
The greatness of the lords of the gods, asuras, and sages is due to his grace.
(Through this very worship alone, Viśvāmitra attained the status of being the creator of the universe and other cosmic functions):
In former times, the supreme [knowledge], difficult to attain, was proclaimed to Viśvāmitra by Śiva;
that great sage himself became a creator equal to Śiva. (16)
The Lord himself alone became the agent of creation and dissolution.
(Regarding its nature as the knowledge of Brahman:
This is the most secret of all sciences, the exclusive knowledge of Brahman. 17.

(Conclusion regarding the qualified practitioner for the worship of this Vidyā): One whose heart is always full of bliss, who is devoted to the bliss of non-duality, who is devoted to the Guru, and who has conquered the senses, should practice the fifth [Vidyā]. || 18 ||
(The excellence of this [Vidyā]): It consists of all sacred fords, it consists of all mantras, it is supreme;
it consists of all deities, it is pure, it consists of all powers, and it is auspicious. (19)
(On the excellence of those who know the fifth Vidyā: Among men on earth, he is the most excellent who knows the fifth [Vidyā]. || 20 ||
He who knows the supreme Great Vidyā consisting of five peaks shall become a sky-walker eternally through practice; there is no doubt in this matter. (21)
A yogi whose self is purified by the authentic tradition, even if devoted to worldly enjoyments,
attains liberation in every way, provided he knows the fifth [state].
He is to be honored in all worlds; he is a god and not a human being. || 22 ||
Endowed with the conduct of the samaya, he should contemplate the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
through a state of mind purified of conceptual construction, he shall attain all siddhis. || 23 ||
Having become filled with eternal bliss, the man who meditates upon the fifth [element] shall attain immortality through the thorough knowledge of the five principles;
he should worship the fifth as the form of causal bliss.
(The nature of the five principles as being the forms of Brahmā and the others:
The five principles consist of the five deities beginning with Brahmā;
likewise, there are five Śaktis, with the fifth [Śakti] being identical with the fifth principle.
The five [syllables] are arranged in the manner of a peak, or as three peaks, beginning with the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]. || 25 ||
Now the fifth [syllable] (therein is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa):
Smara, Yoni, Māyā, Kṣiti; then the head marked with Kalā; Madhādeva; Vahni whose body is fashioned from Śūnya.
A person who has recited this secret seed-syllable, the supreme cause of all poetic composition, one hundred thousand times becomes equal to the preceptor of the gods. || 26 ||

Therein, first, regarding the statement "the fifth [syllable] shall be the venerable Tripurā," he explains the twenty-five-syllable mantra composed of five *kūṭas* belonging to the fifth *Śrīvidyā* as taught in the second chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, beginning with the word "Smara" (*smara*), by first defining the *Vāgbhava-kūṭa*: "Smara" is the letter *ka*; "Yoni" is the letter *e*; "Māyā" [is the letter *ī*].

The letter *ī* is the earth, and the letter *la*; by this, "ka-e-ī-la" is obtained. Now, the word "atha" (then) means immediately after these four seed-syllables. Mahādeva, whose head is marked by a digit—the letter *ī*—is the letter *ha*. Vahni is the letter *ra*.
Likewise, "composed of the void" means joined with the void, that is, with the *bindu*. Thus, his body is formed.
He whose body is fashioned from these—the vowels *ī*, *ā*, *r*, and the nasal bindu—is such [a one]. By this, "hrīṃ" is obtained.
Thus, it results that "ka e ī la hrīṃ" is the first *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). This is clearly stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"O Goddess, [the syllable] 'kā' joined with Viṣṇu, then 'śakti', 'māyā', and 'indra'."
Thereafter, one should extract the seed-syllable Vāgbhava from Mahāmāyā.
Thus; the rest is clear.
This Vāgbhava seed-syllable has been thus declared [as the three peaks of Kāmarāja].
I shall state the remainder:

one should utter the supreme *śambhu*, *soma*, *ravi*, *mahī*, and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Goddess (*bhagavatī*) in sequence; then the supreme seed-syllable of Bhavānī, which is declared as *kandarpa-ari-ravi-īśa-śakra*.
One should duly extract the seed-syllables of Kāma, Śambhu, Samīraṇa, Indra, and Girijā in their proper order. || 27 ||

Having thus described the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), he begins to explain the *kāmarāja*, which consists of three peak-syllables, with the words "this" (*etad*) and so forth. The connection is that by the preceding statement, the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable was declared; "the remainder" means that he will now speak of the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable. Among those, the first peak-syllable of the *kāmarāja*, which is composed of three peak-syllables, is...

He explains [the first seed-syllable] with the words "Śambhu," and so forth: Śambhu is the letter *ha*; Soma (the seed-syllable of the Moon) is the letter *sa*; Ravi (the Sun) is the letter *ka*; Mahī (the seed-syllable of the Earth) is the letter *la*;
and Bhagavatī (the seed-syllable of Māyā) is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ* is the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja. This is clearly stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
Then follows the sky-moon (viyat-candra), after which, in the Kali age, there is the *nakuli* and fire (*vahni*), joined with the vowel *māyā* (ī), and endowed with the *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*.
This is the first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja, which is most difficult to obtain. Thus it is said.

He states the second *kūṭa*: "Kandarpa," etc. *Kandarpāri* (Śiva) is the letter *ha*; *ravi* (the Sun) is the letter *ka*; *īśa* (the Lord) is the letter *ha*; *śakra* (Indra) is the letter *la*. The word "next" (*param*) means that after this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhavānī, namely *hrīṃ*. Thus, it is established that the second *kūṭa* is *ha ka ha la hrīṃ*. He states this explicitly in the *Tantrasāra*: [text follows].
"Viyat joined with Viṣṇu, Kāma, Haṃsa, and Śakra thereafter;
after that, Mahāmāyā—this is called Svapnāvatī.
This [mantra] is indeed the second *kūṭa* of Kāmarāja, known as the Svapnāvatī-vidyā.
This should be understood from this statement of the *Tantrasāra*. It will also be explained by [the author] himself further on.

He states the third peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) with the words "Kāma" and so forth. Kāma is the letter *ka*; Śambhu is the letter *ha*; Samīraṇa is the letter *ya*; Indra is the letter *la*; and the seed-syllable of Girijā is *hrīṃ*. Thus, it results that the third peak-syllable is *ka ha ya la hrīṃ*.
The *Tantrasāra* clearly states [the fruit of reciting these three syllables]: "This supreme seed-syllable, composed of three peaks, is known as the venerable Kāmarāja."
