Having recited this, one shines throughout the three worlds, accompanied by the entire host of gods and great sages.
(The Śakti-kūṭa:
I shall now declare another supreme [mantra], the sole sovereign of the entire universe and the granter of all desires.
One should extract Śambhu, together with Manmatha, Śakra, and Soma, and the Goddess in their proper sequence.

(The excellence of this [mantra]): May this Śrī Tripurā, the supreme benefactor who brings about the attainment of the goals of knowledge, enter my red mental lotus, which is presided over by the seat of Kāma.
"Mādana, the seed-syllable of Śiva, and then the seed-syllable of Vāyu;
after that, the seed-syllable of Indra, and then one should extract Mahāmāyā.
This is indeed the third peak-syllable (kūṭa) of Kāmarāja, which will be described further on as the "Madhumatī Vidya."
He states the fruit of reciting the Kāmarāja-mantra composed of these three *kūṭas* with the words beginning "This" (*etad*) and so forth.
Having thus described the four *kūṭas*, he describes the fifth, the *śakti-kūṭa*, with the words beginning "I shall declare another" (*vakṣye 'nyad*) and so forth. Śambhu is the letter *ha*;
Manmatha is the letter *ka*; Śakra is the letter *la*; Soma (the seed-syllable of the Moon) is the letter *sa*; and Devī (the seed-syllable of Māyā) is *hrīm*.
And thus, *evaṃ ha ka la sa hrīṃ* is the fifth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*). This is clearly stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Then one should apply the seed-syllable of Śiva, followed by Kāma, Indra, and the Goddess;
thereafter, one should extract Mahāmāyā, which is the Peak of Power (*śaktikūṭa*)."

In this regard, the following should be noted: this mantra, consisting of twenty-five syllables, is composed of five *kūṭas*. Here, the word *kūṭa* signifies a collection, as in the terms *kāraṇakūṭa* and others used by the Vaiśeṣikas and other schools. Thus, the first is the *vāgbhava-kūṭa*, consisting of the aforementioned five syllables; the second consists of the aforementioned fifteen syllables.

The *kāmarāja-kūṭa* and the third, the *śakti-kūṭa*, which consists of five syllables according to etymological derivation (*nirukta*); thus, taken together, this mantra consists of twenty-five syllables. This is stated in the *Gandharva-tantra*, within the third chapter of the *Kuloḍḍīśa* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*: [The text continues with the specific mantras.]
"The first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) is Vāgbhava, and the fifth is Śakti;
O Goddess, the three middle peaks are the enchanting Kāmarāja.
Thus, for the easy understanding of practitioners, the arrangement of these peak-syllables is demonstrated by means of a line-drawing.
Her pair of lotus feet are adorned by the magnificent pearl necklaces from the crowns upon the heads of Brahmā, Ananta, and Purāri; her face is as pure as the full moon. || 29 ||
This Vidyā-cūḍāmaṇi is said to be difficult to obtain in all schools;
this Vidyā, consisting of five kūṭas, shall consist of twenty-five syllables.

(Regarding the specific distinction within the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*): I shall explain the *Kāmarāja*, which is very difficult to obtain, by means of its various *kūṭas*; having known it, one may constantly accomplish even that which is impossible to achieve on this earth. (31)
The first peak-syllable (kūṭa) is auspiciousness, which bestows great good fortune;
the three peaks in the form of words are the Kāmarāja, the great state.
Thus, by means of these three peaks, the Vidyā takes the form of auspiciousness.
(The first and fifth [syllables] consist of twenty-five letters each):
the Vāgbhava peak and the Kāmarāja peak.
The peak of power (śaktikūṭa) is *ka ha*.
Ha ka ha.
And that is it.

Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ.
Hrīṃ hrīṃ, O you who possess dreams.

Regarding the "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*) which was previously mentioned as the three-fold *kāmarāja-kūṭa*, he states another method by means of the verse beginning with "saubhāgyam": "saubhāgya" refers to that which belongs to Saubhāgyā, namely the Śāktalopāmudrā who is about to be described.

The meaning is "the first peak" (*kūṭa*). This mantra is demonstrated by the arrangement of lines: (-). By this, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ* is the first peak of the Kāmarāja [mantra]. Regarding the term "three peaks" (*trikūṭa*): here, the word "three" (*tri*) signifies "third. Thus, it refers to the third [peak] with respect to the Vāgbhava peak.
This [goddess], however, who possesses five peaks and eternally resides upon the three peaks, is difficult to find in all the worlds; she is the most beautiful of all auspicious beings. (33)

(The fruit of reciting the middle peak-syllable of Kāmarāja): Having recited the middle syllable of the very middle peak of this same vidyā, one becomes filled with bliss and shall obtain every desire. (34)
This is the lore named Svapnāvatī, difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
it is a lore that effects summoning and brings delight to the mind. (35)
(Madhumatī) The Antakūṭa of Svapnāvatī is called Madhumatī;
it is a lore that bestows great enjoyment and grants the great siddhis. || 36 ||
The Vidyā consists of five peaks; as the fifth, she is composed of the five principles.
(The fruit of propitiating her according to the etymological meaning of "fifth"):
Having performed her propitiation, what on this earth would not be accomplished? || 37 ||
(Another method:
the *vāgbhava* peak-syllable and the *kāmarāja* peak-syllable.
The peak-syllable of power is *ka-ha*.

so it is.

The meaning is that one should employ the "Great Word" (mahatpada), namely Kāmarāja, in the form of the syllable *hrīṃ hrīṃ* as a peak-syllable (*kūṭapada*). By the phrase "the Great Word," [it refers to] this peak-syllable.

The state of having six syllables is indicated. By that, the third peak (kūṭa) is *sa ka ha la hrīṃ*. And thus, because this [mantra] is composed of six syllables, the fifth power-peak (*śaktikūṭa*) consists of four syllables, *sa ka la hrīṃ*, like the *Kāmarāja-vidyā*.
The first peak and the fourth peak are as before. This is another variation.
There is entry into another's body, one may assume any form at will, and there are collyrium, pills, and other such sciences that are very difficult to obtain. (38)
Once this is known by the practitioner, he becomes a sky-walker (khecara);
the powers of atomization (aṇimā-siddhi) arise, and the deities become subject to his will. || 39 ||
Lions, tigers, and the like, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, and birds,
all flee from afar at the mere sight of the practitioner.
By virtue of his constant compassion for him, the mantra-practitioner shall become equal to Śiva;
that supreme adept, liberated while living, shall become a creator and a destroyer in heaven.
This knowledge, difficult to obtain in the three worlds, is the fifth among all categories;
it is declared to be the single-syllable [mantra], which is indeed nothing other than the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). 42.
That power which exists within all beings in the form of universal consciousness—that Goddess is the fifth Vidyā, whose essential nature is the support of all. (43)
Its divisions are many, as are its splendors and qualities;
there exists nothing else superior to it within the three worlds. (44)
The form of men, the form of women, and whatever other form is spoken of—all that is the supreme form of her alone; of this there is no doubt. (45)
(Regarding the specific results of recitation according to specific times:
If a practitioner performs [recitation] at night in a cremation ground on a day sacred to the Great Elements, what on this earth cannot be accomplished by means of one thousand repetitions? 46.
Whoever should mutter this fifth knowledge, supreme and difficult to obtain in the three worlds, shall become a liberated soul whose nature is yoga, solely through various enjoyments. 47.
Through practice for just one year, the practitioner becomes perfectly accomplished.
(The secret nature of this:
This knowledge, which is extremely difficult to obtain, must not be given to just anyone. 48.
(That it should be imparted to a true disciple:
This fifth knowledge should be given to one of noble birth, who is pure, devoted to the Guru and the Deity, to a son, and to one who would give up his own life for it. 49.
(There is a distinction regarding another mantra within that Śaktikūṭa):
Now I shall fully declare another most auspicious Śaktikūṭa, which brings about the consummation of supreme bliss and was revealed in the Kuloḍḍīśa. 50.
Having extracted the *prāṇa* and *jīva*, one should extract the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*).
Below that, one should join the seed-syllable of Śakra with the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśvarī*). 51.
(Herein is the arrangement of the *vāgbhava* and *kāmarāja* clusters:
The *vāgbhava* was declared first; the *kāmarāja* consists of three [syllables].
This Vidyā is the Great Vidyā, bestowing dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation. 52.

Now, following the doctrine of the Kuloḍḍīśa, he states the seed-syllable of Śakti: "Now another... As previously shown, the fifth peak among the five peaks constituting the aforementioned [mantra] is the peak of Śakti; now, an alternative formulation of that very peak of Śakti is presented by this [verse]. Thus, due to the twofold nature of the peak of Śakti, the mantra also [is twofold].

The twofold nature is to be understood. He explains that very division of the Śakti-kūṭa with the words beginning "Prāṇa" and so forth: Prāṇa is the letter *ha*; Jīva is the letter *sa*; the Kāma-bīja is the letter *ka*; the Indrabīja is the letter *la*; Bhuvaneśvarī is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ* is the second Śakti-kūṭa.
(Another opinion) Furthermore, I shall proclaim another supreme doctrine concerning the nectar of the Kula. 53.
(Regarding the specific distinction in the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa* within this very Vidyā): In this same Madhumatī Vidyā,
the best of practitioners should omit the *samīraṇa* and join the *jīva*.
This is to be known as the secret, supreme [teaching], which bestows the fruit of the goals of human existence.

(Another mantra) Now I shall describe another peak-syllable (*kūṭa*), which is difficult for all to obtain; this peak-syllable, more essential than the essence itself, has been revealed in the *Śrīkrama*. (55)

By means of this second *Śakti*-kūṭa, he explains the sequence for accomplishing the five-kūṭa nature of the mantra with the words beginning "Vāgbhava" (*vāgbhavam*). Thus, as before, here too the first is the *Vāgbhava*-kūṭa, then the three *Kāmarāja*-kūṭas, and then the aforementioned *Śakti*-kūṭa; in this way, the five-kūṭa nature of this mantra is established.

It should be understood that this second Vidyā, consisting of five parts, is differentiated by the various divisions of its constituent *kūṭas*. This is demonstrated by the falling of the *rakha* [the seed-syllable]:

The letter *ka* is *gotrabhit*; the letter *la* is *māyā*, which is *hrīṃ*. Thus, *ha āṃ e ī ka la hrīṃ* constitutes the first *kūṭa*.
